checks.label: Explain
checks.meaning: Say it in plain words in under a minute, with no notes.

checks.label: Draw
checks.meaning: Sketch the diagram (or class diagram) from memory.

checks.label: Apply
checks.meaning: Use it in a real design question and say exactly where it fits.

checks.label: Trade-offs
checks.meaning: Say what it costs, when not to use it, and the alternative.

confidentRule: A topic is finished when you pass all four checks, not when you finish a video. Be strict: if you needed your notes, it is not ticked yet.
howToStudy: The notes on every topic are written to be enough on their own. The free resources are optional: a second explanation and extra practice.
Start with Phase 0. Its first topic is a map of every building block; then learn the step-by-step answer frameworks.
HLD track: Phases 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, then practise with Phase 8.
LLD track: Phases 5 → 6, then practise with Phase 7. You can run it alongside the HLD track.
AI/ML track: Phase 9, once the core concepts and the ML Foundations AI-engineering topics feel solid.
Graduate and junior interviews focus on the "Must know" topics. Learn those first; come back for the rest.
Interview tomorrow? Use Revise mode with "Must know only".

phases.title: How system design interviews work
phases.goal: Learn the step-by-step way to answer any design question before you learn the parts. Without a method, even good knowledge comes out messy under pressure.
phases.bigPicture: Interviewers grade how you think: do you ask the right questions, size the problem, start simple and then improve the weak spots? A clear method shows all of that, even when you don't know every technology.

topics.name: Meet the building blocks: a map of a typical web system
topics.definition: Most large web systems are built from the same dozen parts — clients, DNS, a CDN, load balancers, app servers, caches, databases, queues, workers and object storage — connected in a familiar shape.
topics.problem: System design questions use many technical words at once. If you don't know what each part does, answers sound like a list of jargon. Learning the map first makes every later topic easier, because each one is a closer look at one box on this map.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U["Client
(phone or browser)"] -->|"1 where is api.example.com?"| DNS["DNS"] U -->|"photos, scripts"| CDN["CDN
(nearby copies)"] U -->|"2 API request"| LB["Load balancer"] LB --> A1["App server"] LB --> A2["App server"] A1 --> C[("Cache")] A1 --> DB[("Database")] A1 -->|"slow job"| Q[["Queue"]] Q --> W["Worker"] A1 --> OS[("Object storage")] CDN -.->|"on a miss"| OS
diagram.caption: Follow the numbers. The client finds the servers through DNS, then sends its request to the load balancer. App servers read the cache and database, hand slow jobs to the queue, and keep files in object storage, which the CDN serves to users.

topics.idea: A user's app (the client) sends a request over the internet. DNS finds your servers' address, a CDN serves files like photos from somewhere nearby, and a load balancer spreads the other requests across many identical app servers. App servers run your code: they read quick copies of data from a cache and the real data from a database. Slow jobs go onto a queue for background workers, and big files live in object storage.
howItWorks: Client: the phone app is the client. It sends a request: 'upload this photo with this caption'.
DNS: the app asks DNS for the address of api.example.com and gets back an IP address — like a phone number for a server.
Load balancer: the request reaches the load balancer, which picks one of many app servers that is healthy and not too busy.
App server: your code checks who the user is, gets an upload link from object storage, and saves the caption and photo details in the database.
Database: the permanent record of users, posts and likes. It's the source of truth.
Queue and workers: the app server puts a message 'make thumbnails for photo 42' on a queue and replies straight away. A background worker picks it up and makes the thumbnails.
Cache: when friends open the post, the app server checks the cache (fast memory) first, and only reads the database on a miss.
CDN: the photo itself is downloaded from a CDN server near each friend, not from your own servers.
topics.analogy: A big restaurant chain. The phone book tells you where the nearest branch is (DNS). A host at the door sends you to a free waiter (load balancer). Waiters take orders and serve them (app servers). The pantry holds everything (database), but cooks keep the most-used ingredients on the counter (cache). Washing up happens in the back without making customers wait (queue and workers). The cold store holds big, bulky stock (object storage), and takeaway hatches around town hand out popular items fast (CDN).
topics.breaks: A waiter remembers your table. Good app servers deliberately remember nothing between requests (they're 'stateless'), so any server can handle your next request. That's exactly what makes it easy to add more servers.
topics.example: Netflix, Instagram, Uber and a small startup all share this shape. What changes is the size of each box and which boxes matter most: Netflix leans on its CDN, Uber on live location, a bank on its database and transactions.
keyPoints: Client: the app or browser the user holds.
DNS: turns a name (example.com) into a server's address.
CDN: servers around the world that keep copies of files close to users.
Load balancer: spreads requests across many servers and skips broken ones.
App server: runs your code; usually stateless, so you can add more.
Cache: fast memory holding copies of often-read data (often Redis).
Database: the permanent, trusted store of your data.
Queue and workers: a waiting line of jobs, and the background programs that do them.
Object storage: cheap, huge storage for files like photos and videos (for example Amazon S3).
mistakes: Learning tool names (Redis, Kafka) before knowing what job each box does.
Thinking every system needs every box. A small app may only need one server and one database.
Treating the cache as the place where data really lives. The database is the source of truth.
topics.interviewAnswer: Most designs start from the same shape. Clients reach us through DNS; files come from a CDN; a load balancer spreads requests across stateless app servers; those servers read from a cache and a database, push slow work onto a queue for workers, and keep large files in object storage. Then I scale whichever box the requirements stress most.

followUps.q: Which box is usually the hardest to scale?
followUps.a: The database, because it holds data that must stay correct. App servers are easy to copy; data is not.

followUps.q: Why put a queue between the app server and the workers?
followUps.a: So the user doesn't wait for slow work, and so a burst of jobs waits in line instead of overloading the workers.

practice.explain: Name the nine building blocks and say what each one does, in one sentence each, from memory.
practice.draw: Draw the map from memory: client, DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, cache, database, queue, workers and object storage, with arrows.
practice.apply: Pick an app you use every day, such as a food-delivery app. For one action, like placing an order, say which boxes the request passes through and why.
practice.tradeoffs: For a tiny app with 100 users, which boxes would you leave out, and why?

resources.title: ByteByteGo: system design concepts for beginners

explain.answer:
• Client: the app or browser in the user's hand; it sends the requests.
• DNS: turns a name like api.example.com into the IP address of a server.
• CDN: servers spread around the world that keep copies of files (photos, scripts, video) close to users.
• Load balancer: receives every request and passes it to one healthy app server, so no single server is overloaded.
• App servers: run your code; they keep nothing between requests (stateless), so you can add more.
• Cache: fast memory (often Redis) holding copies of data that is read a lot, so the database is asked less often.
• Database: the permanent, trusted record of the data: the source of truth.
• Queue and workers: a waiting line of slow jobs, and the background programs that take jobs off it and do them.
• Object storage: cheap, almost unlimited storage for big files such as photos and videos (Amazon S3).

draw.answer:
Two paths leave the client: files go to the CDN, and API requests go through the load balancer to the app servers. Everything behind the app servers is reached only through them. The CDN pulls from object storage when it doesn't have a file yet.

Check yours for the three arrows people most often miss: client to DNS first, the queue feeding the workers (not the other way round), and CDN to object storage on a miss.
draw.code:
Client (phone or browser)
 │ 1. "where is api.example.com?"
 ├──────────► DNS
 │ photos, scripts
 ├──────────► CDN ─── on a miss ───┐
 │ 2. API request                  │
 ▼                                 │
Load balancer                      │
 ├──► App server ──┐               │
 └──► App server ──┤               │
                   ├──► Cache      │
                   ├──► Database   │
                   ├──► Queue ──► Workers
                   └──► Object storage

apply.answer:
Placing an order in a food-delivery app:

1. Client: you tap "Place order". The app sends POST /orders with the basket and the delivery address.
2. DNS: the app already looked up api.fooddelivery.com earlier and cached the address, so this costs nothing now.
3. Load balancer: picks a healthy order-service server. If one server has crashed, your order still goes through.
4. App server: checks who you are, checks the restaurant is open, and works out the price.
5. Cache: the menu and prices are read from the cache: every user reads them, and they rarely change.
6. Database: the order is written to the database, inside a transaction with the payment record. This must never be lost or half-saved, so it goes to the source of truth, not the cache.
7. Queue and workers: the server puts "order 123 placed" on a queue and replies "order received" straight away. Workers then tell the restaurant, send you a push notification and start finding a courier. You don't wait for any of that.

The CDN and object storage did their job earlier: the restaurant photos you scrolled past came from a CDN server near you.

tradeoffs.answer:
With 100 users, keep only the client, DNS, one app server and one database (with backups). Leave out:

• Load balancer and extra app servers: one small server handles thousands of requests a second; 100 users send a handful. (A managed platform can add a second server later in minutes.)
• Cache: the database answers 100 users easily, and a cache brings its own bugs: stale data, and invalidation.
• Queue and workers: do the few slow jobs inline, or with a simple scheduled task.
• CDN: serve the few static files from the app server or a static host.

Maybe keep object storage if users upload files: it is cheap, simple, and better than putting files in the database.

The reason: every box costs money, adds something to run and monitor, and adds a new way to fail. Add a box when a number (traffic, latency, data size) says you need it, not before.

topics.name: The high-level design interview: a step-by-step answer framework
topics.definition: A repeatable order of steps for answering any 'Design X' question in about 45 minutes.
topics.problem: Under pressure, most people either freeze or start drawing boxes before they understand the question. Both lose marks. A fixed method gives you something to do in every minute, and shows the interviewer how you think.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR R["1 Requirements
about 5 min"] --> E["2 Estimates
about 3 min"] --> A["3 API
about 3 min"] --> D["4 Data model
about 3 min"] D --> H["5 High-level design
about 10 min"] --> X["6 Deep dives
10–15 min"] --> W["7 Wrap-up
trade-offs"]
diagram.caption: Work left to right. Each box is one stage of the interview, with roughly how long to spend on it.

topics.idea: Interviewers judge how you think, not whether you reach one 'right' design. A framework stops you jumping straight to boxes and arrows. The usual order: clarify requirements, estimate the scale, define the API, sketch the data model, draw a simple design that works, then go deep on the hardest parts and discuss trade-offs.
howItWorks: Requirements: ask who uses the system and what the 3–4 core features are. For a URL shortener: 'Do we need custom aliases? Expiry? Click analytics?' Then the non-functional side: 'How many users? Is a slightly stale read acceptable?' Write the answers in a corner of the board.
Estimates: turn the numbers into requests per second and storage. Say each assumption out loud, for example 'I'll assume 100 reads for every write'.
API: write 2–4 endpoints with their inputs and outputs. This fixes exactly what the system must do.
Data model: list the main tables or objects and their keys. Ask yourself: what is the main query, and which key does it use?
High-level design: draw client → load balancer → service → database, and walk one request through it. Make it work before you make it big.
Deep dives: find the bottleneck from your estimates (reads, writes or storage) and fix it with caching, replicas, sharding or queues. Explain each choice and what it costs.
Wrap-up: summarise the design in three sentences, name its weak spots, and say what you would monitor.
topics.analogy: An architect meeting a client. They ask how many people will live in the house and what it is for before they draw anything.
topics.breaks: A client answers once. In an interview you keep checking in ('does this match what you had in mind?'), and the interviewer may change the requirements halfway on purpose to see how you adapt.
topics.example: For 'Design a URL shortener': 3 minutes on requirements (shorten, redirect, custom alias? expiry?), 3 on estimates (100 million new links a month), 3 on the API (POST /urls, GET /{code}), then the simple design, then a deep dive on generating unique short codes.
keyPoints: 1. Requirements (about 5 min): functional (what it does) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Write them down.
2. Estimates (about 3 min): users, requests per second, storage, bandwidth. Only as much as changes a decision.
3. API (about 3 min): the main endpoints with inputs and outputs.
4. Data model (about 3 min): the main entities, and which kind of database fits.
5. High-level design (about 10 min): the simplest design that works end to end.
6. Deep dives (10–15 min): fix the bottlenecks — caching, sharding, queues, failure handling.
7. Wrap-up: the trade-offs you made, what you'd do with more time, how you'd monitor it.
tradeOffs: Don't over-design early: start simple, then scale only the parts the numbers say need it.
Think out loud. If you are silent, the interviewer can't give you credit for good reasoning.
mistakes: Designing before asking a single question.
Adding Kafka, microservices and sharding to a system that gets 10 requests a second.
Long silences. The interviewer can only give credit for what you say.
Never stating trade-offs. Every choice has a cost, and naming it is what earns the strongest marks.
topics.interviewAnswer: Before I design anything, I'd like to clarify the requirements and the scale. Then I'll propose a simple design that works end to end, and we can go deep on the parts you care about most, discussing the trade-offs as we go.

followUps.q: What if they mention a technology you don't know?
followUps.a: Say so honestly, then reason from first principles: describe what the component must do (for example, 'a durable queue that keeps order per user') and the properties you need.

followUps.q: How detailed should the estimates be?
followUps.a: Rough powers of ten are enough. The point is to decide things like 'one database is enough' or 'we need sharding', not to get exact numbers.

practice.explain: Say the 7 steps from memory, with the rough minutes for each.
practice.draw: Draw the framework as a timeline for a 45-minute interview.
practice.apply: Run the framework out loud for 'Design a to-do list app' in 15 minutes. Record yourself and listen back.
practice.tradeoffs: Name two common mistakes candidates make (for example, going deep too early) and how the framework prevents each one.

resources.title: Hello Interview: system design delivery framework
Hello Interview: a framework for system design interviews
ByteByteGo: system design interview step by step

explain.answer:
1. Requirements, about 5 minutes: the core features (functional) and the scale, speed, availability and consistency needed (non-functional). Write them down.
2. Estimates, about 3 minutes: users, requests per second, storage, bandwidth. Only what changes a decision.
3. API, about 3 minutes: the 2 to 4 main endpoints, with inputs and outputs.
4. Data model, about 3 minutes: the main entities, their keys, and which kind of database fits.
5. High-level design, about 10 minutes: the simplest design that works end to end, with one request walked through it.
6. Deep dives, 10 to 15 minutes: fix the bottlenecks the numbers point to (caching, sharding, queues, failures), with the cost of each.
7. Wrap-up, a few minutes: summarise, name the trade-offs and weak spots, and say what you'd monitor.

draw.answer: About 44 minutes of design, and a few minutes at the end for your questions. The two big blocks are the high-level design and the deep dives; the four small steps before them should feel quick.
draw.code:
0 min ┬ 1 Requirements        5 min
       │
 5     ┼ 2 Estimates           3
 8     ┼ 3 API                 3
11     ┼ 4 Data model          3
14     ┼ 5 High-level design  10
       │
24     ┼ 6 Deep dives         15
       │
       │
39     ┼ 7 Wrap-up             3
42     ┼ Your questions        3
45     ┴ end

apply.answer:
A 15-minute version, about a third of each step:

1. Requirements (2 min): create, edit, complete and delete tasks; group them into lists; due dates and reminders; sync across phone and laptop. Out of scope: shared lists. Non-functional: 10 million users, 1 million a day; fast; a task I just added must show on my other device (read-your-own-writes).
2. Estimates (1 min): 1 million users × 20 reads and 5 writes a day ≈ 200 reads and 50 writes a second. Storage: 10 million users × 200 tasks × 500 bytes ≈ 1 TB. Small: one database is enough.
3. API (2 min): GET /lists, POST /lists/{id}/tasks, PATCH /tasks/{id} (edit or tick), DELETE /tasks/{id}, and GET /tasks?since=cursor for sync.
4. Data model (2 min): users, lists (list_id, user_id) and tasks (task_id, list_id, title, done, due_at, updated_at). Relational fits; index tasks by (user_id, updated_at) for sync and by due_at for reminders.
5. High-level design (4 min): client → load balancer → stateless API servers → PostgreSQL with a read replica. A reminder worker runs every minute, finds tasks due now, and puts push notifications on a queue.
6. Deep dive (3 min): offline edits on two devices. Each change carries updated_at (or a version number); the server keeps the newest per field and sends changes since the device's cursor.
7. Wrap-up (1 min): simple, cheap design. Weak spots: one primary database (add automatic failover), and a burst of reminders at 9:00 (spread them through the queue).

When you listen back, check: did you ask before designing, say your assumptions out loud, and keep talking?

tradeoffs.answer:
1. Going deep too early: designing the perfect sharding scheme before the basic flow exists, then running out of time with no working design. The framework puts a simple end-to-end design (step 5) before the deep dives (step 6), and time boxes keep each step short.

2. Designing before understanding: drawing boxes in minute one, then finding out the interviewer wanted something else. Step 1 forces questions first, and writing the requirements on the board lets you check them.

3. Over-engineering: adding Kafka, microservices and sharding for 10 requests a second. Step 2 gives you numbers, and each deep dive must be justified by one.

4. Never naming trade-offs. The wrap-up step makes you say what each choice costs, which is where the strongest marks are.

topics.name: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
topics.definition: Quick, rough maths to estimate traffic, storage and bandwidth, so your design decisions are based on scale.
topics.problem: Without numbers you can't tell whether one server is enough or you need a hundred. Estimation turns a vague 'big app' into numbers that decide the design.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD U["Daily users
10 million"] --> A["× actions per user
20 reads, 1 post"] A --> R["Reads per day
200 million"] --> RS["÷ 100,000 seconds
≈ 2,000 reads/s"] A --> W["Writes per day
10 million"] --> WS["÷ 100,000 seconds
≈ 100 writes/s"] W --> S["× 1 KB each
≈ 10 GB a day"] --> Y["× 365 days × 3 copies
≈ 11 TB a year"] RS --> P["× 2–5 for the peak"]
diagram.caption: Start from users, multiply by actions, divide by about 100,000 seconds in a day for per-second numbers, and multiply by item size for storage.

topics.idea: You turn the number of users into requests per second (QPS), storage per day and per year, and bandwidth. Rough is fine. A day has 86,400 seconds, about 100,000, so 1 million requests a day is about 12 per second. Peak traffic is often 2–5 times the average.
howItWorks: Start from users: daily active users × actions per user per day = actions per day.
Divide by about 100,000 (the seconds in a day, rounded) to get the average per second, then multiply by 2–5 for the peak.
Split reads and writes. Example: 10 million users each read 20 pages and post 1 item a day → 200 million reads (about 2,000 a second) and 10 million writes (about 100 a second).
Storage: writes per day × size of each item × days kept. 10 million posts × 1 KB = 10 GB a day, about 3.6 TB a year, or about 11 TB with 3 copies.
Bandwidth: requests per second × response size. 2,000 reads a second × 100 KB = 200 MB a second going out.
Then decide: is that one database or many? Does the hot data fit in a cache's memory? Do we need a CDN?
topics.analogy: Working out how much food to buy for a party: number of guests × how much each person eats, plus extra for the hungry ones (the peak).
topics.breaks: Party guests are a fixed number. Real traffic has spikes, like a viral post or a sale, that can be 10 times normal or more, so you design for the peak, not the average.
topics.example: A Twitter-like app: 300 million daily users, each posting 2 tweets a day, gives 600 million tweets a day, about 7,000 writes per second on average and maybe 15,000–20,000 at peak. At about 300 bytes each, that's 180 GB of text a day, or about 65 TB a year before media and replication.
keyPoints: Use powers of ten for speed: KB ≈ 10³ bytes, MB ≈ 10⁶, GB ≈ 10⁹, TB ≈ 10¹², PB ≈ 10¹⁵.
Seconds per day ≈ 10⁵. Requests per day ÷ 10⁵ ≈ requests per second.
Read-to-write ratio matters: many apps read 10–100 times more than they write, which points to caching and read replicas.
Latency ladder: memory read ≈ 100 ns; SSD read ≈ 100 µs; round trip inside a datacentre ≈ 0.5 ms; across a continent and back ≈ 100–150 ms.
Storage = items per day × size × days kept × copies (often 3 for replication).
Rough capacity: one app server handles thousands of simple requests per second; one SQL database handles thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second.
mistakes: Spending 10 minutes on exact arithmetic. Round hard: 86,400 ≈ 100,000.
Using the average and forgetting the peak.
Mixing up bits and bytes: network speeds are in bits, so 1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB a second.
Working out numbers and then never using them to make a decision.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'll estimate the scale first, because it decides the design. For example, 100 million requests a day is only about 1,200 per second on average, maybe 5,000 at peak. A few load-balanced app servers and one database with read replicas can handle that. If it were 100 times more, I'd plan for sharding and heavy caching.

followUps.q: Why multiply by a replication factor?
followUps.a: Data is usually stored about 3 times for durability and availability, so real disk use is roughly 3 times the raw data.

followUps.q: What if your estimate is wrong?
followUps.a: That's fine. State your assumptions clearly; the interviewer cares that the design changes sensibly when the numbers change.

practice.explain: Explain why 1 million requests a day is only about 12 requests per second.
practice.draw: Write the latency ladder (memory, SSD, datacentre round trip, cross-continent round trip) from memory, with rough numbers.
practice.apply: Estimate QPS, storage per year and bandwidth for a photo app with 50 million daily users, each uploading one 2 MB photo a day and viewing 50.
practice.tradeoffs: When is detailed estimation a waste of interview time, and when does a number change your design?

resources.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know

explain.answer:
A day has 86,400 seconds, about 100,000. The requests are spread over the whole day, so 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6, about 12 requests a second. (With the rounded 100,000 you get 10, which is close enough.)

"A million a day" sounds big, but 12 a second is easy for one server. Even with a peak of 2 to 5 times the average (25 to 60 a second), one server copes. The lesson: always turn per-day numbers into per-second numbers before deciding anything.

draw.answer:
Each step down is a big jump: memory to SSD is about 1,000 times slower, and a round trip across a continent is about 200 times slower than one inside a datacentre.

What it tells you: keep hot data in memory (a cache); avoid many round trips in a row; and put data near users (CDN, regions), because nothing beats the speed of light across an ocean.
draw.code:
Memory read                ~100 ns
SSD random read            ~100 µs  (0.1 ms)
Round trip, same DC        ~0.5 ms
Round trip, across a
continent and back         ~100–150 ms

(L1 cache ~1 ns; spinning-disk seek ~10 ms)

apply.answer:
Assumptions: 50 million daily users; each uploads one 2 MB photo and views 50 a day; a day ≈ 100,000 seconds; peak ≈ 2 to 5 times the average.

QPS
• Uploads: 50 million a day ÷ 100,000 ≈ 500 a second (578 exactly), so 1,000 to 2,500 at peak.
• Views: 50 million × 50 = 2.5 billion a day ≈ 25,000 a second (about 29,000 exactly), so 50,000 to 125,000 at peak.
• Reads outnumber writes 50 to 1.

Storage
• 50 million × 2 MB = 100 TB a day.
• × 365 ≈ 36.5 PB a year; × 3 copies ≈ 110 PB a year (before thumbnails).

Bandwidth
• In: 500 uploads a second × 2 MB ≈ 1 GB a second (8 Gbps).
• Out: 25,000 views a second × 2 MB ≈ 50 GB a second (400 Gbps) if every view were full size.

What the numbers decide: photos go in object storage, not a database (petabytes); a CDN is essential (400 Gbps can't come from your own servers); serve smaller thumbnails for feeds, which cuts the 50 GB a second hugely; and metadata reads (50:1) want a cache and read replicas.
apply.code:
users = 50e6
uploads_per_s = users / 1e5            # 500
views_per_s = users * 50 / 1e5         # 25,000
tb_per_day = users * 2 / 1e6           # 100 TB (2 MB each)
pb_per_year = tb_per_day * 365 / 1e3   # 36.5 PB
pb_with_copies = pb_per_year * 3       # 109.5 PB
gb_in_per_s = uploads_per_s * 2 / 1e3  # 1 GB/s
gb_out_per_s = views_per_s * 2 / 1e3   # 50 GB/s
print(uploads_per_s, views_per_s, pb_per_year, pb_with_copies, gb_in_per_s, gb_out_per_s)
# 500.0 25000.0 36.5 109.5 1.0 50.0

tradeoffs.answer:
A waste of time when the number can't change any decision:
• The scale is obviously small (an internal tool, 1,000 users): say "this fits on one server" and move on.
• Exact arithmetic: 86,400 vs 100,000 never changes a design. Round to powers of ten.
• Low-level design questions, or when the interviewer tells you to skip it.

A number changes the design when it crosses a limit:
• Requests per second vs what one machine handles (thousands): one server, or a fleet with a load balancer?
• Data size vs one database or one machine's memory: one database, or sharding? Does the hot set fit in a cache?
• Read-to-write ratio: 100 to 1 points to caches and read replicas; write-heavy points to queues, batching and write-friendly stores.
• Bandwidth: hundreds of Gbps out means a CDN.
• Storage growth: petabytes a year means object storage, and deciding how long to keep things.

The rule: estimate only what you will use, and say out loud which decision each number made.

topics.name: The low-level design interview: a step-by-step approach
topics.definition: A repeatable way to answer 'Design the classes for X' (a parking lot, an elevator, Splitwise) and write the key code.
topics.problem: LLD questions are open-ended: 'design a parking lot' could mean almost anything. Without a method you write random classes, or code that breaks the moment the interviewer adds a requirement.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U["Use cases"] -->|"nouns"| E["Entities
(classes)"] U -->|"verbs"| M["Methods"] E --> CD["Class diagram"] M --> CD CD --> P["Patterns where
behaviour varies"] P --> C["Code the
main flows"] C --> T["Stress-test: concurrency,
edge cases, new features"]
diagram.caption: Nouns in the use cases become classes and verbs become methods. Draw them, add patterns where things vary, code the main flow, then test the design against harder situations.

topics.idea: Low-level design (LLD) tests object-oriented design: clear classes, good relationships, sensible patterns, and code that is easy to extend. Clarify the scope, list the entities, draw a class diagram, pick patterns where things vary, code the main flows, then discuss concurrency and how you'd add new features.
howItWorks: Clarify: write 4–6 use cases as short sentences ('a car enters', 'the system assigns a spot', 'the driver pays on exit'). Agree what's out of scope.
Find the entities: underline the nouns in the use cases (car, spot, ticket, payment). They're your candidate classes. The verbs (assign, pay) become methods.
Draw the class diagram: fields, key methods and relationships. For each relationship ask: is it 'is-a' (inheritance) or 'has-a' (composition)?
Spot what varies: pricing rules, vehicle types, payment methods. Put each behind an interface (Strategy, Factory or State).
Code the main flow, such as park() and leave(), with clear names, and show how the classes call each other.
Stress-test it: two cars at two gates at the same moment (concurrency), a lost ticket (an edge case), and 'now add electric charging' (an extension). Say what changes.
topics.analogy: Planning a kitchen before building it: decide which stations you need (classes), who passes what to whom (relationships), and only then build the cupboards (code).
topics.breaks: A kitchen is built once. A software design keeps changing, so interviewers will add a new requirement ('now add electric-car charging') to see if your design bends instead of breaks.
topics.example: Parking lot: clarify (floors? vehicle types? payment?), list entities (ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment), draw relationships, use Strategy for pricing and spot assignment, code park() and leave(), then explain how two gates avoid giving out the same spot.
keyPoints: 1. Clarify requirements and scope: the main use cases, what's out of scope.
2. Identify entities (nouns) and actions (verbs) from the use cases.
3. Draw a class diagram: fields, methods, relationships (composition, inheritance, interfaces).
4. Apply patterns where behaviour varies: Strategy, State, Factory, Observer.
5. Code the core flows with clean names; skip trivial getters.
6. Discuss concurrency (two users at once), edge cases and extensibility.
Use SOLID to justify your choices out loud.
mistakes: One giant class (a 'god class') that does everything.
Deep inheritance trees where composition would be simpler.
Using patterns that don't fit, just to mention them.
Ignoring concurrency when two users can act on the same thing.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'll confirm the use cases first, then pull the main entities out of them and sketch a class diagram. Where behaviour is likely to change, like pricing, I'll put it behind an interface. Then I'll code the core flow and finish with concurrency and how the design extends.

followUps.a: The one you're strongest in. Python and Java are both fine; clean structure matters more than syntax.
The main classes and the one or two core flows, written cleanly. Not every getter, setter or menu.

practice.explain: Say the 6 steps from memory.
practice.draw: Draw the class diagram for a simple library system (books, members, loans) in 10 minutes.
practice.apply: Run the full approach out loud for 'Design a tic-tac-toe game' in 20 minutes, including code for making a move and checking for a winner.
practice.tradeoffs: What are the risks of using many design patterns just to impress the interviewer?

explain.answer:
1. Clarify: write 4 to 6 use cases, and agree what is out of scope.
2. Find the entities: the nouns in the use cases become classes, and the verbs become methods.
3. Draw the class diagram: fields, key methods, and relationships (has-a or is-a).
4. Spot what varies (pricing, vehicle types, payment methods) and put each behind an interface: Strategy, State, Factory or Observer.
5. Code the core flows cleanly, such as park() and leave(); skip trivial getters.
6. Stress-test: two users at the same moment (concurrency), edge cases, and "now add a new feature". Say what changes.

draw.answer:
The key decision is splitting Book (the title, of which the library may own several) from BookCopy (one physical copy, which is what you actually lend). A Loan joins one Member to one BookCopy, with dates; that is also where a late fee would be worked out (a FeePolicy interface, if fee rules vary).

Use cases it must support: search books, lend a copy, return a copy, see a member's loans, and refuse a loan if the member is at their limit.
draw.code:
Library
 ├─ books: Book[]          (has many)
 ├─ members: Member[]      (has many)
 ├─ lend(member, copy) → Loan
 └─ return_copy(copy)

Book     1 ───── *  BookCopy
 isbn, title,        copy_id,
 author              is_available

Member   1 ───── *  Loan  * ───── 1  BookCopy
 member_id,          borrowed_on,
 name,               due_on,
 max_loans = 3       returned_on

apply.answer:
1. Clarify: two players, X and O, take turns on a 3 × 3 board (maybe n × n later). A move must be on the board and on an empty square. The game ends with a win (a full row, column or diagonal) or a draw (board full). Out of scope: a computer player, a user interface.
2. Entities: Game, Board, Player (a name and a symbol), Move. Verbs: make a move, check for a winner, check for a draw.
3. Class diagram: a Game has one Board and two Players; the Board holds the cells; the Game has a status (in progress, won, draw).
4. What varies: the board size, and later perhaps the win rule or a computer player (a Strategy for choosing moves). Not worth a pattern today.
5. Code (below): Board checks and stores moves and knows whether a symbol has won; Game handles turns and status.
6. Stress-test: a move after the game ended is refused; a taken square is refused. Faster win check: only check the lines through the last move (O(n)), or keep a counter per row, column and diagonal (O(1)). Concurrency: two players send a move at once; take a lock per game, and check it is that player's turn.

tradeoffs.answer:
• More code, less clarity: every pattern adds classes and indirection. A tic-tac-toe game with a Factory, an Observer and a Singleton is harder to read than one without.
• Lost time: you spend the interview wiring patterns and never finish the core flow, which is what is being marked.
• It looks memorised: the interviewer wants to see you notice a problem and pick a tool for it, not recite a list.
• Hard follow-up questions: "why is this a Singleton?" If the honest answer is "to mention one", you lose marks.
• Harder to change: the wrong abstraction makes the next requirement harder, not easier.

The rule: name the problem first ("pricing rules will change"), then the pattern that solves it (Strategy). If you can't name the problem, leave the pattern out (YAGNI: you aren't gonna need it).

phases.title: Networking and APIs
phases.goal: Understand how a request travels from a phone or browser to your servers and back, and how to design the API it calls.
phases.bigPicture: Every design starts at the edge: DNS finds your servers, a connection carries the request, a proxy or gateway receives it, and an API defines what can be asked. Getting these basics clear makes every later diagram easier to explain.

topics.name: Client–server, DNS, and what happens when you type a URL
topics.definition: Clients (browsers, apps) send requests; servers process them and send responses. DNS turns a name like example.com into an IP address the client can connect to.
topics.problem: Computers find each other by IP address, but people remember names. Between typing a name and seeing a page there are several steps, and each can be slow or fail. Knowing them lets you explain latency, failover and where caching helps.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant R as DNS resolver
  participant S as Web server
  B->>R: Where is example.com?
  R-->>B: 203.0.113.10 (kept for its TTL)
  B->>S: TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
  B->>S: TLS handshake (certificate and keys)
  B->>S: GET / (Host example.com)
  S-->>B: 200 OK and the page
diagram.caption: Time runs from top to bottom. First the browser finds the address, then it opens a connection, secures it, and only then asks for the page.

topics.idea: When you type a URL, the browser asks DNS for the server's IP address (often from a cache), opens a TCP connection, does a TLS handshake for HTTPS, and sends an HTTP request. The request usually reaches a load balancer, which passes it to an application server. That server may read a cache or database, then sends the response back.
howItWorks: You type example.com. The browser checks its own DNS cache, then the operating system's.

On a miss, it asks a resolver, often run by your internet provider. The resolver asks a root server ('who handles .com?'), then a .com server ('who handles example.com?'), then example.com's own name server, which returns the IP address, say 203.0.113.10. Every answer is cached for its TTL.
The browser opens a TCP connection to that IP on port 443, with a three-step handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
TLS handshake: the server shows a certificate proving it really is example.com, and both sides agree on encryption keys.
The browser sends the request: 'GET /', with the header 'Host: example.com'. A load balancer receives it and passes it to one of many app servers.
The app server reads from a cache or database, builds the page and sends it back. The browser then requests the images, CSS and scripts, often from a CDN.
topics.analogy: Calling a shop. You look up the number in a phone book (DNS), dial (TCP connection), check you're really talking to that shop (TLS), then ask your question (HTTP request).
topics.breaks: A phone book rarely changes. DNS answers are cached for a set time (the TTL), so when a server's IP changes, some users keep reaching the old address for minutes or hours. That matters when you fail over to a new server.
topics.example: Big sites use DNS to send users to their nearest datacentre (geo-DNS), and to move traffic away from a datacentre that is down.
keyPoints: DNS lookup order: browser cache → operating system cache → resolver (for example your ISP) → root server → top-level domain (.com) → the domain's authoritative server.
TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery. UDP is faster but packets can be lost; it suits video calls, games and DNS itself.
TLS (the S in HTTPS) encrypts the connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate.
Every new connection costs round trips, so clients reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2).
IP address = which machine; port = which program on it (443 for HTTPS).
tradeOffs: Low DNS TTL: faster failover, but more DNS lookups. High TTL: fewer lookups, but slow to change.
mistakes: Forgetting DNS caching when you plan a failover by changing DNS records.
Mixing up TCP (the reliable connection) with HTTP (the request format that travels over it).
Thinking HTTPS only encrypts. It also proves the server's identity.
topics.interviewAnswer: The browser resolves the domain through DNS, usually from a cache, to get an IP address. It opens a TCP connection and does a TLS handshake, then sends the HTTP request. The request typically hits a load balancer, which forwards it to an app server; the server reads from a cache or database and sends back the response.

followUps.q: TCP or UDP for a live video call?
followUps.a: Usually UDP-based protocols. A late video packet is useless, so it's better to skip it than to wait for it to be resent.
The TLS handshake adds round trips before the first request. Reusing connections and TLS 1.3 reduce the cost.

practice.explain: Explain what happens when you type a URL and press Enter, in under a minute.
practice.draw: Draw the full path: browser, DNS resolver, load balancer, app server, database, and back.
practice.apply: Your site moves to a new IP address. Explain why some users still reach the old server for a while, and what you would set in advance.
practice.tradeoffs: Compare TCP and UDP: what each gives up, and one system that should use each.

resources.title: ByteByteGo: what happens when you type a URL into your browser

explain.answer:
1. DNS: the browser needs an IP address for example.com. It checks its own cache, then the operating system's, then asks a resolver (usually your internet provider's), which asks the root servers, then the .com servers, then example.com's own name server. The answer is cached for its TTL.
2. TCP: the browser opens a connection to that IP on port 443 with a three-step handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
3. TLS: the server shows a certificate proving it really is example.com, and both sides agree on encryption keys.
4. HTTP: the browser sends "GET /" with the header "Host: example.com".
5. Server side: a load balancer passes the request to one app server, which reads a cache or the database and builds the response.
6. Back in the browser: it reads the HTML, then fetches the CSS, scripts and images (often from a CDN), and draws the page.

draw.answer: The DNS lookup happens once and is then cached; the TCP and TLS handshakes happen once per connection; every request after that goes straight down the right-hand path and back.
draw.code:
Browser
  │ 1. example.com?
  ▼
DNS resolver ──► root → .com → example.com's
  │                 name server
  │ 2. "93.184.216.34" (cached for the TTL)
  ▼
Browser ── 3. TCP + TLS handshake ──┐
  │ 4. GET / (Host: example.com)    │
  ▼                                 │
Load balancer ◄─────────────────────┘
  │ 5. picks a healthy server
  ▼
App server ──► cache (miss) ──► Database
  │ 6. builds the response
  ▼
Load balancer ──► Browser: HTML, then
                  CSS, JS, images (CDN)

apply.answer:
Why: DNS answers are cached. Browsers, operating systems and resolvers all keep the old answer (the old IP) until its TTL runs out, and some resolvers keep it even longer than they should. Until then, those users go to the old server.

What to set in advance:
1. A day or two before the move, lower the record's TTL, for example from 1 day to 60 seconds. Do this at least one old TTL before the switch, so the long-lived copies have expired.
2. Switch the record to the new IP. Most users move within about a minute.
3. Keep the old server running for a while, forwarding (proxying) its requests to the new one, so stragglers still work. Watch its traffic fall to zero before you switch it off.
4. Raise the TTL again afterwards.

Better still, put a load balancer or a fixed (floating) IP in front, so the address users see never changes and you only swap the servers behind it.

tradeoffs.answer:
TCP gives you a connection, delivery of every packet, in order, and slows down when the network is busy. What it gives up: speed. There is a handshake before any data, and a lost packet holds up everything behind it until it is resent. Use it when every byte must arrive: web pages, APIs, payments, file downloads. Example: a banking API.

UDP just sends packets: no connection, no guarantee they arrive, no ordering. What it gives up: reliability (the program must cope with loss itself). What it gains: low, steady latency. Use it when late data is useless anyway: live video calls, online games, DNS lookups. Example: a video call, where it is better to skip a lost frame than freeze while waiting for it.

(QUIC, used by HTTP/3, builds TCP-like reliability on top of UDP, to get fast setup without head-of-line blocking.)

topics.name: HTTP and REST API design
topics.definition: HTTP is the request–response protocol of the web. REST is a style of API design built around resources (nouns) and standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
topics.problem: Clients and servers are often built by different teams, or even different companies. They need a clear, stable contract for asking and answering; otherwise every change breaks somebody.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  participant D as Database
  C->>S: POST /v1/orders (Idempotency-Key k1)
  S->>D: save the order and key k1
  S-->>C: 201 Created
  Note over C,S: the reply gets lost, so the client retries
  C->>S: POST /v1/orders (Idempotency-Key k1)
  S->>D: has key k1 been used?
  D-->>S: yes, for order 77
  S-->>C: 201 Created (the same order 77, no duplicate)
diagram.caption: A retried request carries the same idempotency key, so the server recognises it and returns the first result instead of creating a second order.

topics.idea: A good API is predictable. Resources have clear URLs like /users/42/orders, methods mean what they say, and status codes tell the client what happened. Lists are paginated, the API is versioned, and requests that may be retried are made idempotent so a retry can't do the work twice.
howItWorks: Name resources as nouns: /users, /users/42, /users/42/orders. Avoid verbs in URLs, like /getUserOrders.
Choose the method by intent: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to change part, DELETE to remove.
Return a status code that tells the truth: 201 after creating, 400 for bad input, 404 when something is missing, 409 for a conflict, 429 when rate-limited, 500 when the server broke.
Paginate lists: return 20 items plus a cursor; the client sends the cursor back to get the next 20.
Make retries safe: the client sends an Idempotency-Key header with POST; the server stores the key with the result and returns the same result if the key comes again.
Version from day one: /v1/. When you must break something, add /v2/ and keep /v1/ running for old clients.
topics.analogy: A restaurant menu with clear sections. You ask for a dish by name (the resource), say what you want done (the method), and the waiter replies 'served', 'out of stock' or 'not on the menu' (the status code).
topics.breaks: A waiter can improvise. An API is a contract: once apps depend on it, you can't change it freely, which is why versioning matters.
topics.example: GET /v1/orders?limit=20&cursor=abc returns 200 OK with 20 orders and a cursor for the next page. POST /v1/orders with an Idempotency-Key header returns 201 Created; retrying with the same key returns the same order instead of creating a second one.
keyPoints: Methods: GET reads (safe), POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes. GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent.
Status codes: 2xx success (200, 201), 3xx redirect (301, 302), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429), 5xx server error (500, 503).
Pagination: offset (simple, but slow and unstable on big, changing lists) or cursor (fast and stable; preferred at scale).
Idempotency key: the client sends a unique key so a retried request isn't processed twice. Essential for payments.
Versioning: /v1/ in the path or a header, so old clients keep working.
Alternatives: GraphQL (the client chooses the fields it wants) and gRPC (fast, typed calls between services).
tradeOffs: REST: simple and cacheable, but may need several calls per screen.
GraphQL: flexible queries, but harder caching and rate limiting.
gRPC: fast and strongly typed, but less browser-friendly.
mistakes: Returning 200 OK with an error message hidden in the body.
Using GET for actions that change data (crawlers and browser prefetching may call it).
No pagination, so one request can return a million rows.
Breaking changes without a new version.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd design the API around resources with standard methods and status codes, paginate lists with cursors, version it, and require an idempotency key on any create or payment endpoint so client retries are safe.

followUps.a: 401 means not authenticated (we don't know who you are). 403 means authenticated but not allowed to do this.

followUps.q: Why is cursor pagination better than offset?
followUps.a: Offset has to skip rows, which is slow for page 10,000, and pages shift when new rows arrive. A cursor continues from the last item seen, so it's fast and stable.

practice.explain: Explain idempotency, and why POST isn't idempotent by default.
practice.draw: Write the API for a small library app (list books, borrow a book, return a book) with methods, URLs and status codes.
practice.apply: Design the API for sending money between two bank accounts, including how a retried request is handled.
practice.tradeoffs: When would you choose gRPC or GraphQL instead of REST?

resources.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

explain.answer:
An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. "Set my email to a@b.com" (PUT) is idempotent: the second time changes nothing. "Delete order 7" (DELETE) is too: after the first time it is already gone. GET reads, so it changes nothing at all.

POST usually means "create a new one". Send "create an order for £50" twice and you get two orders. That matters because networks fail: if the reply is lost, the client can't tell whether the order was made, and the safe-looking retry creates a duplicate.

The fix is an idempotency key: the client makes one unique key per real action and sends it with every retry. The server saves the key with the first result, and returns that same result when the key comes again, instead of creating a second order.

draw.answer: Resources are nouns (books, loans); borrowing creates a loan, and returning updates it, so history is kept. Status codes say exactly what went wrong, so the app can show the right message.

apply.answer:
The endpoint:
POST /v1/transfers
Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>, Idempotency-Key: <a UUID made once per transfer by the client>
Body: from_account, to_account, amount_minor (integer pence, never a float), currency, reference.

Responses: 201 Created with transfer_id and status; 400 for bad input; 401 or 403 if the caller can't use from_account; 404 for an unknown account; 422 for not enough money; 409 if the same key comes with a different body; 429 when rate-limited. GET /v1/transfers/{id} lets the client check what happened.

On the server, in one database transaction: insert the idempotency key (a UNIQUE column), insert the transfer, then write the two ledger entries (debit and credit). Store the response with the key. Either all of it happens, or none of it.

A retried request (say the reply timed out) carries the same key:
• If the key is found and finished, return the stored response: the money moves once.
• If the first attempt is still running, return 409 "in progress" (or wait for it).
• Keys expire after, say, 24 hours.

The client's rule: on a timeout or a 5xx, retry with the same key and back off; never make a new key for the same transfer.

tradeoffs.answer:
Choose gRPC for calls between your own services: it is fast (binary messages over HTTP/2), strongly typed (the .proto file is the contract, and client code is generated from it), and supports streaming in both directions. The cost: browsers can't call it directly without a proxy, and it is harder to inspect by hand than JSON.

Choose GraphQL when many different clients (web, iOS, Android) need different slices of the same data, and REST would mean several round trips per screen or a lot of unused fields. The client asks for exactly the fields it needs, in one request. The costs: HTTP caching is harder (one endpoint, POST bodies), rate limiting must look at how expensive a query is, and careless resolvers cause N+1 database queries.

Stay with REST for public APIs, simple CRUD, and anything that benefits from plain HTTP caching and tooling. A common mix: REST or GraphQL at the edge for apps, gRPC inside between services.

topics.name: Real-time communication: polling, long polling, WebSockets, SSE
topics.definition: Ways for a server to get new data to a client quickly: the client keeps asking (polling), waits on an open request (long polling), keeps a two-way connection open (WebSockets), or receives a one-way stream (server-sent events, SSE).
topics.problem: Normal HTTP lets the client ask but not the server tell. Chat, notifications, live prices and multiplayer games need updates pushed to the user within a fraction of a second.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["User A"] <-->|"WebSocket"| G1["Gateway 1"] B["User B"] <-->|"WebSocket"| G2["Gateway 2"] G1 -->|"1 message for B"| CS["Chat service"] CS -->|"2 where is B connected?"| R[("Redis
user → gateway")] CS -->|"3 forward"| G2
diagram.caption: Each user keeps an open connection to one gateway. To reach B, the chat service looks up B's gateway in Redis and forwards the message there.

topics.idea: Normal HTTP is 'the client asks, the server answers'. Chat, live scores and notifications need the server to push. Polling is simple but wasteful. Long polling holds a request open until there's news. WebSockets keep one connection open for messages in both directions. SSE is a simpler one-way stream from server to client.
howItWorks: Short polling: the client asks 'anything new?' every few seconds. Simple, but most answers are 'no'.
Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request open until there's news (or a timeout of about 30 seconds). The client immediately asks again.
WebSocket: starts as an HTTP request with an 'Upgrade' header. After that, the same connection stays open and either side can send a message at any time.
SSE: the client opens one HTTP request and the server keeps sending events down it; the browser reconnects automatically if it drops.
At scale: users connect to many gateway servers. When user A messages user B, the system looks up B's gateway in a registry (such as Redis) and forwards the message there.
topics.analogy: Polling is a child asking 'are we there yet?' every minute. Long polling is asking once, and the driver only answers when you arrive. A WebSocket is an open phone line both people can talk on.
topics.breaks: An open phone line costs nothing to keep open. Each WebSocket holds memory and a connection on a server, so millions of users need many connection servers, and a way to find which server each user is connected to.
topics.example: WhatsApp-style chat: each user keeps a connection to a gateway server, and a lookup store records which gateway holds each user, so a message can be routed to the right one.
keyPoints: Short polling: simple, but most responses are empty; high load, and a delay of up to one polling interval.
Long polling: fewer empty responses; works everywhere; one request per message.
WebSockets: two-way and low latency, but connections are stateful, which makes load balancing and scaling harder.
SSE: one-way, server to client, over normal HTTP; reconnects automatically; good for feeds and notifications.
Stateful connections need a 'who is connected where' registry, often in Redis.
mistakes: Choosing WebSockets for one-way updates, where SSE is simpler.
Forgetting that open connections make servers stateful: you need a connection registry and reconnect logic.
No plan for messages missed while a client was disconnected.
topics.interviewAnswer: For chat I'd use WebSockets, because messages flow both ways with low latency. Users connect to a fleet of gateway servers, and Redis maps each user to their gateway so a message can be pushed to the right connection. For one-way updates like live scores, SSE is simpler.

followUps.q: What happens when a WebSocket server crashes?
followUps.a: Clients reconnect (with backoff) to another server, re-register where they are, and fetch any missed messages using the last message ID they saw.

followUps.q: Why not just poll every second?
followUps.a: With millions of users, that's millions of mostly empty requests every second: huge cost for little benefit.

practice.explain: Explain polling, long polling, WebSockets and SSE with the 'are we there yet?' picture.
practice.draw: Draw how a message travels from user A to user B when they are connected to different WebSocket servers.
practice.apply: Choose a method for: a stock price ticker, a chat app, a nightly report, and a delivery-tracking map. Justify each.
practice.tradeoffs: What does it cost to hold 10 million open WebSocket connections, and how would you spread them across servers?

resources.title: ByteByteGo: polling vs long polling vs websockets vs SSE
Hello Interview: design a chat system

explain.answer:
• Short polling: the child asks "are we there yet?" every minute. Simple, but almost every answer is "no", and you can be up to a minute late hearing "yes".
• Long polling: the child asks once, and the driver stays quiet until they arrive (or for at most 30 seconds), then answers. The child asks again straight away. Fewer wasted questions, and the answer comes the moment it is true.
• WebSocket: an open phone line. Once the call is connected, either person can speak at any time, in both directions.
• SSE (server-sent events): the driver's announcements over the car speaker. The driver talks whenever there is news; the child only listens. One-way, and it reconnects by itself if it drops.

draw.answer: Gateways hold the open connections but don't know where other users are; the registry does. The message is also saved before it is forwarded, so B can fetch it later if B was offline or the forward failed.
draw.code:
User A ═══ WebSocket ═══ Gateway 1
                            │ 1. "message for B"
                            ▼
                       Chat service
                         │   │ 2. save the message
                         │   └──────────► Database
                         │ 3. where is B?
                         ├──────────────► Redis
                         │ ◄── "Gateway 2" ┘
                         │ 4. forward
                         ▼
User B ═══ WebSocket ═══ Gateway 2

apply.answer:
• Stock price ticker: SSE. Updates only flow from server to client, many times a second, and SSE is a simple stream over normal HTTP that reconnects by itself. (If the same screen also places trades, a WebSocket can carry both.)
• Chat app: WebSockets. Messages go both ways, typing indicators and read receipts need low latency, and one open connection is much cheaper than polling.
• Nightly report: none of them. It is ready once a day, so a normal request is enough: email a link or send a notification when it is done, or let the page poll the job status every 30 seconds while someone waits.
• Delivery-tracking map: SSE (or a WebSocket). The courier's position arrives every few seconds and only flows to the customer. Polling every 5 to 10 seconds also works at small scale, and is simpler to build.

The rule: two-way and fast means WebSockets; one-way and frequent means SSE; rare updates mean ordinary requests or polling.

tradeoffs.answer:
The costs of 10 million open connections:
• Memory: each connection holds buffers and some session state, say about 20 KB, so roughly 200 GB of memory in total.
• Servers: a well-tuned server holds about 100,000 to 1,000,000 connections. At 100,000 each, that is 100 gateway servers, plus spare capacity for failures.
• Heartbeats: a ping every 30 seconds per connection is about 330,000 small messages a second, just to keep connections alive.
• File handles, TLS work, and load balancers that must support long-lived connections.

Spreading them:
• Put a layer-4 load balancer (or DNS) in front of a fleet of stateless gateway servers, sending new connections to the least-loaded one.
• Keep a registry (Redis) of user → gateway, updated on connect and disconnect, so any service can route a message to the right gateway.
• Plan for failure: when a gateway dies, its 100,000 users reconnect at once. Clients must back off with random jitter, so they don't stampede the other servers.
• On deploys, drain servers slowly (stop new connections, then close old ones gradually), rather than dropping everyone at once.
tradeoffs.code:
connections = 10_000_000
memory_gb = connections * 20e3 / 1e9          # about 20 KB each
servers = connections / 100_000               # 100k per server
pings_per_s = connections / 30                # one ping every 30 s
print(memory_gb, servers, round(pings_per_s))
# 200.0 100.0 333333

topics.name: CDN (content delivery network)
topics.definition: A network of servers around the world that caches static content (images, video, scripts) close to users.
topics.problem: Distance costs time: a user in Sydney fetching from London waits around a quarter of a second for each round trip, and every byte you send costs bandwidth. Big files and users all over the world make this much worse.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U1["User in Sydney"] --> E1["Edge server
Sydney"] U2["User in London"] --> E2["Edge server
London"] E1 -.->|"miss: fetch once"| O["Origin server
(yours)"] E2 -.->|"miss: fetch once"| O
diagram.caption: Users talk to the edge server near them. Only on a miss does the edge fetch the file from your origin; after that, everyone nearby gets the fast local copy.

topics.idea: Instead of every user fetching a video from your one datacentre, copies are served from a nearby 'edge' server. This cuts latency, takes load off your servers and absorbs traffic spikes. Content is pulled into the CDN on the first request (pull CDN) or uploaded in advance (push CDN).
howItWorks: You point a hostname, like cdn.example.com, at the CDN provider.
A user's request goes to the nearest edge server (found through DNS or 'anycast' routing).
Cache hit: the edge already has the file and returns it in a few milliseconds.
Cache miss: the edge fetches the file from your origin server once, stores it, and returns it. Every later user in that region gets the fast copy.
The file stays until its TTL expires. To update it straight away, publish a new file name (app.3f9a.js → app.7c2b.js) or purge the old one.
topics.analogy: Local supermarket branches stocking popular products, so you don't have to drive to the central warehouse.
topics.breaks: A supermarket can check the warehouse for the newest stock. A CDN serves its cached copy until it expires, so after you change a file, users may get the old one unless you put a version in the file name or purge the cache.
topics.example: Netflix places its own CDN boxes inside internet providers' networks, so most video traffic never crosses the wider internet.
keyPoints: Best for static, popular, cacheable content: images, video segments, JavaScript and CSS files.
Pull CDN: fetches from your origin server on a cache miss. Push CDN: you upload content ahead of time.
Control freshness with TTL headers; put a version or hash in file names (app.3f9a.js) so updates appear immediately.
Also helps with DDoS protection, and can handle TLS close to the user.
mistakes: Caching personalised pages at the edge, and showing one user's data to another.
Long TTLs on files that change, without versioned names.
Forgetting that the first request in each region is still slow (a 'cold' cache).
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd serve static assets and media through a CDN, so users download them from a nearby edge server. That lowers latency and takes most of the bandwidth off our origin. I'd use versioned file names so updates show up immediately.

followUps.q: Can a CDN cache API responses?
followUps.a: Sometimes, for short TTLs on public data like a product page. Personalised responses usually can't be cached at the edge.
Pull for most sites (simple and automatic). Push when content is large and known in advance, like a video library.

practice.explain: Explain a CDN with the supermarket picture, and where the picture breaks.
practice.draw: Draw a user, a CDN edge server and your origin, showing a cache hit and a cache miss.
practice.apply: In a YouTube-like design, which data goes through the CDN and which does not?
practice.tradeoffs: You fixed a bug in app.js but users still get the old file. Why, and how do you prevent it next time?

explain.answer:
A CDN is like a supermarket chain. Instead of everyone driving to the central warehouse (your origin server), each town has a branch (an edge server) that stocks the popular products (files). You shop at your local branch: much quicker. When the branch runs out of something, it orders it once from the warehouse (a cache miss) and then has it for everyone in town.

Where the picture breaks: a supermarket can check the warehouse for the newest version. A CDN keeps selling its copy until it expires (its TTL), even if you have changed the file at the warehouse. So after an update, users may get the old file unless the new one has a new name (app.3f9a.js) or you purge the cache. Also, a supermarket only stocks things everyone buys: anything personal to one user (their account page) should not be stored at the edge.

draw.answer: On a hit the user never touches your servers. On a miss the edge fetches the file once from the origin, keeps a copy until its TTL runs out, and every later nearby user gets a hit.
draw.code:
Cache hit
  User (Sydney) ──► Edge (Sydney)
                     has the file
  User ◄──────────── reply, ~10 ms

Cache miss
  User (Sydney) ──► Edge (Sydney)
                     not there yet
                       │ fetch once
                       ▼
                    Origin (London)
                       │ file
                       ▼
                    Edge stores a copy
                    (until the TTL ends)
  User ◄──────────── reply, ~300 ms

  Next user in Sydney: a hit.

apply.answer:
Through the CDN (public, large, read by many people, the same for everyone):
• Video segments: each video is cut into chunks of a few seconds, at several qualities (240p to 4K). This is almost all of the bandwidth.
• Thumbnails, channel pictures and banners.
• The website's static files: JavaScript, CSS, fonts, icons.

Not through the CDN (personal, changing, or writes), straight to your API servers:
• Uploads: they go to object storage, often through a signed upload URL, then to the transcoding pipeline.
• The home feed and recommendations, which are different for every user.
• Watch history, likes, comments, subscriptions: writes, and data about one user.
• Search, sign-in and payments.
• View counts and analytics events.

A middle case: rarely watched "long-tail" videos may be served from the origin or a regional cache, because caching them at every edge wastes space.

tradeoffs.answer:
Why: app.js has the same name as before, and copies are cached with a long TTL in two places: the CDN's edge servers and users' browsers. Neither knows the file has changed, so both keep serving the old one until their copy expires.

Right now: purge app.js from the CDN. That fixes the edge, but browsers that already have it may still use their copy until it expires.

Next time: put a fingerprint of the contents in the file name (app.3f9a.js, made by the build tool). A changed file gets a new name, so no cache has ever seen it, and you can give these files a very long TTL ("immutable"). The HTML page that names the file is cached briefly (or revalidated every time), so it picks up the new name within seconds.

topics.name: Proxies, reverse proxies and API gateways
topics.definition: A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers and receives requests on their behalf. An API gateway is a reverse proxy with API features: authentication, rate limiting and routing to the right service.
topics.problem: With many services, every client would need to know every service's address, and every service would repeat the same login checks, rate limits and logging. That's duplicated, inconsistent work.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Clients"] --> G["API gateway
TLS · auth · rate limit · logging"] G -->|"/users/..."| US["User service"] G -->|"/orders/..."| OS["Order service"] G -->|"/payments/..."| PS["Payment service"]
diagram.caption: Every request goes through one front door. The gateway checks and logs it, then sends it to the right service based on its path.

topics.idea: Clients talk to one entry point instead of many servers. That entry point can handle TLS, compress responses, cache, check tokens, apply rate limits, and send /orders to the order service and /users to the user service.
howItWorks: The client sends every request to one address, for example api.example.com.
The gateway handles TLS, then checks the token (who is this?) and the rate limit (are they allowed this many requests?).
It looks at the path: /orders/… goes to the order service, /users/… to the user service.
It forwards the request, waits for the answer and sends it back, logging the request and how long it took.
Behind it, each service may run several copies, so a load balancer (often built into the gateway) picks one.
topics.analogy: A hotel reception. Guests don't walk into the kitchen or the laundry; reception checks who they are and passes each request to the right department.
topics.breaks: A reception desk with one person is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. A gateway must itself be replicated and kept fast, or every request suffers.
topics.example: Nginx or Envoy as a reverse proxy; a managed API gateway that checks tokens and allows 100 requests per minute per API key before anything reaches the services.
keyPoints: Forward proxy: acts for clients (for example, a company's web proxy). Reverse proxy: acts for servers.
Gateway jobs: routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS, request logging, API versioning.
A load balancer spreads traffic across copies of a service; a gateway decides what's allowed and which service it goes to. Many products do both.
Keep business logic out of the gateway.
mistakes: Putting business rules in the gateway, so it slowly becomes a hidden monolith.
Running a single gateway instance: a single point of failure.
Doing heavy work in the gateway that slows down every request.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd put an API gateway at the edge to authenticate requests, apply rate limits and route each path to the right microservice, so services don't each re-implement those concerns. It's replicated, so it isn't a single point of failure.

followUps.a: A load balancer spreads requests across copies of one service. A gateway handles API concerns like auth, limits and routing between different services. Often you use both.

followUps.q: What's the downside of a gateway?
followUps.a: An extra network hop, and a central component that must scale and stay up.

practice.explain: Explain reverse proxy versus forward proxy in two sentences.
practice.draw: Draw client → gateway → three services, and label what the gateway checks.
practice.apply: List what your gateway would do for a mobile banking app.
practice.tradeoffs: What goes wrong if business logic slowly creeps into the gateway?

explain.answer:
A forward proxy works for clients: it sits in front of users and sends their requests out to the internet for them, for example a company proxy that filters and logs staff web browsing.

A reverse proxy works for servers: it sits in front of your servers and receives requests from the internet for them, handling TLS, caching and load balancing, and hiding the servers behind it.

draw.answer: The checks run in order and stop early: a request without a valid token never costs a rate-limit lookup or reaches a service. Routing is by path, and every request is logged with how long it took.
draw.code:
Client
  │ HTTPS
  ▼
API gateway, in order:
  1 TLS ends here
  2 token valid?          no → 401
  3 allowed this call?    no → 403
  4 under the rate limit? no → 429
  5 log it, route by path
  │
  ├─ /users/…    ──► User service
  ├─ /orders/…   ──► Order service
  └─ /payments/… ──► Payment service

apply.answer:
For a mobile banking app, the gateway would:
• End TLS, with modern settings only (the app also pins the certificate).
• Check the access token on every request (signature, expiry, audience), and that its scopes allow the call: a "read balance" token can't make payments.
• Rate-limit per user, per device and per IP, strictly on login and one-time-code endpoints, to slow down password guessing.
• Route by path: /accounts to the accounts service, /payments to payments, /cards to cards.
• Reject bad requests early: too large, wrong content type, missing required headers (such as an Idempotency-Key on POST /payments).
• Add a request ID and tracing headers, and write an audit log, with card numbers and personal data masked.
• Handle API versions, and tell very old app versions to upgrade.
• Apply timeouts to each backend, and stop calling a failing one for a while (a circuit breaker).
• Block known bad traffic (a web application firewall, bot detection).

What it would not do: work out balances, check payment limits or run fraud rules. That is business logic, and it belongs in the services.

tradeoffs.answer:
• It becomes a hidden monolith: every team needs changes in the one shared gateway, so releases queue up behind it and teams are tied together again, which is what microservices were meant to stop.
• Rules end up split: half a rule in the gateway, half in the service, and nobody can see the whole thing or test it in one place.
• It is hard to test and debug: gateway logic often lives in configuration or plugin scripts, without the tests, reviews and tooling of normal code.
• A bigger blast radius: a bug in the gateway breaks every service at once, not just one.
• Everything gets slower: heavier work in the gateway adds latency to every single request, and makes the gateway harder to scale.

Keep the gateway to jobs that are the same for every service (TLS, authentication, rate limits, routing, logging), and keep decisions about the business in the services.

phases.title: Core concepts: scale, reliability and speed
phases.goal: The ten ideas every high-level design uses: scalability, availability, fault tolerance, load balancing, caching, consistency and CAP, rate limiting, asynchronous processing, and observability.
phases.bigPicture: Almost every design answer is a combination of these ideas: copy things for availability, spread load for scale, cache for speed, queue slow work, and watch everything. Learn each one well enough to say when to use it and what it costs.

topics.name: Scalability: vertical vs horizontal
topics.definition: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load by adding resources.
topics.problem: A system that works for 100 users can fall over at 100,000. You need a way to add capacity without rewriting everything.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD LB["Load balancer"] --> S1["App server"] LB --> S2["App server"] LB --> S3["App server
(added by auto-scaling)"] S1 & S2 & S3 --> R[("Redis
sessions")] S1 & S2 & S3 --> P[("Database leader")] P --> RR[("Read replica")]
diagram.caption: Horizontal scaling: identical, stateless app servers behind a load balancer. Because sessions live in Redis, any server can handle any user, so adding a server is easy.

topics.idea: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine (more CPU and memory). It's simple, but there's a ceiling, and that one machine can fail. Horizontal scaling means more machines behind a load balancer. It has no hard ceiling and survives failures, but needs stateless app servers and shared storage. The key trick: keep app servers stateless, and keep sessions and data in shared stores.
howItWorks: Find the bottleneck first: is the CPU at 100%, the database slow, memory full, or the network saturated?
Make app servers stateless: no sessions or files kept on the server; put them in Redis and object storage instead.
Put a load balancer in front and add servers. With auto-scaling, servers are added automatically when CPU use or latency rises.
Take reads off the database: cache hot data and add read replicas.
When writes become the bottleneck, shard the database by a key.
Move slow work off the request path with queues.
topics.analogy: A busy restaurant can buy a bigger oven (vertical) or open more kitchens (horizontal).
topics.breaks: More kitchens only help if any kitchen can cook any order. If half of a customer's order is in kitchen 2, it has to go back there. That's 'state', and it's why app servers should be stateless.
topics.example: Moving login sessions from server memory into Redis lets any server handle any user, so you can add servers freely.
keyPoints: Stateless app servers plus a shared session store = easy horizontal scaling.
Databases are the hard part: read replicas for more reads, sharding for more writes.
Scale the real bottleneck: measure first (CPU, memory, database, network).
Auto-scaling adds and removes servers based on load.
Scalability is not speed: a system fast for one user can still collapse under many.
tradeOffs: Vertical: simple, no code changes, but a ceiling and a single point of failure.
Horizontal: almost unlimited and fault tolerant, but needs statelessness, load balancing and distributed data.
mistakes: Adding app servers when the database is the real bottleneck.
Keeping sessions in server memory, then adding more servers.
Sharding far too early: it adds a lot of complexity.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd keep the application tier stateless so it scales horizontally behind a load balancer with auto-scaling. State goes into shared stores: sessions in Redis, data in the database. For the database, I'd add read replicas first and shard only when write volume needs it.

followUps.q: When is vertical scaling the right answer?
followUps.a: Early on, or for a database that's hard to split. It's simple and modern machines are very large. Just plan the horizontal path for later.
It keeps data that later requests depend on, like a session in memory or an uploaded file on its local disk.

practice.explain: Explain vertical and horizontal scaling with the restaurant picture.
practice.draw: Draw a stateless app tier behind a load balancer, with a shared session store and a database with replicas.
practice.apply: An app saves uploaded files on each server's local disk. Explain what breaks when you add a second server, and fix it.
practice.tradeoffs: Give one case where you'd scale vertically first, and why.

resources.title: Hello Interview: scale from zero to millions of users

explain.answer:
A busy restaurant has two ways to cook more meals.

Vertical scaling is buying a bigger oven: one machine with more CPU and memory. It is simple (nothing about how the kitchen works changes), but there is a biggest oven you can buy, and if that one oven breaks, nobody eats.
