Horizontal scaling is opening more kitchens: more machines behind a load balancer. There is no hard limit, and if one kitchen closes the others keep cooking. But it only works if any kitchen can cook any order. If half of a customer's order is sitting in kitchen 2 (state, like a session kept in one server's memory), their next request has to go back there. That is why app servers are made stateless, with sessions and files kept in shared stores.

draw.answer: The app servers are identical and keep nothing between requests, so the load balancer can send any user to any of them, and auto-scaling can add or remove one at any time. All state lives below them: sessions in Redis, data in the database, where the leader takes writes and the replicas serve reads.
draw.code:
Clients
              │
        Load balancer
     ┌────────┼────────┐
     ▼        ▼        ▼
    App      App      App   ← stateless,
   server   server   server   auto-scaled
     │        │        │
     ├────────┴────────┤
     ▼                 ▼
Redis (sessions)   Database leader ── writes
                       │ copies changes
                 ┌─────┴─────┐
                 ▼           ▼
             Replica      Replica ── reads

apply.answer:
What breaks: a user uploads a photo and the load balancer sends that request to server 1, which saves it on its own disk. Their next request, "show my photo", goes to server 2, which has never seen the file: a broken image or a 404. It looks random, because it depends on which server you happen to hit. And if server 1 dies or is replaced, its files are gone for good.

The fix: keep no files on the app servers. Store uploads in shared object storage (such as Amazon S3), and save only the file's key in the database. Better still, have the server hand the client a short-lived signed upload URL, so the file goes straight to object storage and never passes through the app server at all. Serve files to users through a CDN in front of the storage.

Now every server sees the same files, any server can handle any request, and you can add or remove servers freely.

tradeoffs.answer:
The main database of a growing product, early on.

Say the PostgreSQL primary is running out of CPU at 5,000 queries a second. Moving it to a machine twice as big takes an hour and needs no code changes. Sharding it means choosing a shard key, rewriting the queries that join across shards, moving the data and running many databases: weeks of work and a permanent increase in complexity.

Modern machines are huge (hundreds of cores, terabytes of memory), so vertical scaling can carry a database a long way. Do it first, together with the cheap horizontal steps around it (a cache, read replicas), and plan the sharding path for when the biggest machine is no longer enough. Also: keep a standby replica, because one big machine is still a single point of failure.

topics.name: Availability: nines, SLAs and redundancy
topics.definition: Availability is the share of time a system works and responds correctly, usually written in 'nines', like 99.9%.
topics.problem: Machines, disks, networks and whole datacentres fail. If your system has only one copy of anything important, that one failure takes everything down.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD
  LB["Load balancer (redundant pair)"]
  subgraph ZA["Availability zone A"]
    A1["App server"]
    DBA[("Database leader")]
  end
  subgraph ZB["Availability zone B"]
    B1["App server"]
    DBB[("Database standby")]
  end
  LB --> A1
  LB --> B1
  DBA -->|"copies every change"| DBB
diagram.caption: Everything has a copy in a second zone. If zone A goes down, the load balancer sends traffic to zone B and the standby database takes over.

topics.idea: 99.9% ('three nines') allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year; 99.99% about 53 minutes. You raise availability by removing single points of failure: run several copies across machines and zones, with health checks and automatic failover. An SLO is your internal target; an SLA is the promise to customers, often with refunds if you miss it.
howItWorks: Agree the target. 99.9% means about 43 minutes of downtime a month.
List every component a request touches and ask: if this dies, what happens?
Add redundancy: at least two copies of each component, in different availability zones.
Add detection: health checks that notice a failure within seconds.
Add automatic failover: the load balancer stops sending traffic to dead servers, and a database replica is promoted when the leader dies.
Practise it: test failover regularly, because untested backups often don't work when you need them.
topics.analogy: A hospital with backup generators. When the mains power fails, a generator starts and the lights stay on.
topics.breaks: A generator is one independent backup. Real systems also fail in shared ways — a bad deployment, a whole region going down, a shared database — so backups only help if they fail independently.
topics.example: Two parts in series, each 99.9% available, give about 99.8% overall (0.999 × 0.999). Two redundant copies in parallel, each 99%, give 99.99% (1 − 0.01²), as long as they fail independently.
keyPoints: Downtime per year: 99% ≈ 3.65 days; 99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours; 99.99% ≈ 53 minutes; 99.999% ≈ 5 minutes.
Dependencies in series multiply availability down; parallel copies multiply the chance of failure down.
Remove single points of failure: load balancers, databases, DNS, the gateway itself.
Spread across availability zones (separate datacentres in one region); for more safety, across regions.
Active–passive: a standby takes over. Active–active: all copies serve traffic all the time.
SLI = what you measure; SLO = your target; SLA = your contract.
tradeOffs: Each extra nine costs much more: extra regions, more complex failover, more testing.
mistakes: Two copies that share one point of failure (the same rack, the same power supply, the same bad deployment).
Forgetting the database, DNS or load balancer when removing single points of failure.
Promising 99.99% when one of your dependencies only offers 99.9%.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd first agree a target, say 99.9%. Then I'd remove single points of failure: several app servers across availability zones, a replicated database with automatic failover, redundant load balancers and health checks. I'd also remember that every dependency in series lowers the overall availability.

followUps.a: Availability: is it up and responding? Reliability: does it do the right thing over time, without errors or data loss? A system can be up but returning wrong answers.
Active–active uses all capacity and fails over faster, but must handle conflicting writes. Active–passive is simpler, but the standby sits idle and failover takes longer.

practice.explain: Explain what 'three nines' means in hours of downtime per year.
practice.draw: Draw a system with no single point of failure across two availability zones.
practice.apply: Your app depends on 4 services in series, each 99.9% available. Calculate the best-case overall availability, and suggest one fix.
practice.tradeoffs: Why does going from 99.99% to 99.999% cost so much more?

resources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch 4 (service level objectives)
ByteByteGo: availability and the nines explained

explain.answer:
99.9% available means it may be down 0.1% of the time.

A year has 365 × 24 = 8,760 hours, and 0.1% of 8,760 is 8.76 hours. So three nines allows about 8 hours and 45 minutes of downtime a year, which is about 43 minutes a month, or about 10 minutes a week.

Each extra nine divides that by 10: four nines (99.99%) allows about 53 minutes a year; five nines, about 5 minutes.

draw.answer: Every box has a twin in the other zone, and nothing is shared between the zones except the network. If zone A goes dark, the load balancers stop sending traffic there (health checks fail) and the standby database is promoted to leader. DNS points at both load balancers, so even the front door has a copy.
draw.code:
DNS (two records)
           ┌──────┴──────┐
           ▼             ▼
┌──── Zone A ────┐ ┌──── Zone B ────┐
│ Load balancer  │ │ Load balancer  │
│   │       │    │ │   │       │    │
│  App     App   │ │  App     App   │
│   │            │ │   │            │
│ DB leader ─────┼─┼─► DB standby   │
│                │ │  (promoted if  │
│                │ │   A fails)     │
└────────────────┘ └────────────────┘

apply.answer:
In series, every service must be up for a request to work, so you multiply:
0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.996 (99.6%).

That is about 35 hours of downtime a year, four times the 8.8 hours each service allows on its own. And this is the best case: it assumes your own code never fails.

One fix: take a service off the critical path. If one of them is not needed to answer the user (say, recommendations or analytics), call it asynchronously or with a timeout and a fallback, so it failing no longer fails the request. Three in series gives 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%.

Another: give the weakest service a redundant copy in parallel. Two copies at 99.9% each give 1 − 0.001² = 99.9999%, so that link almost stops counting.
apply.code:
series = 0.999 ** 4
print(round(series, 4), round((1 - series) * 8760, 1))   # 0.996 35.0 hours a year
print(round(0.999 ** 3, 4))                               # 0.997
print(round(1 - 0.001 ** 2, 6))                           # 0.999999

tradeoffs.answer:
99.99% allows about 53 minutes of downtime a year; 99.999% allows about 5. That changes how you have to work:

• No time for people: 5 minutes a year is less than it takes to page an engineer and open a laptop. Every failure must be detected and fixed automatically, in seconds.
• More regions: a whole region going down for an hour would use up ten years of budget, so you need several regions serving traffic at once (active–active), with data copied between them and a way to resolve conflicting writes.
• Every dependency must be better than five nines, including DNS, the cloud provider, and the database. Anything that isn't must be made redundant or removed from the critical path.
• Changes are the biggest cause of outages, so every deploy and configuration change needs canary releases and automatic rollback.
• Constant testing: failover drills and chaos experiments, or the failover won't work when you need it.

Each nine roughly multiplies the cost in money, complexity and people, while the benefit (48 fewer minutes a year) gets smaller. So pick the target from what downtime really costs the business.

topics.name: Fault tolerance: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers
topics.definition: Fault tolerance means the system keeps working, perhaps in a reduced way, when parts of it fail.
topics.problem: In a system of many services, something is always slow or broken. Without protection, one slow dependency makes its callers wait, they run out of threads, and the failure spreads until everything is down.

diagram.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: too many failures
  Open --> HalfOpen: after a cool-down
  HalfOpen --> Closed: test calls succeed
  HalfOpen --> Open: test calls fail
  Closed: Closed - calls go through
  Open: Open - fail fast, use the fallback
  HalfOpen: Half-open - a few test calls
diagram.caption: The three states of a circuit breaker. Arrows show what makes it switch from one state to another.

topics.idea: In distributed systems something is always failing: a server, a network link, a slow dependency. The defences: timeouts (never wait forever), retries with exponential backoff and jitter (try again, gently), circuit breakers (stop calling a broken service for a while), fallbacks (return cached or default data), and bulkheads (separate resources so one failure can't sink everything).
howItWorks: Timeout: decide how long a call may take, say 300 ms. After that, give up instead of waiting forever.
Retry: if the failure looks temporary and the call is safe to repeat, try again after 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms (exponential backoff), each with a little randomness (jitter).
Circuit breaker: count failures. If, say, half the calls fail within 10 seconds, 'open' the breaker and fail instantly for the next 30 seconds without calling the service at all.
Half-open: after the wait, let a few test calls through. If they succeed, close the breaker; if not, open it again.
Fallback: while the breaker is open, return something useful: cached data, a default, or the page without that feature.
topics.analogy: A fuse box. When one circuit overloads, its fuse trips, so the whole house doesn't catch fire.
topics.breaks: A fuse stays off until someone resets it. A circuit breaker tests the service again on its own after a cool-down (the 'half-open' state) and closes again when calls succeed.
topics.example: Checkout calls a recommendations service. If it's slow, a 200 ms timeout plus a circuit breaker lets checkout still load, just without recommendations.
keyPoints: Always set timeouts on network calls.
Only retry safe (idempotent) operations; use exponential backoff plus random jitter to avoid retry storms.
Circuit breaker states: closed (normal) → open (fail fast) → half-open (test) → closed.
Graceful degradation: lose a feature, not the whole product.
Cascading failure: a slow service ties up threads in the services calling it, which then slow down too.
Test it: chaos engineering breaks things on purpose, in a controlled way.
mistakes: No timeouts, or a timeout longer than the caller's own timeout.
Retrying operations that aren't safe to repeat, like charging a card.
Retrying instantly without backoff, which turns a small outage into a big one.
topics.interviewAnswer: Every network call gets a timeout. Idempotent calls are retried with exponential backoff and jitter. Calls to non-critical dependencies sit behind a circuit breaker with a fallback, so the core feature keeps working when they fail. That stops one slow service from causing a cascading failure.

followUps.a: Without it, all clients retry at the same moments and hit the recovering service in synchronised waves.
Separate pools of threads or connections for each dependency, so one slow dependency can't use them all up.

practice.explain: Explain the three circuit-breaker states with the fuse-box picture.
practice.draw: Draw service A calling service B through a circuit breaker, and show what A returns when the breaker is open.
practice.apply: Write the retry function below, then simulate 100 clients retrying against a service that recovers after 2 seconds, with and without jitter.
practice.tradeoffs: When are retries dangerous? Give an example of an operation you must not blindly retry.

resources.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
Site Reliability Engineering, Ch 22 (addressing cascading failures)

explain.answer:
A circuit breaker is like the fuse box in a house.

• Closed (the normal state): the fuse is in, electricity flows. Calls to the other service go through, and the breaker counts the failures.
• Open: too many failures, so the fuse trips. Now calls aren't even attempted: they fail at once and the caller uses a fallback. That protects both sides: the caller doesn't tie up threads waiting, and the struggling service gets room to recover.
• Half-open: this is where the fuse picture breaks. A fuse stays off until a person resets it. A circuit breaker tries again by itself after a cool-down: it lets a few test calls through. If they succeed it closes again; if they fail it opens again for another cool-down.

draw.answer: The breaker sits inside service A, in front of every call to B. While it is open, B receives nothing at all, and A answers its own caller straight away from the fallback, so a slow or broken B no longer makes A slow.
draw.code:
Service A
  │ wants data from B
  ▼
Circuit breaker (inside A)
  │
  ├─ CLOSED:    call B normally,
  │             count the failures
  │
  ├─ OPEN:      don't call B at all.
  │             Return the fallback at once:
  │             · cached data
  │             · a default value
  │             · the page without that part
  │
  └─ HALF-OPEN: let a few test calls
                through to B
  │
  ▼
Service B

apply.answer:
The retry function is the lesson's: exponential backoff (0.1 s, 0.2 s, 0.4 s…), each wait multiplied by a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5 (jitter).

The simulation fakes the clock, so it runs instantly and gives the same numbers every time. 100 clients fail at the same moment; the service is down for 2 seconds; every client keeps retrying with the same backoff.

Without jitter, all 100 clients wait exactly the same time, so every retry wave hits the service with all 100 calls in the same instant, including the wave that arrives just after it recovers (a "thundering herd"): 100 calls in one 50 ms slice. With jitter, the same 600 calls are spread out, and the busiest 50 ms after recovery sees only 7, so a recovering service isn't knocked straight back over.

The cost is visible too: with jitter, the unluckiest client gets through at 5.8 s instead of 3.1 s. Jitter trades a little extra waiting for some clients for a much smoother load on the service.

tradeoffs.answer:
Retries are dangerous when:
• The operation is not safe to repeat. A timeout doesn't mean it failed; it may have worked and only the reply was lost. Retrying "charge this card £50" can charge twice.
• The service is overloaded. Each retry is more load on a service that is already drowning, so retries turn a slowdown into an outage. Retries also multiply through layers: if three layers each try 4 times, one user click can become 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 calls at the bottom.
• The error is permanent. Retrying a 400 Bad Request or a 403 just fails again, more slowly.
• The retries outlast the caller's own timeout, so the work continues after nobody is waiting for it.

Example: POST /payments/charge. Never retry it blindly. Send an idempotency key so the provider can recognise the repeat, or first ask "did charge X go through?" before trying again. Elsewhere: retry only at one layer, cap the attempts, back off with jitter, and use a retry budget (for example, retries may add at most 10% to the traffic).

topics.name: Load balancing
topics.definition: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across several servers and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones.
topics.problem: One server can only handle so much, and if it dies, everyone using it is affected. You need to spread requests across many servers and route around the broken ones.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Clients"] --> LB["Load balancer"] LB -->|"request 1"| S1["Server 1 ✓"] LB -->|"request 2"| S2["Server 2 ✓"] LB -.->|"failed health check:
no traffic"| S3["Server 3 ✗"]
diagram.caption: Requests are shared between healthy servers. Server 3 failed its health check, so it gets no traffic until it recovers.

topics.idea: It makes many servers look like one, enables horizontal scaling and hides failures. Layer 4 balancers route by IP address and port (fast). Layer 7 balancers read the HTTP request, so they can route by path, header or cookie. Common algorithms: round robin, least connections, and hashing (the same user always goes to the same server).
howItWorks: Clients connect to the load balancer's address, never directly to a server.
For each request or connection, it picks a healthy server using an algorithm: the next in turn (round robin), or the one with the fewest active connections.
Every few seconds it calls each server's health endpoint. After a few failures in a row it stops sending traffic there, and adds the server back when it recovers.
A layer 7 balancer can read the URL and send /api to API servers and /images to image servers.
So the balancer itself isn't a single point of failure, run two of them (one active, one standby, sharing an address) or use a managed service.
topics.analogy: A supermarket worker sending shoppers to the shortest checkout queue, and closing a till when it breaks.
topics.breaks: Shoppers are fairly similar. Requests aren't: one may take 5 ms and another 5 seconds, so 'the same number of requests' isn't 'the same amount of work'. Least connections helps.
topics.example: An AWS Application Load Balancer (layer 7) sends /api/* to API servers and /images/* to a media service, and checks each server's /health endpoint every few seconds.
keyPoints: Algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, IP or consistent hashing.
Health checks remove failed servers automatically.
Layer 4: fast and protocol-agnostic. Layer 7: smarter routing and TLS handling, but more work per request.
Sticky sessions tie a user to one server; avoid them by keeping servers stateless.
The load balancer itself must be redundant (a pair, or a managed service).
Load balancers are also used between internal services, not only at the edge.
mistakes: Sticky sessions that tie one user to a server forever, which breaks when that server dies.
Health checks that only test 'is the process running?', not 'can it reach its database?'.
Forgetting that the load balancer needs redundancy too.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd put a layer 7 load balancer in front of the stateless app servers, with health checks and least-connections routing. It runs as a redundant pair or a managed service, so it isn't a single point of failure.

followUps.q: How does a load balancer know a server is down?
followUps.a: Health checks: it calls an endpoint regularly and removes the server after several failures in a row.

followUps.q: When would you route by hashing?
followUps.a: When requests for the same key should reach the same server, for example a cache shard, so the data already in its memory gets reused.

practice.explain: Explain layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing in two sentences each.
practice.draw: Draw a load balancer with three servers, one of them failing its health check.
practice.apply: Pick an algorithm for: identical short API calls; long video uploads; a cache cluster. Justify each.
practice.tradeoffs: Why are sticky sessions a problem when you scale out or a server dies?

explain.answer:
Layer 4: the load balancer looks only at the network level, the IP addresses and ports, and forwards whole connections without reading what is inside them. It is very fast and works for any protocol, but it can't route by URL or user.

Layer 7: the load balancer reads the HTTP request itself, its path, headers and cookies, so it can send /api to API servers and /images to an image service, and handle TLS. It is smarter, but does more work per request, and it must decrypt the traffic to read it.

draw.answer: The load balancer calls each server's /health endpoint every few seconds. Server 3 failed several checks in a row, so it gets no traffic until it passes again; requests are shared between servers 1 and 2. A good health check also tests what the server needs (can it reach its database?), not just that the process is running.
draw.code:
Clients
                 │
           Load balancer
    ┌────────────┼ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ┐
    │            │             ╎ no traffic
    ▼            ▼             ▼
Server 1     Server 2      Server 3
/health ✓    /health ✓     /health ✗ ✗ ✗
requests     requests      (back in when
1, 3, 5…     2, 4, 6…       it passes again)

apply.answer:
• Identical short API calls: round robin. Every request costs about the same, so taking turns spreads the work evenly, and it is the simplest algorithm. (Least connections works too.)
• Long video uploads: least connections. An upload can last seconds or an hour, so "the same number of requests" is not "the same amount of work". Round robin could stack several long uploads on one server while another sits idle; least connections sends each new upload to the server with the fewest open ones.
• A cache cluster: consistent hashing on the cache key. The same key must always reach the same node, or every request misses (the data is in another node's memory). Consistent hashing also means that adding or removing a node only moves about 1 in n keys, instead of reshuffling almost all of them.

tradeoffs.answer:
Sticky sessions pin each user to the server that served them first. That causes problems:

• Scaling out doesn't help straight away: new servers only get new users, while the existing users stay on the overloaded old servers.
• Uneven load: a few heavy users stuck on one server can overload it while others idle, and the balancer isn't allowed to move them.
• A server dies: everything stored in its memory for its users is lost. They are logged out, lose their basket or their half-filled form.
• Deploys and scaling in are slow: you have to wait for sessions to drain before you can remove a server.

The fix is to make servers stateless: keep sessions in a shared store like Redis (or in a signed token on the client), so any server can serve any request and the balancer is free to spread the load.

topics.name: Caching
topics.definition: A cache keeps a copy of frequently used data in fast storage, usually memory, so it can be served without repeating slow work.
topics.problem: Reading from a database on disk, or recalculating a result, is slow and expensive compared with reading memory. When the same data is read again and again, repeating the work is waste.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as App server
  participant C as Cache (Redis)
  participant D as Database
  A->>C: get product 42
  alt cache hit
    C-->>A: product (under 1 ms)
  else cache miss
    C-->>A: nothing
    A->>D: read product 42
    D-->>A: product (5–20 ms)
    A->>C: store product 42 for 5 minutes
  end
diagram.caption: Cache-aside. The app always asks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database and saves a copy in the cache for next time.

topics.idea: Caches exist at many layers: the browser, the CDN, the application (Redis or Memcached) and the database. The usual pattern is cache-aside: read from the cache; on a miss, read the database and store the result with a TTL. The hard parts are keeping the cache in step with the database (invalidation) and choosing what to remove when it's full (eviction, often LRU).
howItWorks: A request needs product 42. The app asks Redis for the key 'product:42'.
Hit: Redis has it and returns it in under a millisecond.
Miss: the app reads the database (perhaps 5–20 ms), returns the result, and stores it in Redis with a TTL of, say, 5 minutes.
When product 42 changes, the app deletes 'product:42' from Redis, so the next read loads the fresh value.
When Redis is full, it evicts keys, usually the least recently used ones.
Measure the hit rate: 95% means only 1 read in 20 reaches the database.
topics.analogy: Keeping the books you use every day on your desk instead of walking to the library each time.
topics.breaks: Books on your desk don't change by themselves. Data does: when the database changes, your cached copy is stale until it's updated or expires. That's the hardest problem in caching.
topics.example: A product page is read 1,000 times for every update. Cache-aside in Redis with a 5-minute TTL serves almost every read from memory, and the database sees a tiny share of the traffic.
keyPoints: Cache-aside (lazy loading): check the cache → on a miss, load from the database and fill the cache. The most common pattern.
Write-through: write the cache and database together (fresh, but slower writes). Write-back: write the cache, save to the database later (fast, but data can be lost).
Eviction: LRU (least recently used), LFU (least frequently used), TTL expiry.
Invalidation: delete or update the cache entry when the data changes; the TTL is your safety net.
Problems to know: stale data, cache stampede (many misses at once), hot keys, cold start.
Cache only data that is read often and can be slightly out of date.
topics.code:
def get_product(product_id):
    key = f"product:{product_id}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached:
        return cached                          # hit: fast path
    product = db.query_product(product_id)    # miss: slow path
    redis.set(key, product, ex=300)           # keep for 5 minutes
    return product
mistakes: Caching data that changes constantly, or is hardly ever read.
No TTL, so stale data lives forever if one invalidation is missed.
No plan for a stampede when a very popular key expires.
Treating the cache as the source of truth. It can be emptied at any moment.
topics.interviewAnswer: Reads far outnumber writes here, so I'd add a Redis cache using cache-aside with a TTL. On writes I'd delete the cache key so the next read loads fresh data. I'd watch the hit rate, and protect hot keys from stampedes by letting one request rebuild while others wait.

followUps.a: A popular key expires and thousands of requests miss at the same moment and all hit the database. Fixes: let one request rebuild while the others wait, add random jitter to TTLs, or refresh early.

followUps.q: Update or delete the cache on a write?
followUps.a: Usually delete. It's simpler and avoids races where two writers leave an old value behind.

practice.explain: Explain cache-aside step by step, then explain invalidation with the books-on-your-desk picture.
practice.draw: Draw the read path for a cache hit and a cache miss, and the write path that invalidates the cache.
practice.apply: Implement an LRU cache class with get and put in O(1), using a dict and a doubly linked list.
practice.tradeoffs: Compare write-through and write-back: what does each risk, and where would you use each?

explain.answer:
Cache-aside, for "get product 42":
1. Ask the cache for the key product:42.
2. Hit: it is there; return it (under a millisecond).
3. Miss: read the database (5 to 20 ms), return the result, and save a copy in the cache with a TTL, say 5 minutes.
4. When product 42 changes, write the database, then delete product:42 from the cache, so the next read fetches the fresh value.

Invalidation, with books on your desk: you keep the books you use every day on your desk instead of walking to the library. But if the library gets a new edition, the copy on your desk is now out of date, and it won't update itself. Invalidation is the rule for when you take the old copy off your desk: when you hear the library changed it (delete on write), or after a set time anyway (the TTL), in case you missed the news.

draw.answer: Reads go to the cache first and only reach the database on a miss. Writes go to the database (the source of truth) and then delete the cache key, rather than updating it: that avoids two writers racing and leaving an old value behind. The TTL is the safety net if a delete is ever missed.
draw.code:
READ, cache hit
  App ──get product:42──► Cache ── found ──► App   (<1 ms)

READ, cache miss
  App ──get product:42──► Cache ── nothing
  App ──SELECT … id = 42──► Database ──► App  (5–20 ms)
  App ──set product:42, TTL 300 s──► Cache

WRITE
  App ──UPDATE products … id = 42──► Database
  App ──delete product:42──► Cache
  (the next read misses and loads the new value)

apply.answer:
The dict finds a key's node in O(1). The doubly linked list keeps the nodes in order of use, most recent at the front; with links in both directions, a node can be unlinked from the middle in O(1). Two dummy "sentinel" nodes at the ends mean there is never an empty-list special case.

get moves the node to the front. put either updates and moves an existing node, or adds a new one at the front, first removing the node at the back (the least recently used) if the cache is full.
apply.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=None, value=None):
        self.key, self.value = key, value
        self.prev = self.next = None


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.nodes = {}                          # key -> node
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()    # sentinels: head.next is the most recent
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _unlink(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def _push_front(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        node = self.nodes.get(key)
        if node is None:
            return None
        self._unlink(node)
        self._push_front(node)                   # now the most recently used
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.nodes:
            node = self.nodes[key]
            node.value = value
            self._unlink(node)
            self._push_front(node)
            return
        if len(self.nodes) == self.capacity:
            oldest = self.tail.prev              # least recently used
            self._unlink(oldest)
            del self.nodes[oldest.key]
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.nodes[key] = node
        self._push_front(node)


cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put("a", 1)
cache.put("b", 2)
print(cache.get("a"))      # 1     a is now the most recent
cache.put("c", 3)          # full: evicts b, the least recently used
print(cache.get("b"))      # None
print(cache.get("c"))      # 3
cache.put("a", 10)         # update: a moves to the front
cache.put("d", 4)          # evicts c
print(cache.get("c"), cache.get("a"), cache.get("d"))   # None 10 4

tradeoffs.answer:
Write-through: every write goes to the cache and the database together, and is confirmed only when both have it.
• Risks: slower writes (two stores per write), and filling the cache with data nobody reads. If the two writes aren't atomic, a failure between them can leave them disagreeing.
• Use it when reads must be fresh straight after a write and writes are fairly rare: user profiles, product details, settings.

Write-back (write-behind): writes go to the cache only, and are saved to the database later, in batches.
• Risks: losing data. If the cache crashes before it flushes, those writes are gone. The database is also behind, so anything reading it directly sees old data.
• Use it when writes are very frequent and losing a few is acceptable: view counters, likes, game scores, metrics. You trade some durability for very fast writes and far fewer database writes.

Money, orders and anything you can't lose should never be write-back.

topics.name: Consistency, CAP and PACELC
topics.definition: Consistency (in distributed systems) means every read sees the latest write. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability.
topics.problem: To survive failures and be fast for users everywhere, you keep copies of data on several machines. But copies can't all change at exactly the same instant, and the network between them can break. You must decide what users see in that gap.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD U["User withdraws £80 in London"] --> L["London copy
balance £100"] L ---|"network broken ✗"| P["Paris copy
balance £100"] L --> CP["CP choice: refuse until Paris confirms
always correct, some requests fail"] L --> AP["AP choice: accept, London shows £20
always answers, copies may disagree"]
diagram.caption: The network between the two copies is broken. The system must either refuse (stay consistent) or accept and risk the copies disagreeing (stay available).

topics.idea: When data is copied across machines, the copies can briefly disagree. Strong consistency makes every read return the latest value, but may have to refuse requests when machines can't talk to each other. Eventual consistency always answers, but a read can be briefly out of date. Network partitions will happen, so the real choice is C or A during a partition. PACELC adds: else (normally), you trade latency against consistency.
howItWorks: Picture two replicas, in London and Paris, each holding a balance of £100.
The network between them breaks: a partition. A user in London withdraws £80.
CP choice: London refuses, or only accepts if it can confirm with Paris. Always correct, but some requests fail until the network heals.

AP choice: London accepts and records £20, while Paris still says £100. Both keep answering, but a second £80 withdrawal in Paris would overdraw the account. When the network heals, the system must reconcile the two.
With no partition (normal running), waiting for both copies before confirming is consistent but slower. That's the latency-versus-consistency trade-off in PACELC.
topics.analogy: Two bank branches whose phone line is cut. Either they stop withdrawals until the line is back (consistency), or they keep serving customers and reconcile later, risking an overdrawn account (availability).
topics.breaks: A bank makes this choice once, as a policy. Real systems choose per operation: a social feed can be eventually consistent while the payment inside the same app must be strongly consistent.
topics.example: Bank balance: strong consistency (CP). Likes on a post: eventual consistency (AP); nobody minds seeing 1,203 instead of 1,205 for a second.
keyPoints: C = every read sees the latest write; A = every request gets a non-error response; P = the system keeps working when messages between machines are lost.
Partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, so it's CP or AP during a partition.
Consistency levels: strong, read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads, eventual.
Quorums: with N copies, writing to W and reading from R where W + R > N means every read overlaps the latest write.
PACELC: even without partitions, stronger consistency costs latency.
CAP's C is not ACID's C (which is about the database's rules and constraints).
tradeOffs: CP: correct, but may reject requests during a partition (bank ledger).
AP: always answers, but may return stale data and needs conflict handling (shopping cart, likes).
mistakes: Calling a system 'CA'. With replicas, partitions can't be wished away.
Treating CAP as one choice for the whole system, instead of a choice per type of data.
Confusing CAP's consistency with ACID's consistency.
topics.interviewAnswer: It depends on the data. For money or stock levels I'd choose strong consistency, accepting that some requests fail during a partition. For feeds, likes or view counts I'd choose availability with eventual consistency, because a slightly stale number is harmless and the system stays up.

followUps.q: Is a single-server SQL database CP or AP?
followUps.a: CAP is about distributed systems with replicas. One server has no partition between copies; with replicas, it depends on how replication and failover are set up.
If every write reaches W copies and every read checks R copies, and W + R > N, at least one copy you read must have the latest write.

practice.explain: Explain CAP with the two-bank-branches picture, and why 'CA' isn't a real choice for distributed systems.
practice.draw: Draw two replicas separated by a partition, and show what a CP system and an AP system each do with a write.
practice.apply: Label each as needing strong or eventual consistency: bank balance, Instagram likes, cinema seat booking, profile picture, stock level at checkout.
practice.tradeoffs: With N = 3 copies, compare W = 3, R = 1 with W = 2, R = 2. What does each favour?

resources.title: Distributed Systems lecture series: consistency and consensus
resources.source: Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge · free on YouTube

explain.answer:
Two branches of a bank share every account, and the phone line between them is cut (a network partition). A customer asks the London branch to withdraw £80 from an account holding £100. London can't check with Paris. It has two choices:

• Consistency (CP): refuse, or wait, until the line is back. Every answer it gives is correct, but some customers are turned away.
• Availability (AP): pay out and note it down, and sort things out with Paris later. Everyone is served, but Paris still thinks the balance is £100, so the account could be overdrawn twice over.

Why "CA" isn't a real choice: CA would mean "consistent and available, as long as there are no partitions". But once data lives on more than one machine, the network between them will fail sometimes; you can't choose to have no partitions. So the real question is only what you do when one happens: refuse (C) or answer (A). A single machine is "CA" only because it has nothing to be partitioned from.

draw.answer: The partition is the same in both pictures; the only difference is whether the replica that can't reach the other one keeps accepting writes.
draw.code:
Replica A  ══ ✗ partition ✗ ══  Replica B
(London)                        (Paris)
balance £100                    balance £100

Write: "withdraw £80" arrives at A

CP system
  A can't confirm with B
  → refuses (or waits): error to the user
  → both still say £100: correct, not available

AP system
  A accepts → A says £20, B still says £100
  → the user gets an answer: available
  → copies disagree until the partition heals,
    then they must be reconciled

apply.answer:
• Bank balance: strong. A stale balance lets someone spend the same money twice.
• Instagram likes: eventual. Seeing 1,203 instead of 1,205 for a second harms nobody, and the counter must stay up under huge load.
• Cinema seat booking: strong. Two people must never both get seat F12; the booking must be checked against the latest state (a transaction, or a conditional write).
• Profile picture: eventual, with one exception: the person who changed it should see their own change straight away (read-your-own-writes). Everyone else can catch up in a few seconds.
• Stock level at checkout: strong at the moment of buying (decrement only if stock > 0, atomically), so you never sell the last item twice. The "only 3 left" shown while browsing can be eventual.

tradeoffs.answer:
With N = 3 copies, both settings satisfy W + R > N (3 + 1 = 4, 2 + 2 = 4), so every read overlaps the latest write. What differs is speed and what survives a failure.

W = 3, R = 1:
• Reads are as fast as possible: any one copy will do.
• Writes are slow (they wait for the slowest copy) and fail if any one of the three copies is down.
• It favours read-heavy data that is rarely written, where losing write availability briefly is acceptable.

W = 2, R = 2:
• Both reads and writes wait for two copies: balanced latency.
• Both keep working with one copy down.
• It favours availability, and workloads with a fair mix of reads and writes. This is the common default (a "quorum" of 2 out of 3).

(Going further, W = 1, R = 1 is fastest of all, but 1 + 1 is not more than 3, so reads can be stale: eventual consistency.)

topics.name: Rate limiting and backpressure
topics.definition: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window. Backpressure is a system telling the senders upstream to slow down when it's overloaded.
topics.problem: Without limits, one buggy script, scraper or attacker can send so many requests that everyone else gets errors. And a system that accepts more work than it can do eventually collapses for everyone.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR R["Request from key K"] --> G["Gateway"] G --> D{"Token left in K's bucket?
(kept in Redis)"} D -->|"yes: take 1"| S["Service handles it"] D -->|"no"| X["429 Too Many Requests"] T["Refill: +10 tokens a second,
max 20"] -.-> D
diagram.caption: Each client has a bucket of tokens. A request spends one token; an empty bucket means the request is rejected until the bucket refills.

topics.idea: Rate limits protect services from abuse, bugs and traffic spikes, and enforce fair use, like 100 requests per minute per user. Requests over the limit get HTTP 429. Common algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window and sliding window. Backpressure goes further: queues have size limits, and when they fill, senders are told to wait or requests are dropped on purpose, instead of the whole system falling over.
howItWorks: Choose the rule: for example, 10 requests per second per API key, with bursts of up to 20.
Token bucket: each key has a bucket that holds up to 20 tokens and gains 10 tokens every second.
Each request takes one token. If a token is there, the request goes through.
If the bucket is empty, reply 429 Too Many Requests, with 'Retry-After: 1'.
With many gateway servers, keep each bucket in Redis and update it atomically, so every server shares the same count.
Inside the system, backpressure: when a work queue reaches its limit, stop accepting new work (or drop the least important) instead of letting the queue grow forever.
topics.analogy: A nightclub bouncer lets in a few people per minute (rate limiting). When the club is full, the queue outside stops moving (backpressure).
topics.breaks: A bouncer is one person at one door. A real service runs on many servers, so the limit must be shared between them, usually with counters in Redis, and that shared store must be fast and always available.
topics.example: Token bucket: each user's bucket holds up to 10 tokens and refills at 1 token per second. Each request takes a token; an empty bucket means 429 Too Many Requests. Short bursts are allowed; sustained abuse isn't.
keyPoints: Token bucket: allows bursts up to the bucket size, with a steady refill rate. The most common.
Leaky bucket: processes requests at a fixed rate; smooths out bursts.
Fixed window: a simple counter per minute, but allows double bursts at the window edges.
Sliding window (log or counter): smoother and fairer, slightly more work.
Limit by user, API key or IP address; return 429 with a Retry-After header.
Backpressure: bounded queues, load shedding, and signalling clients to slow down.
mistakes: Limiting per server instead of across all servers.
One global limit, so a single heavy user blocks everyone else.
Unbounded queues that hide overload until memory runs out.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd rate-limit at the API gateway with a token bucket per user or API key, keeping the counters in Redis so every gateway node shares them, and return 429 with Retry-After. Internally I'd use bounded queues and load shedding, so overload slows the system down gracefully instead of crashing it.

followUps.q: Why is the fixed window unfair?
followUps.a: A client can send the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00, doubling the real rate across the boundary.
Decide to fail open (allow requests and risk abuse) or fail closed (block and risk an outage), per API. Many systems fail open with a local backup limit.

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a rate limiter
Using load shedding to avoid overload

explain.answer:
The nightclub bouncer has a bowl of wristbands, and you need one to get in. The bowl holds at most 20, and a helper drops in 10 new ones every second.

• A group of 15 arrives at once: there are wristbands in the bowl, so they all go in. Short bursts are fine, up to the size of the bowl.
• A crowd keeps arriving faster than 10 a second: the bowl empties, and people are turned away until new wristbands drop in (HTTP 429, "come back in a second").
• Over time, nobody gets in faster than 10 a second on average: the refill rate.

That is the token bucket: capacity = the most you allow in a burst; refill rate = the steady limit. Each request spends one token.

draw.answer: The limit is checked once, at the gateway, before any work is done. The counters live in Redis, not in each gateway's memory, so the limit holds no matter which gateway a request lands on. Inside, a bounded queue in front of each service gives backpressure: when it is full, new work is refused instead of piling up.
draw.code:
Clients
  │
  ▼
Load balancer
  ├────────────┬────────────┐
  ▼            ▼            ▼
Gateway 1   Gateway 2   Gateway 3
  │  1. take a token for this
  │     API key (atomic, shared)
  ├───────────────────────► Redis
  │  ◄── allowed / empty ──┘ (one bucket
  │                           per key)
  ├─ empty   → 429, Retry-After: 1
  └─ allowed → service (via a bounded queue)

apply.answer:
Both limiters allow 10 requests a second, and both use a fake clock so the result is the same every run.

A burst of 50 requests in half a second: the fixed window lets the first 10 through and blocks the rest of that second. The token bucket lets 14 through: its 10 stored tokens at once, then about one more every 100 ms as tokens refill.

The real difference is at a window edge. 20 requests between 0.9 s and 1.1 s: the fixed window allows all 20 (10 at the end of the first second, 10 at the start of the next), double the limit in 0.2 seconds. The token bucket allows only 11, because tokens don't reset at a boundary; they only refill at the steady rate.
apply.code:
class FixedWindow:
    def __init__(self, limit, window, clock):
        self.limit, self.window, self.clock = limit, window, clock
        self.current, self.count = None, 0

    def allow(self):
        window = int(self.clock() // self.window)
        if window != self.current:                  # a new window: reset
            self.current, self.count = window, 0
        if self.count < self.limit:
            self.count += 1
            return True
        return False


class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_sec, clock):
        self.capacity, self.rate, self.clock = capacity, refill_per_sec, clock
        self.tokens, self.last = capacity, clock()

    def allow(self):
        now = self.clock()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False


def run(times):
    now = [0.0]
    clock = lambda: now[0]
    fixed = FixedWindow(limit=10, window=1.0, clock=clock)
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=10, refill_per_sec=10, clock=clock)
    fixed_ok = bucket_ok = 0
    for t in times:
        now[0] = t
        fixed_ok += fixed.allow()
        bucket_ok += bucket.allow()
    return fixed_ok, bucket_ok


burst = [i * 0.01 for i in range(50)]              # 50 requests in 0.5 s
edge = [0.9 + i * 0.01 for i in range(20)]         # 20 requests from 0.9 s to 1.1 s
print("burst of 50:", run(burst))                  # (10, 14): fixed window, token bucket
print("20 across the 1 s edge:", run(edge))       # (20, 11)

tradeoffs.answer:
Login endpoint: don't fail fully open. The limit there is a security control: it is what slows down password guessing and credential stuffing, and attackers look for exactly this kind of gap. Fall back to a strict limit kept in each gateway's own memory (for example, 5 attempts a minute per IP and per account, per server). That is weaker than the shared limit, but far from no limit. If even that isn't possible, fail closed: a short login outage is visible and recoverable; a successful mass account takeover is not.

Public search API: fail open, with a generous local limit as a backup. Here the limit protects capacity, not secrets. The worst case of failing open is extra load, which autoscaling and load shedding can absorb, while failing closed would turn a Redis problem into an outage for every user.

The principle: decide per endpoint, by asking which is worse, abuse getting through or real users being blocked.

topics.name: Asynchronous processing and message queues (Kafka, SQS)
topics.definition: Asynchronous processing means doing slow work later, outside the user's request. A message queue holds the work, or events, between the service that produces them and the services that consume them.
topics.problem: Some work is slow (encoding video, sending emails) or comes in bursts (a sale doubles traffic). Doing it inside the user's request makes them wait, and a burst can overwhelm the services behind it.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  API["API server"] -->|"1 put message"| Q[["Queue"]]
  API -->|"2 reply: 202 Accepted"| U["User"]
  Q -->|"3 pull a job"| W1["Worker"]
  Q --> W2["Worker"]
  W1 -->|"4 done: acknowledge"| Q
  Q -.->|"failed too often"| DLQ[["Dead-letter queue"]]
diagram.caption: The API replies at once and leaves the slow work on the queue. Workers take jobs at their own pace; a job is removed only after the worker says it's done.

topics.idea: Instead of making a user wait while you send emails, resize images and update analytics, you put a message on a queue and reply straight away. Workers process messages at their own pace. Queues absorb spikes, decouple services and let you retry failures. SQS-style queues give each message to one worker; Kafka keeps an ordered log that many groups of consumers can read, and re-read.
howItWorks: A user uploads a video. The API stores the file and puts a message {video_id: 42} on a queue.
The API replies straight away: '202 Accepted, processing'.
Worker processes pull messages from the queue. One worker takes message 42 and converts the video.
When it's done, the worker acknowledges the message, and only then is it removed. If the worker crashes first, the message becomes visible again and another worker retries it.
If it fails too many times, it moves to a dead-letter queue for a person to inspect.
If 10,000 uploads arrive at once, they simply wait in the queue; you add workers to clear it faster.
topics.analogy: A restaurant's order rail. The waiter clips the order on the rail and goes back to the customers; the cooks take orders when they're ready.
topics.breaks: A paper order is taken by exactly one cook and then it's gone. Most queues only promise 'at least once' delivery, so a message can arrive twice and consumers must be idempotent. And Kafka keeps messages after they're read, so others can read them again.
topics.example: Upload a video: the API saves the file, puts a 'video uploaded' message on a queue, and replies 202 Accepted. Workers convert it into several resolutions, and the user is notified when it's ready.
keyPoints: Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): spreads work; each message is consumed once, then deleted.
Log or stream (Kafka): ordered, durable, replayable; partitions give order per key and parallel processing.
Delivery guarantees: at most once, at least once (the most common), exactly once (hard; usually 'effectively once' with idempotent consumers).
Dead-letter queue: where messages go after failing too many times.
Pub/sub: one event fans out to many subscribers.
Async means eventual: the user sees 'processing', not the final result straight away.
tradeOffs: Pros: absorbs spikes, decouples services, makes retries easy.
Cons: more moving parts, harder debugging, eventual consistency, and you must handle ordering and duplicates.
mistakes: Assuming each message arrives exactly once. It can arrive twice, so make processing idempotent.
Expecting order across a whole Kafka topic. Order is only kept within one partition.
Using a queue where the user needs an immediate answer.
topics.interviewAnswer: Slow or non-critical work goes on a queue so the request stays fast. For simple task distribution I'd use a queue like SQS with a dead-letter queue. For event streams that many services need, or that I may want to replay, I'd use Kafka, partitioned by a key like user ID to keep each user's events in order. Consumers are idempotent, because delivery is at least once.

followUps.a: SQS: a simple managed queue, each message handled once, no replay. Kafka: a high-throughput ordered log with many independent consumers, replay, and ordering within a partition.

followUps.q: How do you keep messages in order?
followUps.a: Send all messages with the same key (like an order ID) to the same partition. Order is only guaranteed within a partition.

practice.explain: Explain why asynchronous processing makes an API faster, with the order-rail picture.
practice.draw: Draw producer → queue → worker pool → database, plus a dead-letter queue.
practice.apply: Build a tiny producer and consumer with Python's queue module and threads. Make a consumer crash halfway, and show how a message could be processed twice.
practice.tradeoffs: When should something NOT be asynchronous? Give an example where the user must wait for the result.

explain.answer:
Picture a restaurant's order rail. The waiter writes the order, clips it on the rail and goes straight back to the customers: the waiter doesn't stand in the kitchen while the food cooks. The cooks take orders off the rail when they are ready.

An API works the same way. Without a queue, the request does everything before replying (save the video, encode it, email the user), and the user waits the whole time. With a queue, the API does only the essential part (save the file, put "encode video 42" on the queue) and replies at once: "202 Accepted, processing". Workers do the slow part in the background.

The API is faster because the user waits only for the fast part. It is also steadier: a rush of orders just makes the rail longer, instead of overwhelming the kitchen.

draw.answer: The producer only writes to the queue and replies; it never waits for the workers. A worker deletes a message only after the work is safely in the database (it acknowledges it). A message that keeps failing is moved aside to the dead-letter queue, so it can't block or crash the workers forever.
draw.code:
Producer (API)
  │ 1. put message
  ▼
Queue ═══════════════════════════
  │ 2. each worker pulls one job
  ├──────────┬──────────┐
  ▼          ▼          ▼
Worker     Worker     Worker
  │ 3. do the work, save the result
  ▼
Database
  4. acknowledge → message deleted

failed 5 times? ──► Dead-letter queue
                    (a person looks at it)

apply.answer:
Python's queue.Queue forgets a message as soon as get() returns, so the code wraps it in a queue that, like SQS, only deletes a message when the worker acknowledges it. Unacknowledged messages come back (what a visibility timeout does).

The first worker sends emails 1, 2 and 3, but crashes after sending email 3 and before acknowledging it. The queue can't tell "crashed before doing the work" from "crashed after", so it delivers message 3 again, and the second worker sends user 3 a second email. That is at-least-once delivery.

The fix is an idempotent consumer: remember which message IDs have been handled, and skip repeats. In a real system that record must be saved in the same transaction as the work's effect (or passed to the email provider as an idempotency key); otherwise a crash between "send" and "remember" still sends twice.
apply.code:
import queue
import threading


class AtLeastOnceQueue:
    """A message is deleted only when a worker acknowledges it."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.ready = queue.Queue()
        self.in_flight = {}                      # message id -> message
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def put(self, message):
        self.ready.put(message)

    def get(self):
        message = self.ready.get_nowait()        # raises queue.Empty when done
        with self.lock:
            self.in_flight[message["id"]] = message
        return message

    def ack(self, message_id):
        with self.lock:
            del self.in_flight[message_id]

    def redeliver_unacked(self):                 # what a visibility timeout does
        with self.lock:
            for message in self.in_flight.values():
                self.ready.put(message)
            self.in_flight.clear()


def worker(q, handle, crash_on=None):
    while True:
        try:
            message = q.get()
        except queue.Empty:
            return
        handle(message)                          # the work is done...
        if message["id"] == crash_on:
            return                               # ...but the worker dies before it acks
        q.ack(message["id"])


def run(handle):
    q = AtLeastOnceQueue()
    for i in range(1, 6):
        q.put({"id": i, "to": f"user{i}@mail.com"})
    first = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(q, handle), kwargs={"crash_on": 3})
    first.start(); first.join()                  # handles 1, 2, 3, then crashes
    q.redeliver_unacked()                        # 3 was never acked, so it comes back
    second = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(q, handle))
    second.start(); second.join()


sent = []
run(lambda message: sent.append(message["id"]))
print(sent)                                      # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3]: user 3 got two emails

sent, handled = [], set()

def send_once(message):                          # idempotent consumer
    if message["id"] in handled:
        return
    sent.append(message["id"])
    handled.add(message["id"])

run(send_once)
print(sent)                                      # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

tradeoffs.answer:
Keep something synchronous when the user can't continue without the result, or when the next step depends on it:

• Payment authorisation at checkout: the user must know "approved" or "declined" before seeing the confirmation page. You can't say "order placed!" and decline the card later.
• Logging in: you can't show the account until the password has been checked.
• Booking a seat: "is F12 still free?" must be answered before you take the money.
• Validating input: tell the user their form is wrong now, not by email in five minutes.
• Reading data: "show my order history" is a read; there is nothing to defer.

Async also costs something: more moving parts, harder debugging, and the user sees "processing" instead of a result. So use a queue for slow or non-essential work after the critical step (sending the receipt, updating analytics, encoding the video), not for the critical step itself.

topics.name: Observability: logs, metrics and traces
topics.definition: Observability is how well you can understand what a system is doing from the outside, using logs, metrics and traces.
topics.problem: When something goes wrong in a system of many services, you can't attach a debugger to production. Without data coming out of the system, you're guessing.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Request
trace ID abc123"] --> G["Gateway
12 ms"] G --> O["Order service
40 ms"] O --> P["Payment service
1,600 ms ⚠"] O & P --> M["Metrics
dashboards and alerts"] O & P --> L["Logs
tagged with the trace ID"]
diagram.caption: One request's trace shows the time spent in each service, which points straight at the slow one. Metrics and logs from every service carry the same trace ID.

topics.idea: Metrics are numbers over time (requests per second, error rate, latency percentiles), used for dashboards and alerts. Logs are detailed records of events, used for investigating. Traces follow one request across many services and show where the time went. Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, latency against your SLO), not on every CPU blip.
howItWorks: Metrics: every service counts requests, errors and latency, and exports them every few seconds. Dashboards show trends; an alert fires when, say, the error rate stays above 1% for 5 minutes.
Logs: each important event is written as structured JSON, including the request's trace ID, the user ID and timings.
Traces: the first service creates a trace ID and passes it in a header to every service it calls. Each service records how long its part took.
Investigating: the alert tells you something is wrong, the dashboard shows when it started, a trace shows which service is slow, and that service's logs show why.
topics.analogy: A car: the dashboard is metrics, the service history is logs, and a GPS replay of one journey is a trace.
topics.breaks: A car is one machine. A request may cross 20 services, so without a shared trace ID to join the logs together, you can't follow it.
topics.example: The p99 checkout latency jumps from 300 ms to 2 s. The dashboard shows when; a trace shows 1.6 s spent in the payment service's database call; that service's logs show a lock timeout.
keyPoints: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
Use percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages; averages hide the slow users.
Structured logs (JSON), with a request or trace ID on every line.
Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) shows the time spent in each service.
Alert on SLO burn (user impact), and give every alert a runbook.
Health checks and a dashboard per service.
mistakes: Alerting on causes (CPU at 80%) instead of symptoms users feel (errors, slow responses).
Logs without a request or trace ID, so you can't connect them.
Watching averages instead of percentiles.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd emit the four golden signals as metrics for each service, write structured logs with a trace ID, and use distributed tracing to follow requests across services. Alerts fire on user-facing symptoms, like p99 latency or error rate breaking the SLO, so on-call engineers are paged only for real problems.

followUps.q: Why p99 instead of the average?
followUps.a: The average can look fine while 1% of users wait seconds. At scale, that 1% is a lot of people, and often your heaviest users.
Monitoring checks for known failures with dashboards and alerts. Observability lets you ask new questions about failures you didn't predict.

practice.explain: Explain logs, metrics and traces with the car picture.
practice.draw: Draw one request crossing 3 services, and show where the trace ID is passed along.
practice.apply: Choose 4 metrics and 2 alerts, with thresholds, for a payment API.
practice.tradeoffs: Logging everything at debug level in production: what does it cost, and what would you do instead?

resources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch 6 (monitoring distributed systems)

explain.answer:
• Metrics are the car's dashboard: a few numbers, updated all the time (speed, fuel, engine temperature). For a service: requests per second, error rate, latency percentiles. You glance at them to see if anything is wrong, and warning lights (alerts) go on when a number crosses a line.
• Logs are the car's service history: a detailed record of individual events ("12:03: brake pads replaced"). For a service: "order 77 failed: card declined". You read them when you investigate a particular problem.
• A trace is a GPS replay of one journey: exactly where you went and how long each part took. For a request: it entered the gateway, spent 40 ms in orders, then 1.6 s in payments. It shows where the time went.

Where the picture breaks: a car is one machine. One request can cross twenty services, so each one must pass on a shared trace ID, or you can't join the pieces together.

draw.answer: The first service that sees the request creates the trace ID and passes it on in a header (traceparent, in OpenTelemetry) on every call it makes. Every service records its own span (start, duration) under that ID and adds the ID to every log line, so one search finds the whole journey.
draw.code:
Client
  │ GET /checkout
  ▼
Gateway ── creates trace ID abc123
  │ header traceparent: abc123
  ▼                           span: gateway, 12 ms
Order service
  │ header traceparent: abc123
  ▼                           span: orders, 40 ms
Payment service               span: payments, 1,600 ms ⚠

Every log line: {"trace_id": "abc123", ...}
All spans → tracing backend → one timeline

apply.answer:
Four metrics (per endpoint, every few seconds):
1. Traffic: requests per second, split by endpoint and status code.
2. Errors: the share of requests ending in a 5xx (the payment service's fault), kept separate from card declines (normal business results, not errors).
3. Latency: p50, p95 and p99 of request time, plus the latency of calls to the card network or payment provider.
4. Saturation: how full the database connection pool and the worker queue are.

Two alerts (each pages someone, and links to a runbook):
1. Error rate: 5xx above 1% of requests for 5 minutes in a row. Payments failing is the most important symptom.
2. Latency: p99 above 2 seconds for 10 minutes. Users abandon slow checkouts, and slow payments often mean a provider problem.

A useful third, as a warning rather than a page: the authorisation success rate falls more than 10% below its normal level for this time of day, which can mean a provider or fraud-rule problem even when nothing is erroring.

tradeoffs.answer:
What it costs:
• Money and storage: debug logging can easily write 20 lines per request. At 10,000 requests a second and 500 bytes a line, that is 100 MB a second, about 8.6 TB a day, all paid for in ingestion, indexing and storage.
• Speed: writing and shipping all that uses CPU, disk and network on every server, and adds latency.
• Noise: the important lines are buried, so investigations get slower, not faster.
• Risk: debug logs tend to include request bodies, so tokens, card numbers and personal data end up in a system with weaker controls.

Instead:
• Log at INFO by default, as structured JSON with the trace ID, and only for meaningful events.
• Log every error, but sample the successes (say 1%).
• Make the log level changeable at runtime, for one service or even one user, so you can turn on debug only while investigating.
• Use metrics for counting and traces (with sampling that keeps the slow and failed ones) for timing, instead of logging both.
• Mask sensitive fields before they are written.
tradeoffs.code:
requests_per_s, lines, bytes_per_line = 10_000, 20, 500
mb_per_s = requests_per_s * lines * bytes_per_line / 1e6
tb_per_day = mb_per_s * 86_400 / 1e6
print(mb_per_s, round(tb_per_day, 2))          # 100.0 8.64

phases.title: Data: databases, storage and scaling data
phases.goal: Choose the right database, keep data correct with transactions, make queries fast with indexes, and scale data with replication and sharding.
phases.bigPicture: App servers are easy to scale; data is not. Most deep dives in interviews end up here: which store, which key, how many copies, how to split it, and what consistency you promise.

topics.name: SQL vs NoSQL: choosing a database
topics.definition: SQL (relational) databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and support joins and transactions. NoSQL is a family of other models: key-value, document, wide-column and graph.
topics.problem: Different data and different access patterns need different storage. A wrong choice hurts later: slow queries, joins you can't do, or a database that can't keep up with the writes.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD Q{"What do the main reads
and writes look like?"} Q -->|"joins, transactions"| SQL["SQL
PostgreSQL, MySQL"] Q -->|"one key, very fast"| KV["Key-value
Redis, DynamoDB"] Q -->|"self-contained records"| DOC["Document
MongoDB"] Q -->|"huge writes, read by one key"| WC["Wide-column
Cassandra"] Q -->|"relationships"| GR["Graph
Neo4j"]
diagram.caption: Start from how the data is used, then follow the matching arrow to a kind of database.

topics.idea: Start from your data and how it's accessed. Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) suit structured data with relationships and strong consistency. Key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) give fast lookups by key. Document stores (MongoDB) hold flexible JSON-like records. Wide-column stores (Cassandra) handle huge write volumes. Graph databases (Neo4j) suit highly connected data like social networks.
howItWorks: List the main queries: 'get a user's last 20 orders', 'find all messages in a chat by time', 'count the likes on a post'.
If you need joins, transactions and flexible queries over structured data, start with SQL.
If one simple lookup by key dominates, and must be extremely fast or enormous, consider a key-value store.
If each record is a self-contained document with varying fields, consider a document store.
If writes are massive and reads always follow one key (like chat messages by conversation), consider a wide-column store.
If the questions are about relationships ('friends of friends who like X'), consider a graph database.
topics.analogy: SQL is a well-organised filing cabinet with labelled folders and cross-references. NoSQL is a set of specialised containers: a key rack, a box of folders, a giant ledger, a map of connections.
topics.breaks: A filing cabinet can't grow past the office. Relational databases actually scale a long way with replicas and sharding, and many NoSQL stores now support transactions. The line is blurrier than the slogan.
topics.example: An online shop: orders and payments in PostgreSQL (transactions matter); shopping carts and sessions in a key-value store (fast and simple); product search in Elasticsearch; 'people also bought' in a precomputed table or a graph.
keyPoints: Choose by access pattern: what are the main reads and writes, and by which key?
SQL: joins, ACID transactions, a strict schema; scales with replicas and, with more effort, sharding.
Key-value: very fast by key, no complex queries. Document: flexible schema, nested data.
Wide-column (Cassandra): massive write volume; queries designed around the partition key.
Graph: relationships first (friends of friends).
Default in most interviews: start with SQL unless there's a clear reason not to.
Hands-on: the SQL tab teaches the language itself, from SELECT to window functions, with every query runnable.
tradeOffs: SQL: flexible queries and strong guarantees, but harder to scale writes horizontally.
NoSQL: easy scale-out for specific patterns, but limited queries, and you must design around access patterns up front.
mistakes: Choosing NoSQL because it 'scales', without checking the queries you need.
Designing a NoSQL schema like SQL tables, then needing joins.
Forgetting that different parts of one system can use different databases.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd choose based on the access patterns. For orders and payments with relationships and transactions, PostgreSQL. For very high write volume with simple key-based reads, like chat messages, a wide-column store like Cassandra. For sessions and hot data, Redis. Using different stores for different jobs is normal.

followUps.q: Why might chat messages go in Cassandra?
followUps.a: Huge write volume, always read by conversation and time: a natural partition key and sort order, with easy horizontal scaling.
No. It's fast for the access pattern it was designed for. Unplanned queries and joins can be slow or impossible.

practice.explain: Explain the four NoSQL types with one good use for each.
practice.draw: Draw the tables for users, orders and order items, with keys and relationships.
practice.apply: Pick a database for: a bank ledger, IoT sensor readings, user sessions, a social graph, a product catalogue. Justify each.
practice.tradeoffs: A startup used MongoDB for everything and now needs reports that join 5 collections. What went wrong, and what would you do?

resources.title: CMU 15-445 Intro to Database Systems: data models and query languages
resources.source: Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon · free on YouTube

explain.answer:
• Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): a giant dictionary; give it a key, get a value back, very fast. Good for: user sessions, a cache, a shopping cart.
• Document (MongoDB): each record is a JSON-like document, and records can have different fields. Good for: a product catalogue, where a shirt has sizes and a laptop has RAM.
• Wide-column (Cassandra): rows grouped by a partition key and sorted inside it, built for enormous write volumes spread over many machines. Good for: chat messages by conversation, or sensor readings by device and time.
• Graph (Neo4j): nodes and the relationships between them are stored directly, so following links is cheap. Good for: a social network ("friends of friends who like X"), or spotting fraud rings.

draw.answer: One user has many orders, and one order has many item lines; order_items is keyed by the pair (order_id, product_id). Two details worth saying out loud: the item keeps the price at the time of purchase (product prices change later), and orders get an index on (user_id, created_at) for "my latest orders".
draw.code:
users
  user_id       PK
  email         UNIQUE, NOT NULL
  name
  created_at
     │ 1
     │
     │ many
orders
  order_id      PK
  user_id       FK → users.user_id
  status
  total_pence
  created_at
     │ 1
     │
     │ many
order_items
  order_id      PK (part 1), FK → orders
  product_id    PK (part 2), FK → products
  quantity
  unit_price_pence   (the price when bought)

apply.answer:
• Bank ledger: relational (PostgreSQL). Money needs ACID transactions (a transfer is two changes that must both happen), constraints (no negative balance), and exact reports. Correctness matters far more than raw scale.
• IoT sensor readings: a time-series database (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB), or wide-column (Cassandra) partitioned by (sensor, day). Huge numbers of small writes, always appended, read by sensor and time range, and old data is downsampled or deleted.
• User sessions: key-value (Redis). Looked up by session ID on every request, must be very fast, and expire on their own (a TTL). Losing one just means logging in again.
• Social graph: a graph database (Neo4j) for queries several hops deep. At very large scale, many companies keep each user's list of friends in a sharded key-value or wide-column store, and precompute the expensive questions.
• Product catalogue: a document store (MongoDB), or PostgreSQL with JSONB columns, because products have different attributes. Search over it goes in a search engine (Elasticsearch), fed from the main store.

tradeoffs.answer:
What went wrong: the database was chosen for "it scales" rather than for how the data is used. Users, orders, products and payments are relational data, connected by keys, and reports are exactly the cross-collection joins MongoDB is weakest at. So now there are slow $lookup chains, copies of the same data in several documents drifting apart, and reports run against the production database.

What to do:
1. Short term: don't run reports on production. Stream every change (MongoDB change streams) into a relational warehouse (PostgreSQL, BigQuery or Snowflake) and run the five-way joins there. Reports become fast and safe, and nothing in the app changes.
2. Longer term: move the core relational data (orders, payments) into PostgreSQL, where joins and transactions are natural, one part at a time. Keep MongoDB where it fits, such as the flexible product catalogue.

The lesson: choose the store per kind of data, from its access patterns, and expect reporting to need its own copy of the data.

topics.name: ACID transactions and isolation levels
topics.definition: A transaction groups several operations so they succeed or fail together. ACID stands for Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
topics.problem: Real operations change several things at once: take money from A, give it to B. If the system crashes halfway, or two users act at the same moment, money can be created or destroyed.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant DB as Database
  App->>DB: BEGIN
  App->>DB: take £100 from A (only if A has it)
  App->>DB: add £100 to B
  alt everything worked
    App->>DB: COMMIT - both changes are saved
  else something failed
    App->>DB: ROLLBACK - neither change happens
  end
diagram.caption: A transfer is one transaction: it either commits completely or rolls back completely, so money is never lost or created.

topics.idea: Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: the database moves from one valid state to another, so its rules always hold. Isolated: transactions running at the same time don't see each other's half-finished work. Durable: once committed, the change survives a crash. Isolation comes in levels — read committed, repeatable read, serializable — trading safety for speed.
howItWorks: BEGIN starts a transaction. Changes are made, but other users can't see them yet (isolation).
The database writes each change to a write-ahead log on disk.
COMMIT: the log is saved to disk, and only then is success reported. After a crash, the database replays the log, so committed changes survive (durability).
ROLLBACK, or a crash before COMMIT: every change in the transaction is undone (atomicity).
