resources.title: Raft, visualised
resources.source: The Secret Lives of Data, free

resources.title: Distributed Systems lecture series: consistency and consensus
resources.source: Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge · free on YouTube

explain.answer:
Think of a committee that only decides by majority vote. A decision counts only if more than half of all members vote for it, and each member votes once per election.

Why that prevents two leaders: to become leader you need votes from more than half the members. Two different candidates would each need more than half, and two "more than halves" must share at least one member. That member can only vote once in an election (a term), so both can't win the same election.

It also explains what happens when the network splits a 5-node cluster into 3 and 2: the side with 3 is a majority and carries on; the side with 2 can't elect a leader or commit anything, so it waits. They can never both decide different things. Raft adds terms (numbered elections), so an old leader that wakes up after a pause sees a higher term number and steps down instead of acting on stale authority.

draw.answer: The entry is committed the moment a majority (3 of 5, counting the leader itself) has stored it, not when all five have. That is why the cluster keeps working with two nodes slow or down. Followers that were behind catch up from the leader's log later.
draw.code:
Client ── write x = 5 ──► Leader N1
                           │ appends it to its log  (1 of 5)
        ┌─────────┬────────┼─────────┬─────────┐
        ▼         ▼                  ▼         ▼
       N2        N3                 N4        N5
     stored ✓  stored ✓          (slow…)   (down ✗)
        │         │
        └─────────┴──► "stored" ──► Leader

Leader + N2 + N3 = 3 of 5 = a majority
  ★ COMMITTED here: apply x = 5, reply "done"

N4 stores it a moment later; N5 catches up
from the leader's log when it comes back.

apply.answer:
A typical run of the visualisation:

1. All nodes start as followers, each with a random election timeout.
2. One node's timeout runs out first. It becomes a candidate, starts term 1, votes for itself and asks the others for their votes.
3. The others haven't voted in term 1 yet, so they vote for it. With a majority, it becomes the leader.
4. The leader sends heartbeats regularly; each heartbeat resets the followers' timeouts, so no new election starts.
5. A client write arrives at the leader. It appends it to its log (uncommitted) and sends it with the next heartbeat. Once a majority confirm, the leader commits it, applies it and replies to the client; the next heartbeat tells the followers to commit too.
6. The leader is stopped. Heartbeats stop, a follower times out, becomes a candidate for term 2, wins a majority and becomes the new leader.
7. When the old leader comes back, it sees the higher term, steps down to follower, and any entries it had that were never committed are replaced by the new leader's log.

Also worth watching: a split vote. Two candidates time out together and split the votes, so nobody wins; they wait new random timeouts and try again, and one wins the next term.

tradeoffs.answer:
Why writes get slower:
• Every write waits for a round trip to a majority of nodes, and each of them saves it to disk before replying. Across availability zones that adds milliseconds to every write.
• All writes go through one leader, which caps the write rate the group can handle.
• During an election (a few hundred milliseconds or more), no writes are accepted at all, and the minority side of a partition can't write until it heals.

When it is worth it: for small, critical data where two machines disagreeing would be a disaster:
• who the leader is, and locks ("only one worker processes this job");
• cluster configuration and metadata (Kubernetes keeps all its state in etcd);
• the agreed order of transactions in a strongly consistent database (Spanner, CockroachDB).

When it isn't: high-volume data where a little staleness is fine (likes, view counts, logs, metrics). There, faster eventual consistency is the better trade.

topics.name: Security basics: authentication, authorisation, OAuth and JWT
topics.definition: Authentication checks who you are. Authorisation checks what you're allowed to do.
topics.problem: Every system must know who is calling and what they may do, and must keep data safe even if something leaks. Mistakes here are the most expensive kind.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as App
  participant A as Login server
  participant G as Gateway
  participant S as Service
  U->>A: password and one-time code
  A-->>U: access token (15 min) and refresh token
  U->>G: request with the access token
  G->>G: check the signature and expiry
  G->>S: forward, as user 42
  S->>S: does user 42 own this account?
  S-->>U: result
diagram.caption: Authentication happens once at login. After that, every request carries a token, and the service still checks permissions on every request.

topics.idea: A user logs in once and gets a session ID or a token that proves who they are on later requests. A JWT is a signed token that services can check without a database lookup. OAuth 2.0 lets one app act on another service for a user without seeing their password; 'Sign in with Google' adds OpenID Connect on top. Also essential: HTTPS everywhere, passwords stored with a slow salted hash, least privilege, encryption at rest, and no secrets in code.
howItWorks: Login: the user sends their password over HTTPS. The server hashes it with the stored salt and compares the result with the stored hash.
If it matches (and the second factor is valid), the server issues a short-lived access token and a longer-lived refresh token.
Each request carries the access token. The gateway checks its signature and expiry without a database call.
The service checks authorisation: does this user own account 123? This check happens on the server, every time.
When the access token expires, the app swaps the refresh token for a new one. Logging out revokes the refresh token.
topics.analogy: A hotel: reception checks your passport (authentication) and gives you a key card that opens only your room and the gym (authorisation).
topics.breaks: A key card can be switched off at reception instantly. A JWT stays valid until it expires, because services only check its signature, not a central list. So keep JWTs short-lived and use refresh tokens.
topics.example: A banking app: log in with a password plus a one-time code (multi-factor), get a 15-minute access token and a refresh token; the gateway checks the token's signature; the payments service checks the user owns the account before moving any money.
keyPoints: Never store plain passwords: use a slow, salted hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2).
Session cookies (state kept on the server, easy to revoke) or JWTs (stateless, hard to revoke).
OAuth 2.0 = delegated authorisation; OpenID Connect = login and identity on top of it.
Authorisation models: role-based (RBAC) or attribute-based (ABAC). Check on every request, on the server.
Defence in depth: TLS, input validation, rate limiting, least privilege, audit logs.
Common attacks: SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), cross-site request forgery (CSRF), credential stuffing.
mistakes: Checking permissions only in the user interface.
Long-lived JWTs that can't be revoked.
Storing passwords with a fast hash (MD5, SHA-256) or without a salt.
Secrets committed to Git.
topics.interviewAnswer: Authentication goes through an identity provider with multi-factor login, issuing short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens. The gateway verifies tokens, and each service enforces authorisation on every request — for example, that the user owns the account. Passwords are stored with a slow hash, everything runs over TLS, and sensitive data is encrypted at rest.

followUps.q: How do you revoke a JWT?
followUps.a: Keep them short-lived, revoke the refresh token, and for urgent cases keep a small deny-list that the gateway checks.

followUps.q: Why hash passwords with a slow algorithm?
followUps.a: If the database leaks, attackers have to try guesses one at a time, and a slow hash makes every guess expensive.

practice.explain: Explain authentication versus authorisation with the hotel picture.
practice.draw: Draw the login and token-refresh flow for a mobile app.
practice.apply: Write Python functions that hash and check a password with hashlib.scrypt and a random salt, and explain why the salt matters.
practice.tradeoffs: Sessions or JWTs for a web app that must log a user out instantly when fraud is detected?

explain.answer:
At a hotel, reception checks your passport when you arrive. That is authentication: proving who you are. It happens once, at check-in (login).

Reception then gives you a key card. The card opens your room and the gym, but not other guests' rooms or the staff office. That is authorisation: what you are allowed to do. It is checked at every door you try (on every request), not just once.

Where the picture breaks: reception can switch a key card off instantly. A JWT access token keeps working until it expires, because services only check its signature, not a central list. That is why access tokens are kept short-lived and paired with a refresh token that can be revoked.

draw.answer: The access token is short-lived and sent with every request; the refresh token is long-lived, stored securely on the phone, and only ever sent to the login server. Rotating the refresh token on every use means a stolen one is detected the moment both copies are used.
draw.code:
1. Log in
   App ── password + one-time code ──► Auth server
   App ◄── access token (15 min)
           + refresh token (30 days, kept in
             the phone's secure storage)

2. Every request
   App ── request + access token ──► Gateway
          signature ok? not expired? ──► Service
          Service: may user 42 do this?

3. Access token expired
   App ── request ──► Gateway ── 401 expired
   App ── refresh token ──► Auth server
          valid? not revoked?
   App ◄── new access token + new refresh token
           (the old refresh token stops working)
   App ── retry the request ──► ✓

4. Log out, or fraud detected
   Auth server revokes the refresh token:
   no new access tokens; the last one dies
   within 15 minutes

apply.code:
import hashlib
import hmac
import os

N, R, P = 2**14, 8, 1            # cost: how much memory and CPU each guess takes


def hash_password(password):
    salt = os.urandom(16)                                   # a new random salt every time
    key = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=N, r=R, p=P, dklen=32)
    return salt.hex() + "$" + key.hex()                     # store the salt with the hash


def check_password(password, stored):
    salt_hex, key_hex = stored.split("$")
    key = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=bytes.fromhex(salt_hex), n=N, r=R, p=P, dklen=32)
    return hmac.compare_digest(key.hex(), key_hex)          # constant-time comparison


first = hash_password("correct horse")
second = hash_password("correct horse")
print(check_password("correct horse", first), check_password("wrong", first))   # True False
print(first == second)           # False: same password, different salts, different hashes

tradeoffs.answer:
Sessions.

With server-side sessions, the browser holds only a random session ID (in a Secure, HttpOnly cookie), and the session itself lives in a store such as Redis. When fraud is detected, delete the session: the very next request fails, and the user is logged out instantly, on every server.

A JWT is checked by its signature alone, so it stays valid until it expires. To kill one instantly, every request would have to check a deny-list, which is a central lookup on every request: you have rebuilt sessions, with extra complexity.

If JWTs are needed anyway (for example, for many services that check tokens themselves), the compromise is very short-lived access tokens (a few minutes), revocable refresh tokens, and a small deny-list checked at the gateway for emergencies. But for a web app with this requirement, sessions are the simpler and safer choice.

phases.title: Low-level design: OOP and SOLID
phases.goal: The building blocks of good class design: the four pillars of OOP, composition over inheritance, the five SOLID principles, class diagrams, and the concurrency basics LLD questions expect.
phases.bigPicture: Low-level design is about code that's easy to change. SOLID is a set of reasons to split or join classes; patterns (next phase) are proven shapes that follow those reasons. Learn the 'why' here, and the patterns will make sense.

topics.name: OOP: the four pillars
topics.definition: Object-oriented programming organises code into objects that bundle data and behaviour. Its four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
topics.problem: Large programs written as one long list of functions and shared variables become impossible to change safely. OOP groups data with the code that's allowed to change it.

diagram.caption: The arrow with a hollow triangle means 'is a kind of'. Both payment types share the pay() method (polymorphism) and hide their details (the minus sign means private).

topics.idea: Encapsulation hides an object's internal data behind methods, so it can't be put into an invalid state. Abstraction shows callers only what they need. Inheritance lets one class reuse and extend another. Polymorphism lets different classes be used through the same interface, each behaving in its own way.
howItWorks: Group related data and behaviour into a class: a BankAccount holds a balance and has deposit() and withdraw().
Make the balance private, and have withdraw() check there's enough money first. That's encapsulation.
Callers only see deposit(), withdraw() and the balance. That's abstraction.
A SavingsAccount is a kind of BankAccount that also adds interest. That's inheritance.
Code that loops over all accounts and calls monthly_update() gets the right behaviour for each type. That's polymorphism.
topics.analogy: A car. You use the steering wheel and pedals (abstraction) without touching the engine (encapsulation). An electric car is a kind of car (inheritance), and 'press the accelerator' works differently in each (polymorphism).
topics.breaks: Cars are physical and their family tree is shallow. In code, inheritance is easy to overuse: deep class trees become fragile, which is why composition is often the better choice.
topics.example: A payment system: an abstract PaymentMethod with pay(amount); CardPayment and PayPalPayment each implement it differently; checkout simply calls method.pay(amount) without caring which one it has.
keyPoints: Encapsulation: private state, with public methods that keep it valid.
Abstraction: interfaces and abstract classes describe what, not how.
Inheritance: an 'is-a' relationship; reuses code but creates tight coupling.
Polymorphism: one interface, many implementations; replaces long if/else chains on type.
mistakes: Public fields that anyone can set to invalid values.
Using inheritance just to reuse a few lines of code.
Type checks (if isinstance …) where polymorphism would do.
topics.interviewAnswer: Encapsulation protects an object's state, abstraction exposes only what callers need, inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship to reuse behaviour, and polymorphism lets code work with an interface while each class supplies its own behaviour — like checkout calling pay() on any payment method.

followUps.a: An interface only declares methods. An abstract class can also hold shared code and state. In Python both are usually written with ABC.
Overloading: the same method name with different parameters, chosen at compile time (for example in Java). Overriding: a subclass replaces a parent's method, chosen at runtime — that's polymorphism.

practice.explain: Explain the four pillars with the car picture.
practice.draw: Draw a class diagram for Shape with Circle and Rectangle subclasses and an area() method.
practice.apply: Code the Shape example in Python, then add a Triangle without changing any code that uses shapes.
practice.tradeoffs: Give one example where inheritance makes a design worse.

explain.answer:
• Abstraction: to drive, you use the steering wheel, the pedals and the gear stick. You don't need to know how fuel injection works. A class shows callers only the few methods they need.
• Encapsulation: the engine is under the bonnet, out of reach. You can't set the engine speed to an impossible value by hand; you can only press the accelerator, which keeps it within safe limits. A class keeps its data private and only lets it change through methods that keep it valid.
• Inheritance: an electric car is a kind of car. It has everything a car has (wheels, seats, a steering wheel) and adds a battery. A subclass reuses its parent and extends it.
• Polymorphism: "press the accelerator" works on any car, but a petrol car burns more fuel while an electric car draws more current. Code calls the same method on different classes, and each does its own version.

draw.answer: Shape is abstract: it only promises area(). Each subclass keeps its own measurements private (the minus sign) and implements area() its own way. The hollow triangle points from each subclass up to the parent: "is a kind of".
draw.code:
«abstract»
             Shape
        ───────────────
        + area(): float
               △
      ┌────────┴────────┐
   Circle           Rectangle
────────────     ──────────────
- radius         - width
                 - height
+ area()         + area()
  = π × r²         = width × height

apply.answer: total_area only knows about Shape and its area() method. Adding Triangle is one new class; total_area, and any other code that uses shapes, is not touched. That is polymorphism (and the open/closed principle): the caller says "give me your area", and each shape answers in its own way.

tradeoffs.answer:
A stack built by inheriting from a list: class Stack(list).

It looks like neat reuse: a list can already add to the end and pop from the end. But inheritance hands over everything a list can do, and the stack can't take any of it back. Callers can now insert(0, x), sort it, delete from the middle or slice it, all of which break the one promise a stack makes: last in, first out. (Java made exactly this mistake: its Stack class extends Vector.)

Composition fixes it: the Stack holds a list privately and exposes only push(), pop() and peek(). Users can't break it, and the list could later be swapped for something else without anyone noticing.

The general lesson: inherit only for a true "is a kind of", where the child can honour every promise the parent makes. "Uses one internally" is composition.

topics.name: Composition over inheritance, and interfaces
topics.definition: Composition means building a class out of other objects it has ('has-a'), instead of inheriting from a parent ('is-a').
topics.problem: Inheritance looks like free reuse, but every subclass is tied to its parent's details. With several independent features, the number of subclasses explodes.

diagram.caption: A Duck has a flyer and a quacker (the diamond means 'has a'). Dashed arrows mean 'implements': any flyer or quacker can be plugged in.

topics.idea: Inheritance ties a child class closely to its parent's internals, so changes ripple down and deep trees get rigid. Composition plugs behaviour in through small objects behind interfaces, so you can swap them at runtime and test each alone. Rule of thumb: inherit for a true 'is-a' with shared behaviour; otherwise, compose.
howItWorks: With inheritance, 3 kinds of flying × 3 kinds of sound = 9 subclasses, and every new kind multiplies them again.
With composition, a Duck simply holds a flyer object and a quacker object.
Each behaviour is a small class implementing a tiny interface: fly() or quack().
You build a duck by choosing its parts: Duck(Wings(), Quack()) or Duck(NoFly(), Squeak()).
You can even swap a part while the program runs, and test each part on its own.
topics.analogy: A phone with a replaceable camera module, compared with a phone whose camera is moulded into the case. Upgrading the module is easy; re-moulding the case isn't.
topics.breaks: Phone modules have sockets designed in advance. In code you still have to choose good interfaces, and composing everything everywhere can create a maze of tiny objects.
topics.example: Instead of Duck → FlyingDuck → QuackingFlyingDuck classes, a Duck has a flying behaviour and a quacking behaviour. A rubber duck gets NoFly and Squeak.
keyPoints: 'Is-a' → maybe inheritance. 'Has-a' → composition.
Composition lets you change behaviour at runtime and test with fakes.
Program to an interface, not to an implementation.
Dependency injection: pass collaborators in; don't create them inside the class.
mistakes: Using inheritance for 'has-a' relationships (a Car extends Engine).
Creating collaborators inside the class instead of passing them in.
topics.interviewAnswer: I prefer composition: a class holds small collaborator objects behind interfaces, and they're injected. It's more flexible than inheritance, easier to test, and avoids fragile class trees. I use inheritance only for a genuine 'is-a' with shared behaviour.

followUps.a: Giving an object its dependencies from outside, usually through the constructor, instead of creating them inside — so you can swap them, for example a fake payment gateway in tests.

followUps.q: What is the 'fragile base class' problem?
followUps.a: A change to a parent class unexpectedly breaks subclasses that relied on its internal behaviour.

practice.explain: Explain composition over inheritance with the phone-camera picture.
practice.draw: Draw the Duck design with its behaviour objects as a class diagram.
practice.apply: Refactor a Notifier hierarchy (EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier, EmailAndSmsNotifier) into one Notifier that holds a list of channels.
practice.tradeoffs: When is inheritance still the better choice?

resources.title: Inheritance and Composition: A Python OOP Guide

explain.answer:
Two phones. In the first, the camera is moulded into the case. To get a better camera you need a whole new phone: that is inheritance, where behaviour is baked into the class, and changing it means a new subclass. In the second, the camera is a module that clicks into a standard slot. To upgrade, you swap the module; the rest of the phone doesn't change, and you can test a module on its own. That is composition: the object holds a separate part, behind an interface (the slot), and the part can be swapped, even while the program runs.

With inheritance, every combination of features needs its own class (FlyingQuackingDuck, FlyingSqueakingDuck…). With composition, you combine small parts freely: a duck has a way of flying and a way of quacking.

draw.answer: The Duck has its two behaviours (the diamond means it holds them). Each behaviour is an interface, and the small classes below implement it (the dotted line with a hollow triangle). A rubber duck is just Duck(NoFly(), Squeak()): no new subclass needed.
draw.code:
Duck
 - flyer:   FlyBehaviour
 - quacker: QuackBehaviour
 + perform()
   ◆ has a                ◆ has a
   │                      │
   ▼                      ▼
 «interface»            «interface»
 FlyBehaviour           QuackBehaviour
  + fly()                + quack()
   △       △              △        △
   ┊       ┊              ┊        ┊
 Wings   NoFly          Quack    Squeak

apply.answer: With inheritance, every mix of channels needs its own class: with email, SMS and push, that is up to 7 classes (every non-empty combination of 3). With composition, there is one Notifier holding a list of channels, and one small class per channel. Any combination is just a different list, and a new channel is one new class.

tradeoffs.answer:
When there is a true "is a kind of" relationship, the child can keep every promise the parent makes, and they share real behaviour:

• Exception classes: class PaymentDeclined(PaymentError). Code that catches PaymentError should catch every kind of payment error. This is exactly what inheritance is for.
• Framework extension points: a test class extends unittest.TestCase, or a web view extends the framework's base view. The framework is designed to be extended this way and calls your overrides.
• Template method: the parent fixes the steps of an algorithm and the children fill in one or two of them (for example, a report that always loads, formats and saves, where only the formatting differs).
• Shallow, stable hierarchies you own: one or two levels, unlikely to grow.

The warning signs that composition would be better: a hierarchy getting deeper, classes for combinations of features, or a child overriding a method to do nothing.

topics.name: SOLID: S — Single Responsibility Principle
topics.definition: A class should have one reason to change: one job.
topics.problem: When one class does several jobs, unrelated changes collide: a change to the email wording risks breaking the tax calculation, and every change means retesting everything.

diagram.caption: After splitting: each class has one job, and a small service connects them.

topics.idea: If one class holds the business rules, the database saving and the email sending, a change to any one of them risks breaking the others. Split it so each class does one thing well and changes for one reason.
howItWorks: List what the class does, and who asks for changes to each part (finance, the database team, marketing).
Each different 'who' is a separate responsibility.
Move each responsibility into its own class with a clear name.
Connect them in a small coordinating function or service.
topics.analogy: A restaurant where the chef cooks, the cashier takes payments and the cleaner cleans. If the chef also did the accounts, every new tax rule would interrupt the cooking.
topics.breaks: In a tiny café one person does everything, and that's fine. Splitting too early into very small classes adds complexity; apply this when responsibilities really do change separately.
topics.example: Invoice calculates the totals, InvoiceRepository saves it, InvoiceEmailer sends it.
keyPoints: 'A reason to change' usually means a different person or team asking for changes.
Warning signs: huge classes, many unrelated imports, methods that never use each other's data.
The result: smaller classes that are easier to test.
mistakes: Splitting by the number of methods instead of by reason to change.
Creating dozens of tiny classes that are always changed together.
topics.interviewAnswer: Single responsibility means each class has one reason to change. For example, I'd separate invoice calculation, saving and emailing, so a change to the email template can't break the tax logic.

followUps.a: No, it's about cohesion: things that change together stay together, and things that change for different reasons are separated.

practice.explain: Explain SRP with the restaurant picture.
practice.draw: Draw the before and after class diagrams for the Invoice example.
practice.apply: A UserService validates input, hashes passwords, saves users and sends welcome emails. Split it, and write the new class names and methods.
practice.tradeoffs: When does splitting classes make code worse?

resources.title: SOLID: the first 5 principles of object-oriented design

explain.answer:
In a restaurant, the chef cooks, the cashier takes payments and the cleaner cleans. When a new tax rule arrives, only the cashier changes how they work; the kitchen carries on undisturbed.

If the chef also did the accounts, every tax change would interrupt the cooking, and a mistake in the accounts could ruin dinner service. That is a class with several responsibilities: a change for one reason (tax) risks breaking something unrelated (cooking).

The single responsibility principle says each class should have one reason to change, meaning one job, owned by one kind of change. An Invoice works out totals (changes when pricing rules change); a repository saves it (changes when the database changes); an emailer sends it (changes when the email changes).

draw.answer: Before, one class changes for three unrelated reasons, and a change to the email template means redeploying, and risking, the tax logic. After, each class has one reason to change, and each can be tested on its own (the repository with a test database, the emailer with a fake sender).
draw.code:
Before: one class, three reasons to change
┌───────────────────────┐
│ Invoice               │  pricing and tax rules
│  + total()            │  the database
│  + save_to_db()       │  the email template
│  + email_to_customer()│
└───────────────────────┘

After: one reason each
┌────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐
│ Invoice    │  │ InvoiceRepository │  │ InvoiceEmailer │
│  + total() │  │  + save(invoice)  │  │  + send(invoice)│
└────────────┘  └───────────────────┘  └────────────────┘
 pricing          the database           the email

apply.answer:
Four jobs, four classes, each with one reason to change:
• UserValidator.validate(email, password): the sign-up rules.
• PasswordHasher.hash(password): the hashing algorithm.
• UserRepository.save(user) and exists(email): the database.
• WelcomeEmailer.send(user): the email's wording or provider.

A thin UserRegistration.register(email, password) coordinates them in order and holds no rules of its own. Each part can be swapped or tested alone: here the repository and the emailer are in-memory stand-ins.

tradeoffs.answer:
• When the pieces always change together. If every change touches the same three classes, they were one responsibility, and splitting them only scatters it: you now open three files to follow one idea.
• When the classes become too small to mean anything: lots of one-method classes that just pass the call along ("ravioli code"). Following one request means jumping through ten files.
• When you split early, on guesses. Before you know what actually changes, you will often split along the wrong lines, and then have to change several classes for every request.
• When the wiring costs more than the class: every split adds construction, dependency passing and names to remember.

The test is "different reasons to change", meaning different people or rules that change at different times, not "this class has more than 100 lines".

topics.name: SOLID: O — Open/Closed Principle
topics.definition: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification: add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that already works.
topics.problem: Every time a new type of thing appears (a new payment method, a new discount), developers edit the same big if/else, and each edit risks breaking cases that already worked.

diagram.code:
classDiagram
  class DiscountRule {
    <<interface>>
    +apply(price)
  }
  DiscountRule <|.. SaleDiscount
  DiscountRule <|.. StudentDiscount
  DiscountRule <|.. AnyNewRule
  PriceCalculator --> DiscountRule : uses a list of
diagram.caption: The calculator only knows the DiscountRule interface. A new discount is a new class plugged in at the bottom; the calculator never changes.

topics.idea: A long if/elif chain on type ('if card … elif paypal …') must be edited every time a new case appears, which risks breaking the old cases. Instead, depend on an interface and add one new class for each new case.
howItWorks: Find the code that switches on a type: if kind == 'sale' … elif kind == 'student' …
Define an interface for the behaviour that varies: apply(price).
Move each branch into its own class that implements the interface.
The main code just calls rule.apply(price) for every rule it's given.
A new discount is a new class. The main code never changes.
topics.analogy: A power strip: you add a new device by plugging it in, without rewiring the house.
topics.breaks: A power strip has a fixed number of sockets, designed in advance. You can't predict every future change, so apply this where variation is likely, not everywhere.
topics.example: A price calculator takes a list of discount rules. Adding a 'student discount' means adding one new rule class, with no change to the calculator.
keyPoints: Replace 'switch on type' with polymorphism.
Strategy, Decorator and plug-in designs all follow this principle.
Protects tested code from new changes.
mistakes: Adding abstractions for variations that will never happen.
Still having to edit one central if/else to create the new class. Use a registry or configuration instead.
topics.interviewAnswer: Open/closed means I can add behaviour without editing existing code — for example, new discount types as new classes behind a DiscountRule interface, instead of a growing if/else chain.

followUps.q: Does it mean you never edit code?
followUps.a: No. You still fix bugs and refactor. It means designing so that the variations you expect don't require changing working code.

practice.explain: Explain the open/closed principle with the power-strip picture.
practice.draw: Draw the DiscountRule design as a class diagram.
practice.apply: Rewrite a shipping-cost function that uses if/elif for 'standard', 'express' and 'international', so that adding 'drone' needs no edits to existing code.
practice.tradeoffs: Where would applying this principle be over-engineering?

resources.title: SOLID: the first 5 principles of object-oriented design

explain.answer:
With a power strip, you add a new device by plugging it in. You don't rewire the house, and the kettle and the lamp that are already plugged in aren't affected.

The open/closed principle says code should work the same way: open for extension (you can add new behaviour), but closed for modification (you don't edit code that already works). The strip's sockets are the interface: every device has the same plug.

In code: a price calculator that loops over "discount rules", each with an apply() method. A new student discount is a new rule class plugged into the list. Compare that with a long if/elif on the discount type, which you must edit, and might break, every time a new kind appears.

draw.answer: final_price depends only on the DiscountRule interface. Each concrete rule implements apply() its own way. A new rule is a new box at the bottom; nothing above it changes.
draw.code:
final_price(price, rules) ── uses ──► DiscountRule
                                      + apply(price)
                                           △
                     ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
                SaleDiscount        StudentDiscount         (new rules
                apply: price × 0.9  apply: price − £5        plug in here)

apply.answer: Before, a single function had an if/elif branch per method, so adding "drone" meant editing it (and retesting every branch). After, each method is its own class behind a Shipping interface, and the function just looks the method up in a registry. Adding drone delivery is one new class and one line that registers it; shipping_cost and the existing methods are untouched.

tradeoffs.answer:
• Two cases that will probably never become three: VAT on or off, a guest or a member. One if is clearer than an interface and two classes.
• Code you own and can easily change: a private function in one service. If a third case appears, refactor then; editing your own code isn't a crime.
• When you don't yet know how it will vary. Plug-in points built on guesses usually end up in the wrong place, and make the real change harder (YAGNI: you aren't gonna need it).
• When it is really data, not behaviour: shipping prices that differ only in numbers belong in a table or config, not in one class per row.
• Scripts and prototypes that will be thrown away.

Apply it where change is frequent or expected (pricing rules, payment methods, plug-ins), or where other teams or customers extend your code without being able to edit it.

topics.name: SOLID: L — Liskov Substitution Principle
topics.definition: Objects of a subclass must work anywhere the parent class is expected, without breaking the program.
topics.problem: Polymorphism only works if every subtype really behaves like its parent. One misbehaving subclass forces callers to add special cases, and bugs appear far away from their cause.

diagram.caption: The fixed design. Square no longer pretends to be a changeable Rectangle; both are simply Shapes, so neither can break the other's promises.

topics.idea: A subclass must keep its parent's promises. It can't demand more (stricter inputs) or deliver less (weaker results), and it shouldn't throw surprises. If calling code has to check 'is this the special subclass?', the principle is broken.
howItWorks: Write down what callers rely on: 'after set_width(5), the width is 5 and the height hasn't changed'.
Check that every subclass keeps that promise. Square breaks it: setting the width also changes the height.
If a subclass can't keep a promise, it isn't a true subtype for that behaviour.
Fix it with a different hierarchy: Rectangle and Square both implement a Shape interface with area(), and there are no setters that conflict.
topics.analogy: A substitute teacher: lessons should run normally. If the substitute refuses to teach maths, the school timetable breaks.
topics.breaks: A human substitute can explain what's different. Code can't, so the contract — what methods accept and guarantee — must be clear.
topics.example: The classic case: Square inheriting from Rectangle. Code that sets width = 5 and height = 4 expects an area of 20, but a Square keeps its sides equal and gives 16. So Square shouldn't extend a changeable Rectangle.
keyPoints: Subclasses keep the parent's contract: the same or looser inputs, the same or stronger outputs.
Warning signs: overridden methods that throw 'not supported', or isinstance checks in calling code.
Fix: a better abstraction, such as a Shape interface with area().
topics.code:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.h = h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

class Square(Rectangle):
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = self.h = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.w = self.h = h

def resize(r: Rectangle):
    r.set_width(5)
    r.set_height(4)
    assert r.area() == 20        # fails for a Square: its area is 16
mistakes: Overriding a method just to throw 'not supported'.
A subclass that needs more specific input than its parent accepts.
topics.interviewAnswer: Liskov means a subclass must work anywhere its parent does. The classic counter-example is Square extending Rectangle: setting width and height separately breaks for a square, so they shouldn't share that inheritance.

followUps.q: Penguin extends Bird, and Bird has fly()?
followUps.a: A penguin can't fly, so fly() would throw — a Liskov violation. Fix it with a separate FlyingBird type, or give flying as an ability through composition.

practice.explain: Explain Liskov with the substitute-teacher picture.
practice.draw: Draw a better design for Rectangle and Square using a Shape interface.
practice.apply: Run the code below and watch the assertion fail, then redesign it so the check passes for every shape.
practice.tradeoffs: Why do Liskov violations so often show up as isinstance checks?

resources.title: SOLID: the first 5 principles of object-oriented design

explain.answer:
When a teacher is off sick, a substitute takes the class, and the school's timetable carries on as normal: maths at 9, the lesson happens. Nobody has to check who is teaching today. But if the substitute refuses to teach maths, or teaches it only to half the class, the timetable breaks, and the school has to start checking "is this the substitute?" before every lesson.

The Liskov substitution principle says a subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, with no surprises: it accepts at least the same inputs, gives at least the same results, and keeps the same promises. The classic failure is a Square that extends a changeable Rectangle. Code that sets width 5 and height 4 expects an area of 20; the Square keeps its sides equal and gives 16. The "substitute" broke a promise, so it isn't a valid substitute.

draw.answer: Rectangle and Square are both Shapes, but neither is a kind of the other, and Shape doesn't promise set_width or set_height. Each class keeps only the promises it can honour. Code that needs to resize width and height separately asks for a Rectangle; code that only needs an area asks for a Shape.
draw.code:
«interface»
               Shape
            + area()
           △         △
           ┊         ┊
   Rectangle         Square
   - width           - side
   - height
   + set_size(w, h)  + set_side(s)
   + area() = w × h  + area() = side²

No Square → Rectangle arrow: a square
can't keep a rectangle's promise
that width and height change separately.

apply.answer:
The first half is the lesson's code: resize() works for a Rectangle and fails its check for a Square, whose area comes out as 16.

The redesign stops Square pretending to be a Rectangle. Both implement a Shape interface that promises only area(); only Rectangle has set_size(). resize() asks for a Rectangle, so a Square can no longer be passed in, and the check always holds. Both can still go anywhere a Shape is expected.
apply.code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# The original design: Square extends Rectangle.
class OldRectangle:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.h = h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h


class OldSquare(OldRectangle):
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = self.h = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.w = self.h = h


def old_resize(r):
    r.set_width(5)
    r.set_height(4)
    assert r.area() == 20


old_resize(OldRectangle(2, 3))
square = OldSquare(3, 3)
try:
    old_resize(square)
except AssertionError:
    print("the check fails for a square: area =", square.area())   # ... area = 16


# The redesign: both are Shapes; only a Rectangle can change width and height separately.
class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...


class Rectangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def set_size(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h


class Square(Shape):
    def __init__(self, side): self.side = side
    def set_side(self, side): self.side = side
    def area(self): return self.side ** 2


def resize(r: Rectangle):
    r.set_size(5, 4)
    assert r.area() == 20                    # holds for every Rectangle


resize(Rectangle(2, 3))
print([shape.area() for shape in [Rectangle(2, 3), Square(3)]])     # [6, 9]

tradeoffs.answer:
Because an isinstance check is what calling code does when it can no longer trust the parent type.

If every subclass kept the parent's promises, the caller would just call the method and get the right behaviour (polymorphism). When one subclass breaks a promise (a Square that can't set width alone, a ReadOnlyFile that throws on write()), callers get bitten, and the quick fix is a special case: "if isinstance(shape, Square): do something different". The check is the symptom; the broken substitution is the cause.

Those checks then spread: every caller needs one, and every new subclass that breaks the rules needs another branch everywhere, which also breaks the open/closed principle. The real fix is to change the hierarchy (stop the bad inheritance, split the interface), not to teach every caller about the exception.

topics.name: SOLID: I — Interface Segregation Principle
topics.definition: Clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one big one.
topics.problem: Big 'do-everything' interfaces force classes to implement methods that make no sense for them, and every change to the big interface touches classes that don't care.

diagram.caption: Small interfaces. The basic printer implements only Printer; the office machine implements both.

topics.idea: A giant interface forces every class that implements it to write methods it doesn't need (often empty, or throwing errors), and changes ripple into classes that don't care. Split interfaces by what their users actually need.
howItWorks: Look for implementations full of empty methods or 'not supported' errors.
Group the interface's methods by which clients actually call them.
Make one small interface per group: Printer, Scanner, Fax.
Classes implement only what they really do, and each client depends only on the small interface it uses.
topics.analogy: A TV remote with 80 buttons when you only need power, volume and channel. Give most people a simple remote, and an advanced one to those who need it.
topics.breaks: A remote is one physical object. In code, too many tiny interfaces can be confusing too, so group methods that are always used together.
topics.example: A Machine interface with print(), scan() and fax() forces a basic printer to implement fax(). Split it into Printer, Scanner and Fax; an office machine implements all three.
keyPoints: Warning sign: methods that raise NotImplementedError or do nothing.
Split interfaces by what each client needs (role interfaces).
Works hand in hand with single responsibility.
mistakes: One interface per method everywhere, which fragments the design.
Keeping the fat interface 'for convenience'.
topics.interviewAnswer: Interface segregation means small, client-specific interfaces, so classes don't implement methods they don't need — for example separate Printer and Scanner interfaces instead of one big Machine interface.

followUps.a: Single responsibility is about why a class changes. Interface segregation is about what clients are forced to depend on. Both lead to smaller, focused pieces.

practice.explain: Explain interface segregation with the TV-remote picture.
practice.draw: Draw the before (Machine) and after (Printer, Scanner, Fax) designs.
practice.apply: Split a Worker interface with work(), eat() and sleep() so that a RobotWorker isn't forced to implement eat().
practice.tradeoffs: How can you tell when an interface has become too small?

resources.title: SOLID: the first 5 principles of object-oriented design

explain.answer:
A TV remote with 80 buttons, when most people only use power, volume and channel. Everyone has to cope with the buttons they never use, and a remote that must support all 80 is expensive to make. Better: a simple remote for most people, and an advanced one for those who want it.

The interface segregation principle says the same about interfaces: don't force a class to implement methods it doesn't need. A Machine interface with print(), scan() and fax() forces a basic printer to write fake scan() and fax() methods that just throw errors, and any change to fax() touches every printer. Split it into small interfaces by what their users actually need (Printer, Scanner, Fax), and let each class implement only the ones that are true for it.

draw.answer: Before, one fat interface forces BasicPrinter to fake two methods that throw errors. After, each class implements only the interfaces that are true for it, and code that only prints asks for a Printer, so it works with both machines.
draw.code:
Before
  «interface» Machine
   + print()  + scan()  + fax()
       △                     △
  BasicPrinter          OfficeMachine
   print() ✓             print() ✓
   scan()  ✗ raises      scan()  ✓
   fax()   ✗ raises      fax()   ✓

After
  «interface»   «interface»   «interface»
   Printer       Scanner        Fax
   + print()     + scan()       + fax()
      △  △          △             △
      ┊  └┄┄┄┄┄┐    ┊   ┌┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┘
  BasicPrinter  OfficeMachine
  (Printer)     (Printer, Scanner, Fax)

apply.answer: Three small interfaces, one per ability. A human worker implements all three; a robot implements only Workable, so it has no fake eat() that does nothing. Code that runs a shift asks only for Workable, and the lunch break only for Eater, so each part of the program depends only on what it uses.

tradeoffs.answer:
Signs an interface has been split too far:
• The small interfaces are always used together. Every class implements all four, and every caller needs all four, so they are really one role.
• Functions need several parameters for one object: process(doc: Printable, s: Stapleable, c: Collatable) where all three are the same machine.
• You can't name them as roles. Good interfaces are named after what a client needs ("Printer", "PaymentMethod"); if you are reduced to "HasName" and "HasId", you are splitting by method instead of by client.
• There are more interfaces than real implementations, and each has exactly one method and one implementer.

The principle is about clients: split when different callers need different parts. If no caller ever uses one part without the others, merge them back.

topics.name: SOLID: D — Dependency Inversion Principle
topics.definition: High-level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level details.
topics.problem: When business logic creates its own database connection or email client, it's welded to them. You can't test it without a real database, and switching providers means rewriting business code.

diagram.caption: The service depends only on the interface. The real database version and the test version both plug in underneath it.

topics.idea: If OrderService creates a MySQLDatabase directly, you can't swap the database or test without one. Instead, OrderService depends on an OrderRepository interface, and the concrete repository — MySQL in production, an in-memory one in tests — is passed in.
howItWorks: Find a high-level class that creates a low-level one: OrderService creates PostgresRepository() inside itself.
Define the interface the high-level code actually needs: OrderRepository with save(order).
Make the low-level class implement that interface.
Pass the implementation into the high-level class through its constructor.
At start-up, connect the real pieces together. In tests, pass in fakes.
topics.analogy: A standard wall socket. Your lamp depends on 'a standard socket', not on one particular power station, so you can switch energy supplier without rewiring the lamp.
topics.breaks: Socket standards are agreed by whole countries. In code you design the abstraction yourself, and a bad one (leaking database details) gives you none of the benefits.
topics.example: OrderService(repository) uses PostgresOrderRepository in production and InMemoryOrderRepository in tests.
keyPoints: Depend on interfaces; inject the implementations (dependency injection).
Makes testing easy with fakes and mocks.
Lets you swap infrastructure, like the database or email provider, with no change to business logic.
Dependency inversion is the principle; dependency injection is a technique for achieving it.
mistakes: An interface that copies one vendor's API exactly, so the abstraction leaks.
Creating dependencies inside methods 'just this once'.
topics.interviewAnswer: Dependency inversion means business logic depends on interfaces, and concrete implementations are injected. My OrderService depends on an OrderRepository interface, so I can use Postgres in production and an in-memory fake in tests.

followUps.a: Inversion is the design rule: depend on abstractions. Injection is the technique: pass dependencies in, often done for you by a framework like Spring.

practice.explain: Explain dependency inversion with the wall-socket picture.
practice.draw: Draw OrderService, the OrderRepository interface and two implementations, with arrows showing what depends on what.
practice.apply: Write a NotificationService that depends on a MessageSender interface; implement EmailSender and FakeSender, and test with the fake.
practice.tradeoffs: When is adding an interface for a single implementation unnecessary?

resources.title: SOLID: the first 5 principles of object-oriented design
Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern

explain.answer:
Your lamp plugs into a standard wall socket. It doesn't depend on a particular power station; it depends on the standard ("230 V, this plug shape"). So you can switch energy supplier, or run the house on solar panels, without rewiring the lamp. Both sides depend on the standard, not on each other.

Dependency inversion says the same about code: high-level code (OrderService, the business rules) shouldn't depend on low-level details (a MySQL database class). Both should depend on an abstraction (an OrderRepository interface). OrderService is given a repository instead of creating one: a Postgres one in production, an in-memory one in tests. Swapping the database, or testing without one, needs no change to OrderService.

draw.answer: The key detail is the direction of the arrows. OrderService points at the interface, and so do both implementations, so the business code no longer points at the database code. That is the "inversion". The wiring code at startup picks the concrete class and passes it in.
draw.code:
OrderService ── depends on ──► «interface»
 + place(order)                 OrderRepository
                                 + save(order)
                                    △        △
                                    ┊        ┊ implement
                 PostgresOrderRepository   InMemoryOrderRepository
                 (production)              (tests)

main() / start-up code:
  repo = PostgresOrderRepository(connection)
  service = OrderService(repo)        ← injected

apply.answer: NotificationService depends only on MessageSender. EmailSender is the real implementation (it would be given an SMTP client in production, so it isn't run here); FakeSender just records what it was asked to send. The test hands the service a FakeSender and checks exactly one message went out, with no email server, network or mocking library needed.

tradeoffs.answer:
• There will only ever be one implementation, and it is fast and in-process (a price calculator, a date formatter). An interface adds a file and a jump for nothing. Injecting the concrete class still keeps it testable.
• In Python, duck typing already lets you pass any object with the right methods, and test tools can stand in for a class, so a formal ABC is often optional.
• Small scripts, prototypes and glue code that will be rewritten anyway.
• Simple value objects (Money, an Address): there is nothing to swap.

Worth it at the boundaries with slow, external or changing things: databases, other services, payment providers, email and SMS, the clock, the file system. Those are exactly the things you want to replace in tests, and the ones most likely to change.

topics.name: UML class diagrams and relationships
topics.definition: A class diagram shows the classes, their fields and methods, and how they relate to each other.
topics.problem: In an interview, you need to show the structure of your design quickly, before coding. A clear diagram lets the interviewer follow you and correct you early.

diagram.code:
classDiagram
  ParkingLot "1" *-- "many" Floor : composition
  Floor "1" *-- "many" Spot : composition
  Spot "1" --> "0..1" Vehicle : association
  Vehicle <|-- Car
  Vehicle <|-- Truck
  PaymentMethod <|.. CardPayment : implements
diagram.caption: A filled diamond means 'owns'; a plain arrow means 'uses'; a hollow triangle means 'is a kind of'; a dashed triangle means 'implements'. The numbers say how many.

topics.idea: In LLD interviews you sketch the main classes and relationships before coding. The relationships: association (uses or knows about), aggregation (has, but the part can exist alone), composition (owns; the part dies with the whole), inheritance (is-a) and realisation (implements an interface). Multiplicity (1, 0..1, *) says how many.
howItWorks: Draw a box for each class: its name at the top, key fields in the middle, key methods at the bottom.
Connect the boxes with the right line: a filled diamond for 'owns', an empty diamond for 'has', a triangle arrow for 'is a', and a dashed triangle arrow for 'implements'.
Add numbers at the line ends: 1, 0..1 or * (many).
Talk through one use case on the diagram before you write code.
topics.analogy: A family tree combined with an organisation chart: who is a kind of what, and who belongs to whom.
topics.breaks: A family tree records what already happened. A class diagram is a draft: keep it simple, and change it as your design improves.
topics.example: Parking lot: ParkingLot owns Floors (composition), a Floor owns Spots (composition), a Spot holds 0 or 1 Vehicle (association), and Car, Truck and Bike are kinds of Vehicle (inheritance).
keyPoints: Composition (filled diamond): the owner controls the part's lifetime.
Aggregation (empty diamond): shared parts that can exist alone.
Inheritance: a line with an empty triangle. Realisation: a dashed line with an empty triangle.
In an interview, show only the important classes and methods.
topics.code:
ParkingLot 1 ◆──── * Floor        (composition)
Floor      1 ◆──── * Spot         (composition)
Spot       1 ────── 0..1 Vehicle  (association)
Car, Truck, Bike ───▷ Vehicle     (inheritance)
CardPayment ┄┄┄▷ PaymentMethod    (implements an interface)
mistakes: Drawing every getter and setter.
Spending 20 minutes on the diagram and leaving no time to code.
topics.interviewAnswer: I start an LLD answer by listing the main entities, then draw a class diagram with the key fields, methods and relationships: composition for owned parts, inheritance only for a true 'is-a', and interfaces for anything likely to vary.

followUps.a: Composition: the part dies with the whole, like a room in a house. Aggregation: the part can exist on its own, like a player in a team.

practice.explain: Explain the five relationship types with an everyday example of each.
practice.draw: Draw a class diagram for a library: Library, Book, BookCopy, Member and Loan.
practice.apply: Turn your diagram into Python class skeletons with the right attributes.
practice.tradeoffs: How much detail should a class diagram have in a 45-minute interview?

explain.answer:
• Association ("uses", "knows about"): a doctor and a patient. Each exists on its own; they are linked for a while. A plain line.
• Aggregation ("has, but the part lives on"): a football team has players. If the team folds, the players still exist and can join another team. A line with a hollow diamond at the team.
• Composition ("owns; the part dies with the whole"): a house has rooms. Demolish the house and its rooms are gone too. A line with a filled diamond at the house.
• Inheritance ("is a kind of"): a dog is an animal. A solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent.
• Realisation ("implements an interface"): a phone charger implements the USB-C standard; any USB-C device can use it. A dotted line with a hollow triangle pointing at the interface.

Multiplicity says how many: 1, 0..1, * (many) or 1..* (at least one), written at each end of the line.

draw.answer: Book is the title in the catalogue; BookCopy is one physical copy, which is what gets lent. The library owns its catalogue (composition), but members exist without it (aggregation). A Loan links one Member to one BookCopy for a period of time (associations), and a member can have up to max_loans active loans.
draw.code:
◆── composition   ◇── aggregation   ─── association

Library
 + lend(member, copy) → Loan
 + return_copy(loan)
   │
   ├ 1 ◆──── * Book
   │          isbn, title, author
   │            │
   │            └ 1 ◆──── 1..* BookCopy
   │                        copy_id, available
   │                              │ 1
   └ 1 ◇──── * Member             │
              member_id, name     │
              max_loans = 3       │
                │ 1               │
                └──── 0..* Loan * ┘
                       borrowed_on, due_on,
                       returned_on

apply.answer: Each class from the diagram becomes a dataclass with the attributes shown. Composition becomes a list the owner creates and holds (a Book's copies); association becomes a reference to an object that lives independently (a Loan's member and copy). Library.lend() enforces the two rules the diagram implies: a member can't exceed max_loans, and a copy can't be lent twice.
apply.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date, timedelta


@dataclass
class BookCopy:
    copy_id: str
    available: bool = True


@dataclass
class Book:
    isbn: str
    title: str
    author: str
    copies: list[BookCopy] = field(default_factory=list)      # composition


@dataclass
class Member:
    member_id: int
    name: str
    max_loans: int = 3
    loans: list["Loan"] = field(default_factory=list)


@dataclass
class Loan:
    member: Member                                            # association
    copy: BookCopy                                            # association
    borrowed_on: date
    due_on: date
    returned_on: date | None = None


@dataclass
class Library:
    books: dict[str, Book] = field(default_factory=dict)      # composition
    members: dict[int, Member] = field(default_factory=dict)  # aggregation

    def lend(self, member, copy, today):
        active = [loan for loan in member.loans if loan.returned_on is None]
        if len(active) >= member.max_loans:
            raise ValueError("loan limit reached")
        if not copy.available:
            raise ValueError("copy is already on loan")
        copy.available = False
        loan = Loan(member, copy, today, today + timedelta(days=21))
        member.loans.append(loan)
        return loan

    def return_copy(self, loan, today):
        loan.returned_on = today
        loan.copy.available = True


library = Library()
dune = Book("978-0441013593", "Dune", "Frank Herbert", [BookCopy("dune-1"), BookCopy("dune-2")])
library.books[dune.isbn] = dune
asha = Member(1, "Asha")
library.members[asha.member_id] = asha

loan = library.lend(asha, dune.copies[0], date(2024, 3, 1))
print(loan.due_on, dune.copies[0].available)     # 2024-03-22 False
library.return_copy(loan, date(2024, 3, 10))
print(dune.copies[0].available)                  # True

topics.name: Concurrency basics: threads, locks and race conditions
topics.definition: Concurrency is several tasks making progress at the same time. A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing between them.
topics.problem: Real systems serve many users at once. When two of them change the same data at the same moment, results can be silently wrong, like one seat sold twice.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Thread A
  participant S as seats_left
  participant B as Thread B
  A->>S: read - 1 seat left
  B->>S: read - 1 seat left
  A->>S: write 0 (seat sold)
  B->>S: write 0 (seat sold again!)
  Note over A,B: two tickets for one seat. A lock makes read, check and write one step.
diagram.caption: Both threads read before either writes, so both think the seat is free. That's a race condition.

topics.idea: LLD questions like seat booking or elevators often ask: what if two users act at once? If two threads read a counter, add one and write it back at the same moment, one update is lost. Locks (mutexes) make a critical section run one thread at a time; atomic operations and thread-safe queues avoid manual locks. Watch out for deadlock: two threads each waiting for a lock the other one holds.
howItWorks: Thread A reads seats_left = 1. Thread B also reads seats_left = 1.
A sells the seat and writes 0. B also sells the seat and writes 0. Two tickets have been sold for one seat.
Fix: wrap 'read, check, write' in a lock. Now B waits until A has finished, then reads 0 and refuses.
Across many servers, do it in the database with a conditional update — UPDATE seats SET sold = true WHERE id = 7 AND sold = false — and check that exactly one row changed.
topics.analogy: Two people filling in the same paper form at once: both read '3 seats left', both write '2 seats left', and one booking disappears. A lock is a rule that only one person may hold the form at a time.
topics.breaks: People can see each other. Threads can't, and the bug may appear once in a million runs, so you have to reason about it, not just test for it.
topics.example: Seat booking: 'check the seat is free, then mark it booked' must happen as one step — inside a lock within one program, or inside a database transaction with a row lock across many servers.
keyPoints: Critical section: code that touches shared data; protect it with a lock.
Race condition: read–modify–write without protection.
Deadlock needs four conditions; break 'circular wait' by always taking locks in the same order, or use timeouts.
Across several servers, an in-program lock isn't enough: use database transactions or a distributed lock.
Prefer thread-safe queues and data that never changes, where you can.
mistakes: Locking only the write, instead of the whole read-check-write.
Holding a lock while doing slow work, like a network call.
Taking locks in different orders in different places, which causes deadlock.
topics.interviewAnswer: Anywhere two users can change the same thing — like booking the last seat — I'd make 'check and update' a single atomic step: a lock within one process, or a database transaction with a row lock or optimistic versioning across servers. I'd take locks in a fixed order to avoid deadlock.

followUps.a: A process has its own memory. Threads share their process's memory, which makes communication easy but needs synchronisation.
Take locks in one agreed global order, hold them briefly, or use try-lock with a timeout.

practice.explain: Explain a race condition with the paper-form picture.
practice.draw: Draw a timeline of two threads causing a lost update, then the same timeline with a lock.
practice.apply: Run the counter code below with and without the lock using several threads. Then write a tiny deadlock with two locks and fix it by ordering them.
practice.tradeoffs: Why is a Python threading.Lock useless for a seat-booking system running on 10 servers?

resources.title: An Intro to Threading in Python

explain.answer:
Two people are filling in the same paper booking form at the same time. Both read "3 seats left". Both write their booking and change it to "2 seats left". Two seats have gone, but the form says only one did: one booking has silently disappeared, and the hall may be overbooked.

That is a race condition: the result depends on the exact timing of two actors, because "read the value, work out the new one, write it back" is several steps, and the other person can slip in between them.

A lock is the rule that only one person may hold the form at a time. The second person waits until the first has finished writing, then reads "2 seats left" and writes "1". The read-and-write becomes one indivisible step (a critical section).

draw.answer: The race happens because both threads read before either writes, so each writes a value based on stale data. With the lock, thread B can't even read until A has written and released, so its read sees A's result.
draw.code:
Without a lock (count starts at 3)
time   Thread A            Thread B
 t1    read count → 3
 t2                        read count → 3
 t3    write 3 + 1 = 4
 t4                        write 3 + 1 = 4
Result: 4. Expected 5: one update was lost.

With a lock
 t1    take the lock
 t2    read count → 3      wants the lock: waits…
 t3    write 4
 t4    release the lock
 t5                        take the lock
 t6                        read count → 4
 t7                        write 5, release
Result: 5.

apply.answer:
In CPython, count += 1 rarely shows the race on its own, because the interpreter seldom switches threads in the middle of it. Splitting it into read, a forced switch (time.sleep(0)) and write makes the race happen every time. Without the lock, updates are lost: the total comes out below 4,000, and different on every run. With the lock, it is always 4,000.

The deadlock: thread 1 takes lock A then wants B, while thread 2 takes B then wants A. Each waits for the other forever. (Here a timeout lets the program report it instead of hanging.) The fix is to always take locks in the same order: both threads take A, then B, so one simply waits for the other to finish.
apply.code:
import threading
import time

count = 0
lock = threading.Lock()


def add_many(use_lock, n=1000):
    global count
    for _ in range(n):
        if use_lock:
            with lock:
                current = count
                time.sleep(0)        # let another thread run here
                count = current + 1
        else:
            current = count
            time.sleep(0)
            count = current + 1


def run(use_lock):
    global count
    count = 0
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=add_many, args=(use_lock,)) for _ in range(4)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return count


print("without the lock:", run(False) < 4000)    # without the lock: True (updates were lost)
print("with the lock:", run(True))               # with the lock: 4000


# A deadlock: two threads take the same two locks in opposite orders.
a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
results = []


def take(first, second, name):
    with first:
        time.sleep(0.1)                          # both threads now hold one lock each
        if second.acquire(timeout=1):            # a real deadlock would wait forever
            second.release()
            results.append(f"{name}: done")
        else:
            results.append(f"{name}: stuck (deadlock)")


def both(order_1, order_2):
    results.clear()
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=take, args=(*order_1, "thread 1")),
               threading.Thread(target=take, args=(*order_2, "thread 2"))]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return sorted(results)


print(both((a, b), (b, a)))    # ['thread 1: stuck (deadlock)', 'thread 2: stuck (deadlock)']
print(both((a, b), (a, b)))    # ['thread 1: done', 'thread 2: done']: same order, no deadlock

tradeoffs.answer:
A threading.Lock lives in the memory of one Python process. Ten servers run ten separate processes, each with its own lock, and none of them knows about the others.

Two customers click "book seat F12" at the same moment; the load balancer sends one request to server 3 and the other to server 7. Each server takes its own lock (which nobody else is holding), each checks that F12 is free, and each books it. The seat is sold twice, and the locks did nothing.

The check-and-book must happen at a single place that every server shares:
• The database (best): a conditional update, UPDATE seats SET booked_by = :user WHERE seat_id = :seat AND booked_by IS NULL, then check one row changed; or a row lock with SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transaction; or a UNIQUE constraint on (show_id, seat_id) in the bookings table, so the second insert fails.
• A distributed lock (Redis, or etcd/ZooKeeper), with a time limit and a fencing token, for work that isn't a single database write.

phases.title: Design patterns
phases.goal: Ten patterns that come up again and again in LLD interviews and real code: three for creating objects, three for structuring them, and four for behaviour.
phases.bigPicture: A pattern is a proven shape for a common problem, with a name everyone recognises. In an interview, naming the right pattern — and saying why it fits — shows you design for change, not just for today.

topics.name: Singleton
topics.definition: Makes sure a class has only one instance, and gives one global way to reach it.
topics.problem: Some things should exist exactly once per program, like one configuration or one connection pool. Creating several wastes resources or causes conflicting settings.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  A["Code A"] -->|"Config()"| G{"Instance exists?"}
  B["Code B"] -->|"Config()"| G
  G -->|"no, first call"| N["Create it and store it"]
  G -->|"yes"| S["Return the stored one"]
  N --> S
diagram.caption: Whoever asks, and however often, they all get the same single object.

topics.idea: Used for a shared resource like a configuration object or a connection pool. The class controls its own creation. Downsides: it's global state, hides dependencies, makes testing harder, and needs care with threads.
howItWorks: The class keeps a hidden class-level variable for its single instance.
When asked for an instance, it checks that variable. If it's empty, it creates the instance and stores it.
With threads, two could check at the same moment, so creation is wrapped in a lock (and the variable is checked again inside the lock).
Every later request returns the stored instance.
topics.analogy: A country has one official government, and everyone refers to the same one.
topics.breaks: You can't replace a country's government in a test, but code should be replaceable. Many teams prefer creating one instance at start-up and injecting it, which gives 'only one' without the global.
topics.example: A logging configuration, or a database connection pool created once per process.
keyPoints: Use it for a truly single, shared resource.
Make creation thread-safe (double-checked locking), or create the instance eagerly.
In Python, a module is already a natural singleton.
Often criticised as global state; prefer injecting one shared instance.
mistakes: Using Singleton for things that aren't truly single, like 'the current user'.
Hidden dependencies: code reaches for the global instead of receiving what it needs.
topics.interviewAnswer: Singleton guarantees one instance with one access point, for things like configuration or a connection pool. I'd make creation thread-safe, but I usually prefer creating one instance at start-up and injecting it, because a global singleton hides dependencies and makes testing harder.

followUps.q: Why is Singleton sometimes called an anti-pattern?
followUps.a: It's global, changeable state: hidden dependencies, hard to replace in tests, and tricky lifetimes.

practice.explain: Explain Singleton and its main criticism.
practice.draw: Draw its class diagram: the stored instance and the method that returns it.
practice.apply: Implement the thread-safe Singleton below and prove with 10 threads that only one instance is ever created.
practice.tradeoffs: Singleton or injecting one shared instance: compare testing and flexibility.

draw.answer: The instance is stored on the class itself (a class-level field, shown underlined in UML), not on any object. The creation method checks it first: if it is empty, it creates the instance (inside a lock), and either way it returns the stored one.
draw.code:
┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│ Config                            │
├───────────────────────────────────┤
│ - _instance: Config = None        │ ← the one stored
│ - _lock: Lock                     │   instance (class-level)
│ - settings: dict                  │
├───────────────────────────────────┤
│ + __new__(): Config               │ ← returns _instance,
│   (or get_instance() in Java)     │   creating it only the
└───────────────────────────────────┘   first time
          ▲         ▲         ▲
       Config()  Config()  Config()
      every caller gets the same object

apply.answer:
A barrier releases all 10 threads at the same moment, and a short sleep inside creation widens the window where a race could happen. The safe version is created exactly once and all 10 threads get the same object.

The check-lock-check-again ("double-checked locking") matters: the first check skips the lock once the instance exists (fast), and the second check, inside the lock, stops a thread that was waiting from creating a second one. Without the lock, the same test creates several instances.
apply.code:
import threading
import time


class Config:
    _instance = None
    _lock = threading.Lock()
    created = 0

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:
            with cls._lock:                       # one thread at a time past here
                if cls._instance is None:         # check again: another thread may have won
                    time.sleep(0.01)              # slow creation makes a race likely
                    cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
                    cls._instance.settings = {}
                    cls.created += 1
        return cls._instance


class UnsafeConfig:                               # the same, without the lock
    _instance = None
    created = 0

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:
            time.sleep(0.01)
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
            cls.created += 1
        return cls._instance


def ten_threads(cls):
    start = threading.Barrier(10)                 # release all 10 at the same moment
    got = []

    def grab():
        start.wait()
        got.append(cls())

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=grab) for _ in range(10)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return cls.created, len({id(obj) for obj in got})


print(ten_threads(Config))                        # (1, 1): created once, one shared object
print(ten_threads(UnsafeConfig)[0] > 1)           # True: without the lock, several were created

tradeoffs.answer:
Both give the program one shared instance. The difference is who decides that, and how other code gets hold of it.

Singleton: the class enforces "only one", and code fetches it from anywhere with Config().
• Testing: the instance is global, so state leaks between tests, and swapping in a fake means monkey-patching the class.
• Flexibility: "exactly one" is baked in; needing two later (a second database, one config per customer) means changing every caller.
• Hidden dependencies: you can't see from a constructor what a class really uses.
• Convenience: no wiring at all.

Injecting one shared instance: create one Config at start-up (in main) and pass it into the classes that need it.
• Testing: each test passes its own fresh or fake instance. Nothing leaks.
• Flexibility: making two is just calling the constructor twice.
• Dependencies are visible in every constructor.
• Cost: a little wiring code.

In most designs, injection is better: you get "one instance" by choice at start-up, without the downsides of the pattern.

topics.name: Factory: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
topics.definition: A factory creates objects for you, so the calling code asks for 'a notifier' without knowing which concrete class gets built.
topics.problem: If the code that uses an object also decides which concrete class to create, every new type means editing that code in many places.

diagram.caption: The order service asks the factory for a notifier and only ever sees the Notifier interface. Only the factory knows the concrete classes.

topics.idea: Factory Method: one method decides which class to create. Abstract Factory: creates whole families of related objects that must match, such as all dark-theme or all light-theme UI parts. Both keep 'new ConcreteClass()' in one place.
howItWorks: Define a common interface: Notifier with send(message).
Implement it in EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier and PushNotifier.
Put the 'which class?' decision in one factory, using a dictionary from name to class.
Callers ask the factory for 'sms' and use the result only through the interface.
Adding a WhatsAppNotifier means one new class and one new dictionary entry.
topics.analogy: Ordering from a car factory: you ask for 'a family car', and the factory decides the exact model and parts.
