topics.breaks: A car factory has a fixed catalogue. If every new type means editing one big if/else inside the factory, you've just moved the problem. A registry of creators keeps it open for extension.
topics.example: NotifierFactory.create('sms') returns an SmsNotifier, and the order service just calls notifier.send().
keyPoints: Use it when the exact class depends on input or configuration.
Factory Method: one product, a method decides. Abstract Factory: families of related products.
A registry dictionary avoids long if/else chains.
The 'simple factory' (one create function) is the usual interview version.
mistakes: A factory that's just a giant if/else edited for every new type.
Factories for objects that only ever have one type.
topics.interviewAnswer: A factory centralises object creation: callers ask for a type by name or configuration and get an object behind a common interface, so adding a new type doesn't change the calling code. Abstract Factory extends this to whole families of matching objects.

followUps.a: A factory picks which class to create, in one step. A builder assembles one complex object step by step.

practice.explain: Explain Factory Method and Abstract Factory with one example each.
practice.draw: Draw NotifierFactory, the Notifier interface and three notifiers.
practice.apply: Add a 'push' notifier without changing the logic inside create().
practice.tradeoffs: When is a factory just unnecessary indirection?

explain.answer:
Both put the decision "which concrete class do I create?" in one place, so the rest of the code never names a concrete class.

Factory Method: a single method creates one product and decides which class it is. NotifierFactory.create("sms") returns an SmsNotifier; the order service only knows it got "a notifier" and calls send(). Adding a channel changes the factory, not the callers.

Abstract Factory: an object that creates a whole family of related products that must match. A UI has a DarkThemeFactory that makes a dark button, a dark checkbox and a dark menu, and a LightThemeFactory that makes the light versions. The screen asks its factory for parts, so it can never mix a dark button with a light checkbox. Switching theme means switching one factory.

draw.answer: The caller talks to the factory and to the Notifier interface only. The factory's registry maps a channel name to a class; each notifier implements the same send() method, so whichever one comes back is used the same way.
draw.code:
OrderService ── create("sms") ──► NotifierFactory
     │                             - _registry:
     │                               "email" → EmailNotifier
     │                               "sms"   → SmsNotifier
     │                               "push"  → PushNotifier
     │                             + create(channel): Notifier
     │ uses
     ▼
«interface» Notifier
 + send(msg)
   △            △             △
   ┊            ┊             ┊
EmailNotifier  SmsNotifier  PushNotifier

apply.answer: create() is exactly the lesson's one line. The factory gains a register() method, used as a decorator, so a new notifier registers itself where it is defined. Adding "push" touches no existing code: one new class, marked with the channel name.

tradeoffs.answer:
• There is only one concrete class, and no real prospect of another: just call its constructor.
• The caller already knows exactly which class it needs: a factory that takes "email" and returns EmailNotifier() adds a lookup and a file for no gain.
• Construction is trivial: a factory that only wraps a constructor is a layer to read through, not a design.
• In Python, a class is already a factory: you can pass the class itself (or a function) to whoever needs to create objects, without a Factory class around it.

A factory earns its place when the choice depends on something only known at runtime (configuration, user input, the country), when creating the object is complicated (several steps, dependencies to wire), or when a family of objects must match (Abstract Factory).

topics.name: Builder
topics.definition: Builds a complex object step by step, instead of using a constructor with a dozen parameters.
topics.problem: Objects with many optional settings lead to long, confusing constructors, where it's easy to pass arguments in the wrong order.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR B0["PizzaBuilder('large')"] --> B1[".add('mushroom')"] --> B2[".add('olive')"] --> B3[".with_extra_cheese()"] --> B4[".build()
checks it's valid"] --> P["Pizza ✓"]
diagram.caption: Each step sets one part; build() checks everything and returns the finished object.

topics.idea: When an object has many optional parts, a constructor like Pizza(size, cheese, olives, ham, …) is unreadable and easy to get wrong. A builder sets each part with a clearly named method, then build() checks everything and returns the finished object.
howItWorks: Create a builder with sensible defaults for every setting.
Each method sets one thing and returns the builder, so calls can be chained.
build() checks the combination is valid: required fields set, values in range.
build() returns the finished object, which can then be read-only.
topics.analogy: Ordering a custom sandwich at a counter: choose the bread, then the fillings, then the sauce, then say 'done'.
topics.breaks: At the counter you can choose in any order. Some objects need steps in a valid order, or have required parts, so build() must check before returning anything.
topics.example: Building an HTTP request: Request.builder().url(...).method('POST').header(...).body(...).timeout(5).build().
keyPoints: Use it for objects with many optional settings, or multi-step construction.
Fluent style: each step returns the builder, so calls can be chained.
Validate in build(); the finished object can then be unchangeable.
In Python, keyword arguments with defaults often solve the same problem; in Java, Builder is very common.
mistakes: Letting the half-built object escape before build() is called.
Using a builder for objects with only two or three fields.
topics.interviewAnswer: Builder constructs a complex object step by step through readable, named methods, then validates it and returns it, instead of a constructor with many parameters. I'd use it for things like requests or reports with lots of optional settings.

followUps.q: Why is Builder less needed in Python?
followUps.a: Keyword arguments with defaults already make optional settings readable. Builder still helps when construction has several steps or needs validation.

practice.explain: Explain Builder with the sandwich-counter picture.
practice.draw: Draw PizzaBuilder and Pizza as a class diagram.
practice.apply: Write an EmailBuilder (to, cc, subject, body, attachments) whose build() fails if there's no recipient.
practice.tradeoffs: Builder or keyword arguments: when is each the better choice?

explain.answer:
At a sandwich counter you don't shout the whole order in one breath. You build it step by step: "white bread", "chicken", "lettuce", "no mayo", and then "that's it". Each choice is clearly named, you can skip what you don't want, and when you say "done", the person behind the counter checks it makes sense ("you didn't pick a bread") before making it.

A builder does the same for objects with many optional parts. Instead of Pizza("large", None, True, False, ["olive"], …), where nobody can remember which position means what, you call clearly named methods, one per part, each returning the builder so they chain: PizzaBuilder("large").add("olive").with_extra_cheese(). Finally build() checks the rules and returns the finished, complete object.

draw.answer: The builder holds the parts while they are being chosen, and every setter returns the builder itself, which is what lets the calls chain. Only build() creates the Pizza, after checking the rules, so a half-finished pizza can never escape.
draw.code:
PizzaBuilder                          Pizza
 - size                                - size
 - toppings: list                      - toppings
 - extra_cheese: bool                  - extra_cheese
 + add(topping): PizzaBuilder ─┐
 + with_extra_cheese():         ├ return self,
     PizzaBuilder ─────────────┘ so calls chain
 + build(): Pizza ── checks the rules,
                     then creates ──►  Pizza

apply.answer: Each part has its own named method that returns self, so the calls chain and read like a sentence. to(), cc() and attach() can be called several times. build() enforces the one hard rule, at least one recipient, and hands back copies of the lists, so changing the builder afterwards can't change an email already built.

topics.name: Adapter
topics.definition: Lets two incompatible interfaces work together, by wrapping one so it looks like the other.
topics.problem: You often need a library or old system whose interface doesn't match the one your code expects, and you can't (or shouldn't) change either side.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  C["Our checkout code"] -->|"pay(20.00)"| A["LegacyBankAdapter"]
  A -->|"make_payment(2000, 'GBP')"| L["LegacyBankSDK"]
  L -->|"'OK'"| A
  A -->|"True"| C
diagram.caption: The adapter translates in both directions: pounds into pence on the way in, 'OK' into True on the way out.

topics.idea: Your code expects pay(amount_in_pounds), but a third-party SDK offers make_payment(pence, currency). An adapter wraps the SDK and translates the calls, so your code doesn't change.
howItWorks: Write down the interface your code expects: pay(pounds) returning True or False.
Write down what the other system offers: make_payment(pence, currency) returning 'OK' or an error code.
Create an adapter class that implements your interface and holds the other system.
In each method, convert the inputs (pounds → pence), call the other system, and convert the outputs (codes → True/False, or proper exceptions).
topics.analogy: A UK-to-EU travel plug adapter.
topics.breaks: A plug adapter only changes the shape. Software adapters often also convert data (units, formats, errors), and a careless conversion can hide real problems.
topics.example: Wrapping an old XML-based bank service so it fits your new PaymentGateway interface.
keyPoints: Use it to plug in third-party or legacy code without changing your own interface.
Prefer wrapping an object (object adapter) over inheriting from it (class adapter).
Keeps vendor-specific code in one place, so switching vendors is easy.
mistakes: Letting the third-party's types leak through the adapter into business code.
Losing error details during the conversion.
topics.interviewAnswer: Adapter wraps an incompatible class so it matches the interface my code expects — for example making an old bank SDK fit our PaymentGateway interface — so business code doesn't change and vendors can be swapped.

followUps.a: An adapter makes one interface match another that's expected. A facade gives a simpler interface over a complicated set of classes.

practice.explain: Explain Adapter with the travel-plug picture.
practice.draw: Draw PaymentGateway, LegacyBankAdapter and LegacyBankSDK, with arrows.
practice.apply: Write an adapter so that a weather API returning Fahrenheit fits an interface that returns Celsius.
practice.tradeoffs: What can go wrong if an adapter silently converts or swallows errors?

explain.answer:
You bring a UK hair dryer to Spain. The dryer expects a UK socket; the wall has an EU socket. You don't rewire the hotel, and you don't take the dryer apart: you plug a travel adapter in between. It changes the shape of the connection so the two fit, and neither side has to change.

The Adapter pattern is the same in code. Your code expects an interface (pay(pounds)); a third-party SDK you can't change offers something different (make_payment(pence, currency)). An adapter class implements your interface and translates each call into the SDK's form: pounds into pence, a "GBP" argument added, the SDK's "OK" string turned into True. Your code and the SDK both stay exactly as they are.

draw.answer: Our code depends only on PaymentGateway. The adapter implements that interface (dotted line) and holds the SDK it wraps (solid arrow), translating every call. Swapping to a different bank later means writing a different adapter; our code never changes.
draw.code:
Our checkout code
   │ pay(12.50)
   ▼
«interface» PaymentGateway
 + pay(pounds) → bool
   △
   ┊ implements
LegacyBankAdapter
 - sdk
 + pay(pounds):
     make_payment(1250, "GBP") == "OK"
   │ wraps and calls
   ▼
LegacyBankSDK   (we can't change this)
 + make_payment(pence, currency) → str

apply.answer: Our code wants current_celsius(city name). The third-party client offers get_temp(city code) in Fahrenheit. The adapter translates both ways: the city name into the API's code on the way in, and Fahrenheit into Celsius ((F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9) on the way out. Nothing that uses TemperatureSource knows the API exists.

tradeoffs.answer:
An adapter sits exactly where two systems meet, so anything it hides, nobody else sees.

Silent conversion:
• Lost precision: £10.005 rounded to pence, or rounded twice in different places, and the totals stop matching the bank's.
• Wrong assumptions: a timestamp assumed to be UTC that was local time, or a unit assumed to be metres that was feet. Everything "works" and the numbers are quietly wrong.
• Missing data filled with defaults: a missing temperature becomes 0 °C, which is a real temperature.

Swallowed errors:
• The SDK says "DECLINED" in one case and "TIMEOUT" in another, and the adapter returns False for both. The caller can't tell "the card was refused, don't retry" from "we don't know, check before retrying", and may charge twice.
• An exception is caught and logged inside the adapter, so the caller thinks the payment failed when it went through (or the opposite).

A good adapter converts explicitly and with tests, and translates errors into your own error types that keep their meaning (PaymentDeclined, PaymentTimedOut), instead of hiding them.

topics.name: Decorator
topics.definition: Adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, without changing the original class.
topics.problem: You want to add extras like logging, caching or retries to some objects, in different combinations, without writing a subclass for every combination.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Caller"] -->|"read()"| L["LoggingSource
adds a log line"] -->|"read()"| U["UpperCaseSource
upper-cases"] -->|"read()"| D["DataSource
the real data"]
diagram.caption: Each wrapper adds one feature and passes the call inward. The caller only sees read().

topics.idea: Instead of a subclass for every combination (LoggedCachedRetryingClient and so on), you stack small wrappers: a retry wrapper around a cache wrapper around the real client. Each wrapper adds one feature and passes the call along.
howItWorks: Start with an object that implements an interface: read().
Write a wrapper class that implements the same interface and holds another object of that interface.
In its read(), do the extra work (write a log line, check a cache), then call the inner object's read().
Wrap again for more features: Logging(Caching(Real())).
Callers can't tell they're talking to a wrapper; they just call read().
topics.analogy: Wrapping a present in layers: paper, then ribbon, then a card. It's still the same present underneath, and you can add or skip any layer.
topics.breaks: Gift layers don't affect each other. Code wrappers do, so the order matters: caching outside retries behaves differently from retries outside caching.
topics.example: Java's file streams (a BufferedInputStream around a FileInputStream), and Python's @decorators for logging or timing functions.
keyPoints: Same interface as the wrapped object, so wrappers can stack.
Avoids an explosion of subclasses for every feature combination.
Follows open/closed: add features without editing classes.
Python's @ syntax is a related idea for functions.
mistakes: Wrappers that change what the method means, rather than just adding to it.
Wrapping in the wrong order (for example, caching errors).
topics.interviewAnswer: Decorator wraps an object with another that has the same interface and adds one behaviour, like logging, caching or retries. Wrappers can be stacked in any combination, which avoids an explosion of subclasses.

followUps.a: Inheritance fixes behaviour for a whole class when you write the code. Decorators add it to individual objects at runtime, and combine freely.

practice.explain: Explain Decorator with the present-wrapping picture.
practice.draw: Draw the stack of wrappers around DataSource.
practice.apply: Write a TimingDecorator and a RetryDecorator for an HTTP client class, and stack them in both orders. What changes?
practice.tradeoffs: When do many layers of decorators make debugging hard?

explain.answer:
You wrap a present in layers: paper, then a ribbon, then a card. Each layer adds one thing; underneath it is still the same present, and you can add or leave out any layer, in any order.

A decorator does that to an object. Each decorator holds the object inside it, has the same methods (so it looks exactly like the thing it wraps), adds one feature, and passes the call on: a logging layer prints "reading…", an upper-case layer changes the result, a cache layer remembers it. You stack the features you need, LoggingSource(UpperCaseSource(DataSource())), instead of writing a subclass for every combination (LoggedUpperCaseCachedSource…). With three features, that is three small classes instead of seven combinations.

draw.answer: The call goes down through each layer to the real source, and the result comes back up through them. Every layer has the same read() method as the thing it wraps, so any layer can wrap any other, and the caller can't tell how many layers there are.
draw.code:
caller
  │ read()                        ▲ "DATA"
  ▼                               │
LoggingSource   prints "reading…" │
  │ inner.read()                  │ "DATA"
  ▼                               │
UpperCaseSource                   │ upper-cases
  │ inner.read()                  │ "data" → "DATA"
  ▼                               │
DataSource ───── returns "data" ──┘

apply.answer:
Both decorators have the same get() method as the client, so they stack either way. A fake clock and a client that fails twice make the results repeatable.

The order changes what is measured. Timing outside retry measures the whole call, retries included: one entry of 0.3 s, which is what the user waited. Retry outside timing measures each attempt separately: three entries of 0.1 s, which tells you how fast the server is but hides that the user waited three times as long. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions, so choose the order on purpose (or keep both).

tradeoffs.answer:
• The stack is invisible where it is used: the caller just sees "a client". What it actually does depends on how many layers were wrapped around it, in what order, somewhere else (often in start-up code).
• Order changes behaviour, silently: retry inside a cache behaves differently from cache inside retry, and timing inside or outside retry measures different things.
• Layers change things on the way through: a retry layer hides the first two failures, a cache returns old data, an error-handling layer turns an exception into a default. When the result is wrong, you have to work out which layer produced it.
• Stack traces get deep, full of near-identical wrapper frames.
• Duplicated layers multiply: a retry around a client that already retries means 3 × 3 = 9 attempts.
• Identity is lost: isinstance checks and attribute access stop working on the wrapped object.

Keep the stack short, build it in one obvious place, give each layer a clear name, and have each log what it did.

topics.name: Facade
topics.definition: Gives one simple interface to a complicated set of classes.
topics.problem: Using a complex subsystem directly means every caller must know many classes and the right order to call them, and that knowledge gets copied everywhere.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  C["Caller"] -->|"place_order()"| F["CheckoutFacade"]
  F --> I["Inventory"]
  F --> P["Payments"]
  F --> S["Shipping"]
  F --> N["Notifier"]
diagram.caption: One simple call from the caller; the facade deals with the four subsystems in the right order.

topics.idea: Placing an order may involve inventory, payment, shipping and notification classes. A CheckoutFacade with one place_order() method hides those steps, so callers use one method.
howItWorks: Identify the task callers keep repeating: placing an order.
Create a facade class that holds the subsystem objects.
Give it one method per common task, which calls the subsystem pieces in the right order.
Callers use the facade; advanced callers can still use the subsystem directly.
topics.analogy: A hotel concierge: you ask for 'dinner and a taxi at 8', and they deal with the restaurant and the taxi company.
topics.breaks: A concierge knows everything. A facade that keeps growing becomes a 'god class' that does too much, so keep it thin and let it delegate to the subsystems.
topics.example: A video-conversion library: convert(file, 'mp4') hides the codecs, buffers and audio mixing.
keyPoints: Simplifies a subsystem; the subsystem stays available for advanced use.
Reduces coupling between callers and many classes.
Keep it thin: coordination, not business logic.
mistakes: Putting business rules into the facade.
Forcing every caller through the facade even when they need fine control.
topics.interviewAnswer: Facade gives callers one simple method, like place_order(), over a complex subsystem of inventory, payment and shipping classes, which reduces coupling. I keep it thin so it doesn't become a god class.

followUps.a: The same idea at different levels: a facade simplifies classes inside one program; an API gateway simplifies many services for outside clients.

practice.explain: Explain Facade with the concierge picture.
practice.draw: Draw the facade and the four subsystems it calls.
practice.apply: Write a HomeTheaterFacade with watch_movie() that switches on the projector, amplifier and player in the right order.
practice.tradeoffs: How do you stop a facade from turning into a god class?

explain.answer:
A hotel concierge. You say "dinner for two at 8, and a taxi there". You don't phone the restaurant, check the menu, book the table, then call the taxi firm and give the address. The concierge does all of that, in the right order, and you deal with one person.

A facade is the concierge for a set of classes. Placing an order involves inventory, payments, shipping and notifications, each with its own methods and its own order of calls. A CheckoutFacade offers one method, place_order(order), which makes those calls in the right sequence. Callers get a simple front door; the subsystems stay as they are, and anyone with an unusual need can still talk to them directly, the way you could still phone the restaurant yourself.

draw.answer: The facade only coordinates: it calls each subsystem in the right order and holds no business rules of its own. The subsystems don't know the facade exists, and callers can still use them directly for anything unusual.
draw.code:
Caller
  │ place_order(order)
  ▼
CheckoutFacade
  │ 1. reserve(items) ────────────► Inventory
  │ 2. charge(customer, total) ───► Payments
  │ 3. schedule(order) ───────────► Shipping
  │ 4. send(customer, "confirmed") ► Notifier

apply.answer: The facade switches things on in the order that matters: the projector and its input first, then the amplifier at a sensible volume, and the player last, so the film doesn't start before there is a picture and sound. end_movie() switches off in the reverse order. Anyone using the facade needs one call, not six.
apply.code:
class Projector:
    def on(self): return "projector on"
    def input(self, source): return f"projector input: {source}"
    def off(self): return "projector off"


class Amplifier:
    def on(self): return "amplifier on"
    def volume(self, level): return f"volume {level}"
    def off(self): return "amplifier off"


class Player:
    def on(self): return "player on"
    def play(self, film): return f"playing {film}"
    def off(self): return "player off"


class HomeTheaterFacade:
    def __init__(self, projector, amplifier, player):
        self.projector, self.amplifier, self.player = projector, amplifier, player

    def watch_movie(self, film):
        return [
            self.projector.on(),
            self.projector.input("player"),
            self.amplifier.on(),
            self.amplifier.volume(5),
            self.player.on(),
            self.player.play(film),               # last: picture and sound are ready
        ]

    def end_movie(self):                          # the reverse order
        return [self.player.off(), self.amplifier.off(), self.projector.off()]


theater = HomeTheaterFacade(Projector(), Amplifier(), Player())
print(" → ".join(theater.watch_movie("Dune")))
# projector on → projector input: player → amplifier on → volume 5 → player on → playing Dune
print(" → ".join(theater.end_movie()))
# player off → amplifier off → projector off

tradeoffs.answer:
• Keep it thin: it coordinates calls in the right order and nothing more. Business rules ("orders over £1,000 need a fraud check") belong in the subsystems; if you find yourself writing ifs about the business in the facade, move them out.
• One facade per task or use case, not one for the whole system. A CheckoutFacade and a ReturnsFacade stay small; an OrderSystemFacade grows forever.
• Don't make it the only way in. Other code may use the subsystems directly for unusual needs, so the facade doesn't have to grow a method for every case.
• Watch the method count and the number of dependencies: when it holds ten subsystems and twenty methods, split it.
• Test the subsystems on their own, so the facade's tests only check the order of calls.

topics.name: Strategy
topics.definition: Puts a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so you can choose one at runtime.
topics.problem: When an algorithm can vary (pricing, sorting, routing), putting every variant in one method with if/else makes it long, hard to test and risky to extend.

diagram.caption: Ride holds one pricing strategy and can swap it for any other that implements the same interface.

topics.idea: Instead of an if/elif on pricing type inside checkout, each pricing rule is its own class (or function) with the same method. Checkout holds one strategy and can swap it.
howItWorks: Define the interface: price(distance_km).
Write one class per algorithm: NormalPricing, SurgePricing, NightPricing.
The context (Ride) holds one strategy object and calls it.
Choose the strategy at runtime: from configuration, a factory, or the time of day.
topics.analogy: Choosing a route in a maps app: fastest, shortest or avoiding tolls. Same journey, different strategy.
topics.breaks: The maps app chooses for you when you tap a button. In code, something still has to decide which strategy to use, often a factory or configuration.
topics.example: Payment fees, sorting, compression formats, and ride pricing (normal or surge).
keyPoints: Replaces 'which algorithm?' conditionals with polymorphism.
Strategies can be swapped at runtime.
In Python, plain functions can be strategies.
Very common in LLD answers: pricing, payment, parking fees.
mistakes: Strategies that need lots of the context's private data (a sign the interface is wrong).
Creating strategy classes for one fixed algorithm.
topics.interviewAnswer: Strategy puts each interchangeable algorithm, like normal or surge pricing, behind one interface, so the class using it can switch algorithms at runtime, and new ones are added without editing it.

followUps.a: Both swap behaviour objects. With Strategy, the caller chooses the algorithm. With State, the object changes its own state as events happen.

practice.explain: Explain Strategy with the route-choice picture.
practice.draw: Draw Ride with a PricingStrategy interface and two implementations.
practice.apply: Add a 'night pricing' strategy without changing Ride, and write tests for all three.
practice.tradeoffs: When is a simple if/else better than Strategy?

explain.answer:
In a maps app, the journey is the same, from home to the airport, but you choose how the route is worked out: fastest, shortest, or avoiding tolls. The app doesn't care which you pick; it asks the chosen option for a route and follows it. You can switch options without changing anything else.

Strategy is that idea in code. One job (working out a ride's price) has several interchangeable ways of being done (normal pricing, surge pricing). Each way is its own class (or function) with the same method, price(distance). The Ride holds one strategy and calls it, without knowing which one it has. Swapping the strategy changes the behaviour; adding a new one needs no change to Ride. It replaces an if/elif on "pricing type" in the middle of the business code.

draw.answer: Ride holds one PricingStrategy and only ever calls price(). Each implementation is interchangeable. Night pricing is added as one more box at the bottom, without touching Ride.
draw.code:
Ride
 - pricing: PricingStrategy  ◆──► «interface» PricingStrategy
 + fare(km)                         + price(distance_km)
                                      △          △           △
                                      ┊          ┊           ┊
                           NormalPricing   SurgePricing   NightPricing
                           2 + 1.2 × km    normal × 1.5   normal + £3
                                                          (added later)

apply.answer: NightPricing is one new class with the same price() method: here a flat £3 on top of the normal fare. Ride is not changed. Each strategy gets a test for a 10 km ride: normal £14.00, surge (× 1.5) £21.00, night £17.00, and one more test checks that strategies can be swapped on the same ride.

tradeoffs.answer:
• Two or three options that rarely change, each only a line or two: an if/else is shorter and easier to read than an interface and three classes.
• The choice is used in one place only, so nothing else would reuse the strategies.
• The behaviour never needs to be swapped at runtime, configured, or tested separately.
• It is really data, not behaviour: if the options only differ in numbers (a rate per km), a table of numbers is enough.

In Python there is also a lighter middle ground: functions are already strategies. Pass a function, or keep a dictionary from name to function, without writing classes.

Move to Strategy when the options multiply, when each grows its own logic, when other teams add options, or when you want to test each option on its own.

topics.name: Observer
topics.definition: Lets objects subscribe to another object's events, and get notified automatically when something happens.
topics.problem: When one event must trigger several reactions, the code that raises the event ends up calling every reacting component directly, so adding a new reaction means editing it.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["OrderEvents
(the subject)"] -->|"order A123 placed"| E["Email receipt"] O -->|"order A123 placed"| S["Update stock"] O -->|"order A123 placed"| AN["Analytics"]
diagram.caption: One event, many subscribers. The subject doesn't know what each subscriber does with it.

topics.idea: When an order is placed, email, analytics and stock might all need to react. Instead of the order code calling each one, they subscribe; the order publishes 'order placed', and every subscriber is notified. It's the in-program version of publish/subscribe.
howItWorks: The subject keeps a list of subscribers.
Components that care call subscribe(callback).
When the event happens, the subject loops through the list and calls each callback with the event's details.
New reactions subscribe themselves; the subject never changes.
Subscribers can unsubscribe when they no longer care.
topics.analogy: Subscribing to a YouTube channel: when a new video is published, every subscriber is told, and the channel doesn't need to know who they are.
topics.breaks: YouTube handles millions of subscribers reliably. A simple in-memory list of observers is lost if the program crashes, and one slow subscriber can slow the publisher. Across services, you'd use a message broker instead.
topics.example: Button click listeners in user interfaces, stock-price updates, event systems.
keyPoints: Decouples the publisher from its listeners.
Subscribers can be added and removed at runtime.
Watch for memory leaks (forgotten subscribers) and slow or failing subscribers.
At system level, the same idea becomes pub/sub with a message broker.
mistakes: Never unsubscribing, which leaks memory.
Letting one subscriber's error stop the others from being notified.
Relying on subscribers being called in a particular order.
topics.interviewAnswer: Observer lets listeners subscribe to an object's events, so the publisher notifies all of them without knowing who they are — like 'order placed' triggering an email and a stock update. Across services I'd use the same idea with a message broker, for durability.

followUps.a: With Observer, subscribers register directly with the subject, usually inside one program. With pub/sub, a broker sits in between, so publishers and subscribers don't know each other, often across services.

practice.explain: Explain Observer with the YouTube-subscription picture.
practice.draw: Draw the subject, its list of subscribers, and three observers.
practice.apply: Build a StockTicker that notifies subscribers only when a price changes by more than 1%.
practice.tradeoffs: What happens if one subscriber throws an error or is very slow? How would you protect the publisher?

explain.answer:
When you subscribe to a YouTube channel, the channel doesn't need to know who you are or what you'll do with the notification. When a new video is published, YouTube tells every subscriber. People can subscribe and unsubscribe at any time, and the channel keeps publishing the same way.

Observer is that pattern inside a program. The subject (OrderEvents) keeps a list of subscribers. When something happens ("order A123 placed"), it calls each of them. Email sends a receipt, stock is reduced, analytics records the sale, but the order code doesn't call those three things by name; it just publishes. Adding a fourth reaction means subscribing one more function, without touching the order code.

draw.answer: The subject only holds a list of things to call, so it never depends on email, stock or analytics code. New observers subscribe themselves; the publish loop doesn't change.
draw.code:
OrderEvents (the subject)
   - subscribers: [send_receipt, update_stock, record_sale]
   + subscribe(callback)
   + publish(order_id) ── calls each subscriber
          │
  ┌───────┼──────────────────┐
  ▼       ▼                  ▼
Email   Stock              Analytics
send    reduce the         record
receipt stock levels       the sale

apply.answer:
The ticker remembers, for each stock, the last price it told subscribers about, and stays quiet unless the new price is more than 1% away from it. Comparing with the last notified price (not the last price seen) means a slow drift still gets reported once it adds up to more than 1%.

From 100.0: 100.5 is a 0.5% move, so it is ignored; 101.2 is 1.2% above 100.0, so it is sent; 99.9 is 1.3% below 101.2; 98.8 is 1.1% below 99.9.

tradeoffs.answer:
In the simple loop, subscribers run one after another, inside publish():
• One throws: the error comes back into the publisher, so placing an order can fail because analytics broke, and the subscribers after it in the list are never called.
• One is slow: publish() waits for it, so the order request waits, and everything after it is delayed.

Protecting the publisher:
• Wrap each call in try/except, log the error, and carry on with the next subscriber.
• Run subscribers asynchronously, on a thread pool or a queue, with a timeout, so publish() returns straight away.
• Across services, use a real message queue (publish/subscribe): each subscriber gets its own queue, with its own retries and a dead-letter queue, and a broken subscriber can't affect the publisher or the others.
• Decide what must not be an observer: if the order can't be placed without reserving stock, that is part of the main flow, not a fire-and-forget notification.

topics.name: Chain of Responsibility
topics.definition: Passes a request along a chain of handlers; each one either deals with it or passes it on to the next.
topics.problem: A request may need to pass several checks, or be handled by one of several handlers depending on its details. Hard-coding that sequence in one function makes it long and rigid.

diagram.caption: The request travels along the chain until a handler can deal with it.

topics.idea: Good for pipelines of checks or approvals: authentication → rate limit → validation → handler; or expense approval: a team lead up to £100, a manager up to £1,000, a director above that. Each handler is independent, and the chain can be reordered.
howItWorks: Define a handler interface: handle(request).
Each handler decides: deal with the request, or pass it to the next handler it holds.
Link the handlers into a chain, in the order you want.
Send the request to the first handler; it travels along until someone deals with it.
End the chain with a default handler that rejects or logs anything unhandled.
topics.analogy: A customer-support line: first-line support, then a specialist, then a manager, each stepping in only if the one before can't solve it.
topics.breaks: A support line always ends with someone. In code, a request can fall off the end with nobody handling it, so add a final default handler.
topics.example: Web framework middleware, logging levels, and an ATM paying out £50 notes, then £20s, then £10s.
keyPoints: Decouples whoever sends the request from whichever handler deals with it.
Handlers can be added, removed or reordered.
Make sure something handles the end of the chain.
Middleware pipelines are the everyday example.
mistakes: No default at the end, so requests disappear silently.
Very long chains that are hard to trace.
topics.interviewAnswer: Chain of Responsibility passes a request through a sequence of handlers until one deals with it — like expense approvals by amount, or middleware for auth, rate limiting and validation. It keeps each handler small and lets me reorder the chain.

followUps.a: Middleware in web frameworks (Express, Django, Spring filters), and events bubbling up through a web page.

practice.explain: Explain the pattern with the support-line picture.
practice.draw: Draw the approval chain and trace a £450 request and a £20,000 request through it.
practice.apply: Write an ATM dispenser chain for £50, £20 and £10 notes that pays out £180.
practice.tradeoffs: What makes a long chain hard to debug?

explain.answer:
You phone customer support. First-line support takes the call. If they can answer, done. If not, they pass you to a specialist; if the specialist can't, to a manager. Each person either handles the problem or hands it to the next, and you only deal with "support"; you don't choose who answers.

Chain of Responsibility links handlers in a line. A request goes to the first; each handler decides "can I deal with this?" and either handles it or passes it on. An expense of £450 goes to the team lead (limit £100), who passes it to the manager (limit £1,000), who approves it. The sender doesn't know who will handle it, each handler is independent, and the chain can be reordered or extended without changing the others. Web middleware works the same way: authentication, then rate limiting, then validation, then the handler.

draw.answer: Each approver either handles the request or passes it to the next. A request that reaches the end of the chain unhandled must get a clear answer (here a rejection), never silence.
draw.code:
Team lead ──► Manager ──► Director ──► (end of the chain)
≤ £100        ≤ £1,000    ≤ £10,000

£450
  Team lead: over £100, pass it on
  Manager:   £450 ≤ £1,000 ✓
  → "Manager approved £450"

£20,000
  Team lead: pass → Manager: pass → Director:
  over £10,000, and nobody is left
  → "Rejected: over every limit"

apply.answer:
Each dispenser handles one note size: it pays as many of its notes as fit (divmod), and passes the remainder to the next dispenser. £180 is three £50s (£150), then one £20, then one £10. An amount the chain can't finish, such as £185, ends with a clear error instead of paying the wrong sum.

One honest limit of this greedy approach: with only £50 and £20 notes, £60 would fail (£50, then £10 left over), although three £20s would work. A real ATM checks the combination before paying anything out.

tradeoffs.answer:
• It isn't obvious who handled a request. The answer depends on the order of the chain, which is set up somewhere else, so reading the sender's code tells you nothing.
• A request can disappear. If a handler neither handles the request nor passes it on (a missing "else: pass it on"), or the chain ends without a final handler, nothing happens and nobody is told.
• Order bugs: putting validation before authentication, or the £1,000 approver before the £100 one, changes the results without any error.
• Hidden side effects: each handler may change the request on the way through, so the last handler sees something different from what was sent.
• Long chains add a little work to every request, and very long recursive chains get deep stack traces.

Mitigations: build the chain in one visible place; log which handler took each request; put a final handler at the end that fails loudly; keep each handler small and test it on its own.

topics.name: State
topics.definition: Lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by putting each state's behaviour in its own class.
topics.problem: Objects with modes (an order that's paid or shipped, a machine that's idle or dispensing) often end up with if/else on a status field in every method, and invalid actions slip through.

diagram.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Idle
  Idle --> HasCoin: insert a coin
  HasCoin --> Idle: press the button, snack given
  HasCoin --> HasCoin: insert a coin, already has one
  Idle --> Idle: press the button, asks for a coin
diagram.caption: Circles are states; arrows are events. The same event (pressing the button) does different things depending on the current state.

topics.idea: A vending machine reacts differently to 'insert coin' when it's idle, when it already has money, or when it's sold out. Instead of an if/elif on a status variable inside every method, each state is a class that handles the events and decides the next state.
howItWorks: Draw the state diagram: states as circles, events as arrows between them.
Create one class per state, with one method per event.
Each method does what's valid in that state, and may move the object to a new state.
The main object holds its current state and forwards every event to it.
An event that isn't valid in a state returns a clear 'not allowed' instead of doing something wrong.
topics.analogy: A traffic light: what happens on the next tick depends on whether it's red, amber or green, and each colour knows which comes next.
topics.breaks: A traffic light has three simple states. Real systems can have many states and transitions, so draw the state diagram first, or the classes become hard to follow.
topics.example: An order's life (created → paid → shipped → delivered, or cancelled), vending machines, elevators, network connections.
keyPoints: Each state class handles the events that are valid in that state.
Transitions are explicit; invalid actions get a clear response.
Start by drawing a state diagram.
A cousin of Strategy, but here the object changes its own behaviour.
mistakes: States that know too much about each other.
Forgetting some events in some states (like cancel while dispensing).
topics.interviewAnswer: State moves each state's behaviour into its own class, so a vending machine or an order behaves correctly for its current state and the transitions are explicit, instead of an if/else on a status field in every method.

followUps.q: When is an enum and a switch enough?
followUps.a: When there are only a few states and events. The State pattern pays off as the states and rules grow.

practice.explain: Explain State with the traffic-light picture.
practice.draw: Draw the state diagram for an order: created, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled, with the allowed transitions.
practice.apply: Extend the vending machine below with a SoldOut state and a refund action.
practice.tradeoffs: State classes or a transition table (a dictionary of state → event → next state)?

explain.answer:
A traffic light reacts to the same event, "tick", differently depending on its colour: red goes to red-and-amber, green goes to amber, amber goes to red. Each colour knows what comes after it. You don't need one big rule book that says "if red and tick, then…, if green and tick, then…"; the current colour decides.

The State pattern does this in code. An object (a vending machine) behaves differently in different situations (idle, has a coin, sold out). Instead of an if/elif on a status variable inside every method, each state is a class with a method for each event. The machine forwards each event to its current state object, and that state does the right thing and decides which state comes next. A new state is a new class, and each state's rules are in one place.

draw.answer: Only the arrows shown are allowed; any other event in a state is refused with a clear message. An order can be cancelled before it ships (with a refund once paid); after shipping it is a return, not a cancellation. Delivered and cancelled are final.
draw.code:
created ──pay──► paid ──ship──► shipped ──deliver──► delivered
   │               │
   │ cancel        │ cancel (refund the payment)
   ▼               ▼
cancelled ◄────────┘

Final states: delivered, cancelled
Refused, for example:
  ship   while created  (not paid yet)
  cancel while shipped  (use a return instead)
  pay    while cancelled

apply.answer: Every state now handles three events: insert_coin, press and refund. HasCoin.press() sells the snack, reduces the stock and moves to SoldOut if it was the last one, otherwise back to Idle. SoldOut refuses coins (handing them back) and presses. HasCoin.refund() returns the coin. The machine itself contains no if statements about its status: it just forwards each event to its current state.

phases.title: Low-level design questions
phases.goal: Practise the classic LLD questions end to end: requirements, classes, patterns, the key code and concurrency.
phases.bigPicture: Every LLD question tests the same skills: turning requirements into clean classes, using a pattern where something varies, and handling two users acting at once. Do each question yourself first, then compare with the notes.

topics.name: Design a parking lot
topics.definition: Design the classes for a multi-floor car park that assigns spots, issues tickets and charges fees.
topics.problem: It's the classic first LLD question: the entities are clear, there are natural places for patterns (pricing, spot assignment), and there's a real concurrency problem.

diagram.code:
classDiagram
  class PricingStrategy {
    <<interface>>
    +fee(hours)
  }
  class SpotAssignmentStrategy {
    <<interface>>
    +find_spot(vehicle)
  }
  ParkingLot "1" *-- "many" Floor
  Floor "1" *-- "many" Spot
  Spot --> "0..1" Vehicle
  Vehicle <|-- Car
  Vehicle <|-- Truck
  Vehicle <|-- Bike
  Ticket --> Spot
  Ticket --> Vehicle
  ParkingLot --> PricingStrategy
  ParkingLot --> SpotAssignmentStrategy
diagram.caption: The car park owns floors, floors own spots, and each spot holds at most one vehicle. Pricing and spot assignment are pluggable strategies.

functional: Several floors, with spots of different sizes (small, compact, large).
Vehicles (bike, car, truck) park in a suitable free spot.
Issue a ticket on entry; calculate the fee on exit; take payment.
Show free spots per floor on display boards.
nonFunctional: Two vehicles must never get the same spot, even at different gates.
Easy to add new vehicle types or pricing rules.
classes: ParkingLot: floors and gates; finds and assigns spots.
Floor: its spots, and free counts by size.
Spot: id, size, current vehicle (or none).
Vehicle (abstract) → Bike, Car, Truck: each says which spot size it needs.
Ticket: id, vehicle, spot, entry time.
SpotAssignmentStrategy: for example, nearest free spot first.
PricingStrategy: hourly, weekend, and so on.
Payment: amount, method, status.
evolution: Version 1: one floor, one gate, one spot size, a flat fee. Classes: ParkingLot, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket.
Version 2: several spot sizes and vehicle types, a rule for which vehicle fits which spot, and pricing as a strategy.
Version 3: several floors and gates, with display boards observing the free counts.
Version 4: concurrency — claiming a spot atomically — and storing state in a database so gates on different servers agree.
design: Entry: a vehicle arrives → the assignment strategy finds a free spot that fits → the spot is marked taken in one atomic step → a ticket is issued.
Exit: scan the ticket → the pricing strategy works out the fee from the time parked → payment → the spot is freed.
Display boards subscribe to spot changes (Observer) and update their counts.
deepDives: Concurrency: two gates assigning the same spot. Use a lock (per floor, or for the whole lot), or an atomic compare-and-set on the spot.
Fit rules: can a bike use a car spot when bike spots are full? Decide, and say it out loud.
Lost ticket: charge the maximum daily fee.
Extensibility: electric-car charging spots become a new spot type with their own pricing strategy.
mistakes: Putting pricing logic inside Ticket or Vehicle.
Ignoring two gates acting at the same moment.
Vehicle subclasses that override lots of behaviour instead of just declaring their size.
topics.interviewAnswer: Core classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, the Vehicle types, Ticket and Payment. Spot assignment and pricing are strategies, so the rules can change without touching the rest. Parking is one atomic step — a lock or a compare-and-set — so two gates can't take the same spot. Display boards observe spot changes.

followUps.q: How would this work with gates on different servers?
followUps.a: Keep spot state in a database and claim a spot with a conditional update (UPDATE … WHERE spot_id = ? AND vehicle_id IS NULL), trying another spot if no row changed.

followUps.q: How would you add electric-car charging?
followUps.a: A new spot type with a charger, plus a pricing strategy that adds the energy cost. No existing classes change.

practice.explain: Explain your class design in 2 minutes, naming the patterns you used.
practice.draw: Draw the class diagram with relationships and multiplicities.
practice.apply: Complete the code with a PricingStrategy (first hour £2, then £1.50 per hour) and test parking 3 vehicles.
practice.tradeoffs: One lock for the whole car park, one per floor, or a compare-and-set per spot: compare them.

explain.answer:
"A ParkingLot has several Floors, and each Floor has Spots of three sizes: small, compact and large. A Vehicle is abstract; Bike, Car and Truck each say which spot size they need. When a vehicle arrives, the lot asks a SpotAssignmentStrategy for a free spot that fits, for example the nearest one, marks it taken and issues a Ticket with the entry time. On exit, a PricingStrategy works out the fee from the time parked, a Payment is taken, and the spot is freed.

The patterns, and why: Strategy for spot assignment and for pricing, because those are the rules most likely to change (nearest-first, weekend rates, EV charging). A Factory creates vehicles and spots from input. Display boards are Observers of spot changes, so they update their free counts without the lot knowing about them. There is one ParkingLot, created at start-up and injected.

The key risk is concurrency: two gates assigning the same spot. Finding and taking a spot happens in one atomic step under a lock. To extend it, an EV charging spot is a new spot type with its own pricing strategy; nothing else changes."

draw.answer: Composition (the filled diamond) marks parts that belong to one whole: a lot's floors, a floor's spots. A Spot holds at most one Vehicle, and a Ticket links one Vehicle to one Spot. The two strategies are interfaces the lot holds, so they can be swapped.
draw.code:
ParkingLot
 + park(vehicle): Ticket
 + leave(ticket): fee
 - assigner: SpotAssignmentStrategy ──► «interface»
 - pricing:  PricingStrategy ──┐         + find_spot(floors, vehicle)
   │ 1                         │           △ NearestFirst
   ◆                           └──► «interface»
   │ 1..*                            + fee(hours)
 Floor                                 △ Hourly, Weekend
  + free_count(size)
   │ 1
   ◆
   │ 1..*
 Spot ── 0..1 ── Vehicle «abstract»
  id, size,       + size
  vehicle           △ Bike, Car, Truck
   ▲ 1
   │
 Ticket ── 1 ── Vehicle
  id, entry time

 Payment ── 1 ── Ticket (amount, method, status)
 DisplayBoard ┄┄ observes ┄┄► Floor

apply.answer:
The pricing strategy charges £2 for the first hour, then £1.50 for each extra hour or part of one, all in pence to keep money exact. A fake clock makes the fees testable without waiting hours.

Three vehicles park in three spots of the right size; a fourth gets "car park full". The bike leaves after 45 minutes and pays £2.00; the car leaves after two and a half hours (3 started hours) and pays £2 + 2 × £1.50 = £5.00. A new car then gets the compact spot the old car freed, not the bike's small spot.

tradeoffs.answer:
• One lock for the whole car park: the simplest, and obviously correct. Every gate waits its turn to assign a spot, but assigning takes microseconds and a car park has a handful of gates, so the waiting is negligible. The right default.
• One lock per floor: gates on different floors can assign at the same time. But a vehicle that doesn't fit on one floor must move on to the next, and taking locks in different orders invites deadlock, so you need a fixed lock order. More complexity, for contention that a real car park doesn't have.
• Compare-and-set per spot: no locks at all. Each gate scans for a free spot and claims it only if it is still free ("set vehicle if currently empty", atomically); if another gate won, it tries the next spot. The most concurrent, but subtler: retries, and it needs an atomic primitive, which in a distributed system is a conditional database update.

In the interview: start with one lock and say why it is enough. If the gates are separate machines, the lock moves into the database as a conditional update (UPDATE spots SET vehicle = … WHERE id = … AND vehicle IS NULL), which is really compare-and-set per spot.

topics.name: Design an elevator system
topics.definition: Design the classes and scheduling logic for a building's lifts.
topics.problem: It tests state machines, scheduling and concurrency, and there's no single right answer, so your reasoning is what gets marked.

diagram.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Idle
  Idle --> MovingUp: a stop above
  Idle --> MovingDown: a stop below
  MovingUp --> DoorsOpen: reached a stop
  MovingDown --> DoorsOpen: reached a stop
  DoorsOpen --> MovingUp: doors closed, more stops above
  DoorsOpen --> MovingDown: doors closed, more stops below
  DoorsOpen --> Idle: doors closed, no stops
  Idle --> Maintenance: switched off
  Maintenance --> Idle: switched on
diagram.caption: One lift's state machine. There's no arrow from DoorsOpen straight to moving without the doors closing, which is how safety is guaranteed.

functional: Hall calls (up and down buttons on each floor) and car calls (floor buttons inside the lift).
Several lifts; each hall call is assigned to one lift.
Doors open and close; show the current floor and direction.
Emergency stop and maintenance mode.
nonFunctional: Short waiting times; far floors must not be starved.
Safety: never move with the doors open.
classes: ElevatorController: receives calls and dispatches them.
Elevator: id, current floor, direction, state, and its up and down stops.
Request: floor, direction, type (hall call or car call).
DispatchStrategy: chooses a lift for each hall call.
Door, Display, Button: simple parts.
evolution: Version 1: one lift with a list of requested floors, visited in order of arrival.
Version 2: one lift using LOOK scheduling: sweep up, then down.
Version 3: several lifts and a controller that gives each hall call to the lowest-cost lift.
Version 4: safety states (doors, overload, maintenance) and strategies for busy times.
design: Each lift serves its stops with the LOOK algorithm: keep going in one direction, serving stops on the way, then turn around — like a lift operator sweeping up and down.
A controller assigns each hall call to the best lift: idle and near, or already moving towards that floor in the same direction.
Each lift has a state machine that enforces safety: doors must be closed before moving.
deepDives: Dispatch cost = distance + stops on the way + a penalty for the wrong direction.
Peak times: in the morning rush, send idle lifts back to the ground floor.
Concurrency: requests arrive from many buttons at once, so use a thread-safe queue into the controller.
Overload sensor: the doors stay open.
mistakes: First-come, first-served scheduling.
No state machine, so 'moving with the doors open' is possible.
Over-complicating the dispatch algorithm before the basics work.
topics.interviewAnswer: A controller receives hall calls and gives each one to the lift with the lowest cost: near, idle, or already heading that way. Each lift serves its stops with the LOOK algorithm — continue in one direction, then reverse. A state machine per lift guarantees the doors are closed before it moves.

followUps.q: Why not first come, first served?
followUps.a: The lift would zig-zag between floors. Sweeping in one direction serves more people per trip and avoids starving any floor.
Simulate time in steps with scripted requests, check the safety rules (never moving with the doors open) and measure the average wait.

practice.explain: Explain how LOOK scheduling works, using the lift-operator picture.
practice.draw: Draw the lift's state diagram and the class diagram.
practice.apply: Write a small simulation with 3 lifts and 20 random requests; print each lift's path and the average wait.
practice.tradeoffs: Nearest-lift dispatch or zone-based dispatch (each lift serves certain floors): pros and cons.

explain.answer:
Picture an old-fashioned lift operator. They don't rush to whichever button was pressed last. They pick a direction, say up, and keep going, stopping at every floor where someone inside wants to get off or someone outside wants to go up. When there are no more requests above, they turn around and do the same on the way down.

That is LOOK. Each lift keeps two sorted lists of stops: those above it and those below it. While moving up it serves the up stops in order, from the nearest; when none are left above, it switches direction and serves the down stops. Unlike its cousin SCAN, it doesn't travel to the top floor if nobody needs it there; it only goes as far as the last request (it "looks" ahead).

Why it works: every request is served within one sweep, so nobody on a far floor waits forever, and the lift doesn't zigzag between nearby requests while others wait. Serving the nearest request first, by contrast, can starve far floors under heavy traffic.

draw.answer: The state machine enforces the safety rule: the lift only moves from DoorsOpen after the doors are confirmed closed. Maintenance can be entered from any state and serves no calls. The controller holds the lifts and a swappable dispatch strategy.
draw.code:
Lift states
  Idle ── call above ──► MovingUp
  Idle ── call below ──► MovingDown
  Idle ── call on this floor ──► DoorsOpen
  MovingUp / MovingDown ── reached a stop ──► DoorsOpen
  DoorsOpen ── timer, doors closed ──►
      MovingUp / MovingDown (more stops) or Idle (none)
  any state ── maintenance key ──► Maintenance ── key off ──► Idle
  (never move unless "doors closed" is confirmed)

Classes
  ElevatorController 1 ◆── * Elevator
   + request(floor, direction)    - id, floor, direction
   - dispatch: DispatchStrategy   - state: ElevatorState
                                  - up_stops, down_stops
                                  + add_stop(floor), step()
  «interface» DispatchStrategy    Elevator 1 ◆── 1 Door
   + choose(elevators, request)   Elevator 1 ◆── 1 Display
     △ NearestCar, ZoneDispatch
  Request: floor, direction, kind (hall | car)

apply.answer:
Time moves in ticks: in each tick a lift travels one floor. Each lift follows LOOK (keep going while there are stops ahead, then turn). Each new request is given to a lift with the lesson's pick_elevator cost: distance, plus a penalty of 10 if the lift is busy heading the other way. Passengers board when their lift reaches their floor; their wait is the number of ticks since they pressed the button, and their destination becomes a new stop.

20 requests arrive at random times on a 15-floor building, with a fixed seed so the run is repeatable. The printout shows every floor each lift stopped at, and the average and longest wait. Try changing the penalty in the cost function, or using one lift, and watch the waits change.
apply.code:
import random


class Elevator:
    def __init__(self, eid):
        self.id, self.floor, self.direction = eid, 0, 0    # -1 down, 0 idle, 1 up
        self.stops = set()
        self.path = [0]                                     # every floor it stopped at

    def add_stop(self, floor):
        if floor != self.floor:
            self.stops.add(floor)

    def step(self):                                         # one tick: LOOK
        if not self.stops:
            self.direction = 0
            return
        above = any(s > self.floor for s in self.stops)
        below = any(s < self.floor for s in self.stops)
        self.direction = 1 if (self.direction >= 0 and above) or not below else -1
        self.floor += self.direction
        if self.floor in self.stops:
            self.stops.discard(self.floor)
            self.path.append(self.floor)


def pick_elevator(elevators, floor, direction):
    def cost(e):
        heading_there = e.direction == direction and (floor - e.floor) * direction >= 0
        return abs(e.floor - floor) + (0 if e.direction == 0 or heading_there else 10)
    return min(elevators, key=cost)


random.seed(4)
FLOORS = 15
requests = []
while len(requests) < 20:
    start, end = random.sample(range(FLOORS), 2)            # two different floors
    requests.append((random.randrange(40), start, end))     # (time, from, to)
requests.sort()

lifts = [Elevator(i) for i in range(3)]
waiting = {lift.id: {} for lift in lifts}                   # lift -> floor -> [(time, destination)]
waits = []


def board(lift, tick):
    for asked_at, destination in waiting[lift.id].pop(lift.floor, []):
        waits.append(tick - asked_at)
        lift.add_stop(destination)


tick = 0
while requests or any(lift.stops or waiting[lift.id] for lift in lifts):
    while requests and requests[0][0] == tick:
        asked_at, start, end = requests.pop(0)
        lift = pick_elevator(lifts, start, 1 if end > start else -1)
        waiting[lift.id].setdefault(start, []).append((asked_at, end))
        lift.add_stop(start)
    for lift in lifts:
        board(lift, tick)                                   # already on that floor
        lift.step()
        board(lift, tick)                                   # just arrived
    tick += 1

for lift in lifts:
    print(f"lift {lift.id}:", lift.path)
print("average wait:", round(sum(waits) / len(waits), 1), "ticks; longest:", max(waits))
# lift 0: [0, 13, 4, 3, 2, 0, 4, 11, 14, 4]
# lift 1: [0, 4, 14, 4, 1, 10, 13, 3, 1, 0, 6, 8, 13]
# lift 2: [0, 2, 1, 5, 8, 4, 3, 5, 7, 10, 11, 6, 1, 13]
# average wait: 6.8 ticks; longest: 19

tradeoffs.answer:
Nearest-lift dispatch (any lift can serve any floor; pick the cheapest by distance and direction):
• Pros: simple; adapts to whatever traffic appears; every lift is useful all the time; short average waits in low and medium buildings.
• Cons: lifts bunch together and chase the same calls; trips mix short and long journeys, so someone going to floor 40 stops at 5, 9 and 12; under heavy load, waits become unpredictable.

Zone-based dispatch (lifts 1–2 serve floors 1–15, lifts 3–4 serve floors 16–30, often running express through the other zone):
• Pros: fewer stops per trip and faster journeys to high floors; predictable; works well in tall buildings and in the morning rush.
• Cons: an idle lift in one zone can't help a busy zone, so capacity is wasted; when a zone's lifts are busy, its passengers wait even though other lifts are free; changing floors between zones may need a transfer.

Real systems mix them: zones (or destination dispatch, where you enter your floor in the lobby and are told which lift to take) at peak times, and nearest-lift the rest of the day.

topics.name: Design Splitwise (expense sharing)
topics.definition: Design an expense-sharing app where friends split bills and can see who owes whom.
topics.problem: It tests clean modelling of money, validation, and a small algorithm (debt simplification), and it catches people who use floats for money.

diagram.code:
classDiagram
  Group "1" o-- "many" User
  Group "1" *-- "many" Expense
  Expense "1" *-- "many" Split
  Expense --> User : paid by
  Split <|-- EqualSplit
  Split <|-- ExactSplit
  Split <|-- PercentSplit
  BalanceSheet --> User : net balance per user
  DebtSimplifier --> BalanceSheet
diagram.caption: A group has members and expenses; each expense is divided into splits of one of three kinds. The balance sheet and simplifier work out who pays whom.

functional: Users and groups.
Add an expense paid by one person, split equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage.
Show balances: who owes whom, and how much.
Settle up, and simplify the debts in a group.
nonFunctional: Money must be exact: no floating-point errors.
Splits must always add up to the total.
classes: User; Group (members, expenses).
Expense: payer, amount, splits, description.
Split (abstract) → EqualSplit, ExactSplit, PercentSplit.
SplitFactory: creates and validates splits.
BalanceSheet: the net balance per user.
DebtSimplifier: reduces the number of payments.
evolution: Version 1: equal splits only, stored as pairwise 'A owes B' records.
Version 2: exact and percentage splits, behind a split strategy that validates them.
Version 3: one net balance per user, plus debt simplification.
Version 4: groups, several currencies, history and notifications.
design: Add an expense: validate the split (it sums to the total) → each participant now owes the payer their share.
Keep one net balance per user: positive means they're owed money, negative means they owe.
Simplify debts: repeatedly match the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor until everyone is at zero.
deepDives: Store money as whole pence (or Decimal), never as float.
Rounding: £10 split three ways is 334 + 333 + 333 pence; give the extra penny to someone in a fixed, fair way.
The greedy simplification settles n people in at most n − 1 payments.
topics.code:
from collections import defaultdict
import heapq

net = defaultdict(int)       # in pence: + is owed money, - owes money

def add_equal_expense(payer, amount_pence, people):
    share, remainder = divmod(amount_pence, len(people))
    for i, person in enumerate(people):
        owed = share + (1 if i < remainder else 0)    # spread the leftover pence
        net[person] -= owed
        net[payer] += owed

def simplify():
    creditors = [(-v, p) for p, v in net.items() if v > 0]
    debtors = [(v, p) for p, v in net.items() if v < 0]
    heapq.heapify(creditors)
    heapq.heapify(debtors)
    payments = []
    while creditors and debtors:
        c_amt, c = heapq.heappop(creditors)
        d_amt, d = heapq.heappop(debtors)
        pay = min(-c_amt, -d_amt)
        payments.append((d, c, pay))           # d pays c this many pence
        if -c_amt > pay:
            heapq.heappush(creditors, (c_amt + pay, c))
        if -d_amt > pay:
            heapq.heappush(debtors, (d_amt + pay, d))
    return payments
mistakes: Floats for money.
Splits that don't add up to the total.
Losing the leftover pence when rounding.
topics.interviewAnswer: Expenses have a payer and a list of splits, created by a split strategy that checks they add up to the total. Each expense updates a net balance per user, stored in whole pence. To settle a group, I greedily match the largest debtor with the largest creditor, which needs at most n − 1 payments.

followUps.q: Why not use floats for money?
followUps.a: 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 in binary floating point. Money needs whole minor units (pence) or Decimal.
It always finishes in at most n − 1 payments, which is good. Finding the true minimum is NP-hard in general, so greedy is the practical choice.

practice.explain: Explain how balances and debt simplification work, with an example of 3 friends.
practice.draw: Draw the class diagram, including the Split subclasses.
practice.apply: Add percentage and exact splits with validation, and test that £10 split three ways gives 334, 333 and 333 pence.
practice.tradeoffs: Store every pairwise balance, or just one net balance per user? What does each make easy or hard?

explain.answer:
Three friends: Asha, Ben and Chen. Each person has one net balance, in pence: positive means they are owed money, negative means they owe.

1. Asha pays £30 for dinner, split equally: each share is £10. Ben and Chen each owe Asha £10, and Asha's own share cancels out. Balances: Asha +£20, Ben −£10, Chen −£10.
2. Ben pays £12 for a taxi, split equally: £4 each. Balances: Asha +£16, Ben −£2, Chen −£14. (They always add up to zero.)

Simplifying: instead of paying back each expense separately (Ben → Asha £10, Chen → Asha £10, Asha → Ben £4, Chen → Ben £4: four payments), match the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor, again and again:
• Chen (−£14) pays Asha (+£16) £14. Asha is now +£2, Chen is settled.
• Ben (−£2) pays Asha (+£2) £2. Everyone is at zero.
Two payments settle everything. The greedy method always needs at most n − 1 payments for n people.

draw.answer: An Expense owns its splits; the abstract Split has one subclass per way of splitting. SplitFactory builds the right splits and rejects any that don't add up to the total. Every expense updates the BalanceSheet, which DebtSimplifier reads to suggest the fewest payments.
draw.code:
Group 1 ◆── * Expense
 - members: User[*]          - payer: User
                             - amount_pence
                             - description
                             - splits ◆── 1..* Split «abstract»
                                               - user: User
                                               - amount_pence
                                                 △
                               ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
                           EqualSplit        ExactSplit       PercentSplit
                                             (given amount)   (given percent)

SplitFactory
 + create(kind, total, people, values) → Split[]  (checks the sum)
BalanceSheet
 - net: User → pence        ◄── updated by each new Expense
DebtSimplifier
 + simplify(balance_sheet) → [(from, to, pence)]

apply.answer:
Money is whole pence (integers) throughout. Each split type returns who owes what, and refuses splits that don't add up: exact amounts must sum to the total, and percentages must sum to 100. Integer division leaves a few pence over, which are handed out one each, to people in a fixed order, so the shares always add up to the total exactly.

£10 split three ways gives 334, 333 and 333 pence. £9.99 split 50/25/25 gives 500, 250 and 249: the 2 leftover pence go to the first two people.

tradeoffs.answer:
Pairwise balances (for every pair of people, how much one owes the other):
• Easy: showing "you owe Ben £6" directly, per friend and per group; settling up with one particular person; explaining where a number came from.
• Hard: storage grows with the square of the number of people; one expense updates many pairs; and paying everything back pair by pair needs many more payments than necessary.

One net balance per user:
• Easy: tiny storage (one number per person); an expense is a few additions; "am I owed or do I owe, overall?" is instant; simplifying to at most n − 1 payments falls straight out of it.
• Hard: you lose who owes whom. The simplified plan might ask you to pay someone you never shared a bill with, which confuses users, and you can't show a per-friend balance without going back to the expenses.

In practice, keep the expenses as the source of truth (they can always be replayed), keep net balances per group for speed, and work out pairwise views or simplified payments when someone asks to see or settle them.

topics.name: Design a vending machine
topics.definition: Design a vending machine that sells items, accepts coins and gives change.
topics.problem: It's the clearest test of the State pattern: every action means something different depending on the machine's state.

diagram.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Idle
  Idle --> ItemSelected: select an item
  ItemSelected --> HasMoney: enough money inserted
  ItemSelected --> Idle: cancel and refund
  HasMoney --> Dispensing: confirm
  HasMoney --> Idle: cancel and refund
  Dispensing --> Idle: item and change given
  Idle --> SoldOut: stock reaches 0
  SoldOut --> Idle: restocked
diagram.caption: Every state allows only the actions that make sense in it, so the machine can never hand out an item without enough money.

functional: Select an item, insert money, get the item and any change.
Cancel and get a refund.
Restock items and coins (admin).
nonFunctional: Never hand out an item without enough money, and never lose money.
Clear behaviour in every state.
classes: VendingMachine: current state, inventory, coin box.
State (interface) → Idle, ItemSelected, HasMoney, Dispensing, SoldOut.
Inventory: slot → item and count.
Item: name, price.
ChangeCalculator: the coins to give back.
evolution: Version 1: one item, exact coins only.
Version 2: several items, an inventory, and change-making.
Version 3: a State class for each mode, plus cancel and refund.
Version 4: card payments as a strategy, admin restocking, and recovery after a power cut.
design: Idle → select an item → ItemSelected → insert money → HasMoney (once paid ≥ price) → Dispensing → give change → Idle.
Cancel while in ItemSelected or HasMoney → refund → Idle.
An item with no stock left → SoldOut for that item.
deepDives: Change-making: the greedy method works for UK coins when you have plenty of each, but with limited coins it can fail even when exact change is possible (60p with one 50p and three 20p coins). Use dynamic programming, or refuse the sale.
Keep money in whole pence.
Power cut mid-sale: record the transaction before dispensing, so it can be recovered.
mistakes: An if/else on a status string in every method.
Taking money for an item that's sold out.
Assuming change can always be made.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd model the machine with the State pattern — Idle, ItemSelected, HasMoney, Dispensing, SoldOut — so every action is only valid in the right state. Money is in pence; change is worked out from the coins actually available, and the sale is refused if exact change isn't possible.

followUps.a: Every action (insert, select, cancel) behaves differently in each state; state classes avoid an if/else on a status field in every method.
Yes for UK coins with an unlimited supply, but not with limited coin counts. Then use dynamic programming.

practice.explain: Walk through one purchase, naming each state change.
practice.draw: Draw the state diagram, including cancel and sold-out.
practice.apply: Implement make_change, find a case where greedy fails with limited coins, and fix it with dynamic programming.
practice.tradeoffs: State classes or a transition table for this machine?

explain.answer:
Buying crisps priced at 120p:

1. Idle: the screen says "select an item".
2. You press A3. A3 is in stock, so: Idle → ItemSelected. The screen shows "120p".
3. You insert £1. 100p is less than 120p, so it stays in ItemSelected and shows "20p to pay".
4. You insert 50p. 150p is now at least 120p, so: ItemSelected → HasMoney.
5. HasMoney → Dispensing, straight away: the sale is recorded first (so a power cut can't lose it), then the crisps drop, and A3's count goes down by one.
6. Change: 150 − 120 = 30p, worked out from the coins in the machine (a 20p and a 10p) and paid out. Dispensing → Idle.

If A3 had been the last packet, it is now marked sold out, and the next person who presses A3 is told "sold out" instead of being taken to ItemSelected. Pressing cancel in ItemSelected or HasMoney refunds every coin inserted and returns to Idle.

draw.answer: Money is only taken in ItemSelected, so a coin inserted while Idle is simply returned. Dispensing can only be reached once the price is covered, and a cancel before that refunds everything.
draw.code:
select item (in stock)
Idle ───────────────────────────► ItemSelected
 ▲  │                                │ insert coin, paid < price:
 │  │ select item (none left)        │   stay (show what is left)
 │  ▼                                │ insert coin, paid ≥ price
 │ SoldOut message ── back to Idle   ▼
 │                                HasMoney
 │                                   │ automatic
 │ give change                       ▼
 └─────────────────────────────── Dispensing
                                  (record the sale,
                                   drop the item)

cancel in ItemSelected or HasMoney
  → refund every coin inserted → Idle

apply.answer:
The greedy method takes the biggest coin that fits, as many as allowed, then moves on. With plenty of every coin, that works for UK coins. With limited coins it can fail: to give 60p from one 50p and three 20p coins, greedy takes the 50p, and then needs 10p, which the machine doesn't have. But three 20p coins would have worked.

The dynamic-programming version builds up every amount it can reach, using each physical coin at most once, and keeps the way that uses the fewest coins. It finds 3 × 20p for 60p, and agrees with greedy when greedy works.

tradeoffs.answer:
For this machine, state classes, with a short table kept as documentation.

The states here don't just decide the next state; they do real work that differs by state: ItemSelected adds up coins and compares with the price, HasMoney must handle cancel by refunding, Dispensing must record the sale before driving the motor and must recover after a power cut, and SoldOut hands coins straight back. Keeping each state's logic in its own class keeps money handling in one place per state and makes each one testable alone, which matters because mistakes here lose real money.

A transition table (state → event → next state) would be the better choice if the machine were mostly a list of allowed moves with little behaviour, or if the rules had to be configured without new code. It is also the best way to show the whole machine at once, which is why it is worth drawing even when the code uses classes.

topics.name: Design an LRU cache
