topics.definition: Design a fixed-size cache that removes the least recently used item when full, with get and put in O(1).
topics.problem: It tests data-structure design under a strict time limit (O(1) operations), and it's asked both as a coding question and as a design question.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR H["head
(dummy)"] <--> N3["key 3
most recent"] <--> N1["key 1"] <--> T["tail
(dummy)"] M[("Hash map
key → node")] -.-> N3 M -.-> N1
diagram.caption: The list keeps usage order (most recent next to the head) and the map finds any node instantly. When full, the node next to the tail is removed.

functional: get(key): return the value, or nothing if missing; it counts as a use.
put(key, value): insert or update; if the cache is full, remove the least recently used item.
nonFunctional: Both operations in O(1) time.
Optionally thread-safe.
classes: LRUCache: capacity, a hash map from key to node, and a doubly linked list.
Node: key, value, previous, next.
patterns: Strategy, if the eviction policy should be swappable
evolution: Naive: a list kept in order of use. get is O(n), because you must find and move the item.
Better: a dictionary for lookups, but keeping the order still costs O(n).
Final: a dictionary plus a doubly linked list, so both operations are O(1).
Extensions: a TTL per entry, thread safety, or LFU instead of LRU.
design: A hash map finds a key's node in O(1).
A doubly linked list keeps items in order of use: most recent at the front, least recent at the back.
get: move the node to the front. put: update and move to the front, or insert at the front and remove the back node if over capacity.
deepDives: Dummy head and tail nodes remove the edge cases.
Thread safety: one lock around get and put (or several locks for parts of the cache).
In Python, OrderedDict with move_to_end does the same in a few lines; know both versions.
mistakes: A singly linked list, which can't remove a node in O(1).
Forgetting to update the order on get.
Forgetting to delete the evicted key from the dictionary.
topics.interviewAnswer: A hash map from key to node gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list keeps items in order of use. get moves the node to the front; put inserts at the front and removes the back node when over capacity. Dummy head and tail nodes keep the code simple.

followUps.a: To remove a node from the middle in O(1), you need to reach the node before it.
LRU removes the item used longest ago; LFU removes the item used least often. LFU protects popular items better but is more complex.

practice.explain: Explain why you need both a hash map and a doubly linked list.
practice.draw: Draw the list after put(1), put(2), get(1), put(3), with capacity 2.
practice.apply: Implement it from memory, then again with OrderedDict, and test both with the same sequence of calls.
practice.tradeoffs: How would you make it thread-safe, and what does that cost?

explain.answer:
An LRU cache needs two things to be fast:
1. Find an item by its key: is "user:42" in the cache?
2. Know the order of use, and change it cheaply: move an item to "most recently used" on every get, and remove the least recently used one when full.

A hash map does the first in O(1), but has no useful order. A list keeps the order, but finding a key in it takes O(n). So you use both: the map goes from key to the item's node in the list, and the list keeps the nodes in order of use.

Why doubly linked: to move a node to the front, you must unlink it from wherever it is in the middle, which means fixing its neighbours' pointers. With a link back to the previous node, that is O(1). A singly linked list would have to walk from the start to find the previous node, which is O(n). The back of the list (just before the tail sentinel) is always the least recently used item, so eviction is O(1) too.

draw.answer: Front means most recently used. get(1) moves node 1 to the front, so node 2 becomes the least recently used, and it is the one evicted when put(3) overflows the capacity of 2. The map always points at exactly the nodes in the list.
draw.code:
Capacity 2. Front of the list = most recently used.

put(1):  head ⇄ [1:a] ⇄ tail
put(2):  head ⇄ [2:b] ⇄ [1:a] ⇄ tail
get(1):  head ⇄ [1:a] ⇄ [2:b] ⇄ tail     1 moves to the front
put(3):  head ⇄ [3:c] ⇄ [1:a] ⇄ tail     full: 2 (at the back)
                                         is evicted
map after put(3): {1 → node 1, 3 → node 3}

apply.answer:
The first version is the lesson's hash map plus doubly linked list. The second uses OrderedDict, which is exactly that structure built in: move_to_end() marks a key as most recent, and popitem(last=False) removes the oldest.

Both run the same sequence of calls and give the same results. A second check runs 10,000 random gets and puts against both, with a fixed seed, and confirms they always agree.
apply.code:
import random
from collections import OrderedDict


class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=None, val=None):
        self.key, self.val, self.prev, self.next = key, val, None, None


class LRUCache:                                  # from memory: hash map + doubly linked list
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def _add_front(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return None
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_front(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, val):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])
        node = Node(key, val)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add_front(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]


class OrderedLRU:                                # the same with OrderedDict
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.data = capacity, OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)               # most recent at the end
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, val):
        self.data[key] = val
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.cap:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)        # least recent is at the start


def run(cache, ops):
    return [cache.get(op[1]) if op[0] == "get" else cache.put(op[1], op[2]) for op in ops]


ops = [("put", 1, "a"), ("put", 2, "b"), ("get", 1), ("put", 3, "c"), ("get", 2),
       ("get", 3), ("put", 1, "A"), ("put", 4, "d"), ("get", 3), ("get", 1), ("get", 4)]
gets = [r for op, r in zip(ops, run(LRUCache(2), ops)) if op[0] == "get"]
print(gets)                                      # ['a', None, 'c', None, 'A', 'd']
print(run(LRUCache(2), ops) == run(OrderedLRU(2), ops))   # True

random.seed(0)
ops = [("get", random.randrange(20)) if random.random() < 0.5 else ("put", random.randrange(20), i)
       for i in range(10_000)]
print(run(LRUCache(5), ops) == run(OrderedLRU(5), ops))   # True: 10,000 random calls agree

tradeoffs.answer:
The simple way: one lock around both get and put. get has to be inside the lock too, because it changes the list (it moves the node to the front); two threads moving nodes at once would corrupt the pointers. (Python's GIL doesn't help: a get is many steps, and a thread can switch between them.)

What it costs:
• Every operation, even a read, waits its turn, so under heavy concurrency the cache handles one request at a time and threads queue at the lock.
• A read-write lock doesn't help, because every get is a write to the order.

Ways to reduce the cost:
• Shard it: N independent LRU caches, each with its own lock, chosen by a hash of the key. Contention drops by about N; the price is that eviction is only "least recently used" within each shard.
• Approximate the order: record reads in a buffer and apply them in batches (as Java's Caffeine does), or use a CLOCK-style "recently used" bit instead of moving nodes. Redis samples a few keys and evicts the oldest of them.
• Use a well-tested concurrent cache library instead of writing your own.

topics.name: Design an order-matching engine (stock exchange)
topics.definition: Design the core of a stock exchange: an order book that matches buy and sell orders.
topics.problem: It tests data structures (heaps and queues), fairness rules, and why a single-threaded design can be both the fastest and the safest.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR BUY["Incoming: buy 6 at £101"] --> E["Matching engine
one thread per stock"] E -->|"fill 3 at £100"| A1["Ask: sell 3 at £100
(cheapest)"] E -->|"fill 3 at £101"| A2["Ask: sell 5 at £101
(2 left in the book)"] E --> T["Trades published"]
diagram.caption: The buy order fills against the cheapest sell orders first, until its price limit or quantity runs out.

functional: Place limit orders (buy or sell at a price or better).
Match orders by price, then time; allow partial fills.
Cancel orders; publish trades.
nonFunctional: Very low latency; fair and deterministic ordering.
Never lose an order or fill it twice.
classes: Order: id, side, price, quantity, time.
OrderBook (one per stock): bids and asks, first in first out at each price.
MatchingEngine: processes incoming orders against the book.
Trade: buyer, seller, price, quantity.
patterns: Command (orders as objects in a sequenced log)
evolution: Version 1: one list of orders, scanned for a match every time (slow).
Version 2: buy and sell heaps ordered by price, first in first out at each price.
Version 3: partial fills, cancels and market orders.
Version 4: one single-threaded engine per stock, fed by a queue, with an event log for replay.
design: An incoming buy order fills against the cheapest sell orders while their price is at or below the buy price, oldest first at each price.
Any quantity left over rests in the book.
Each stock's book is processed by one thread, in sequence, fed by a queue, so no locks are needed inside the book.
deepDives: Price-time priority: better price first; at the same price, the earliest order first.
One thread per stock gives determinism and avoids locks; parallelism comes from different stocks.
Log every order before processing it, so the book can be rebuilt by replay after a crash.
mistakes: Ignoring time priority at the same price.
Using locks inside the matching loop instead of processing in sequence.
Floats for prices.
topics.interviewAnswer: Each stock has an order book with bids in a max-heap and asks in a min-heap, first in first out within a price. A matching engine processes one stock's orders in sequence on a single thread: an incoming order fills against the best opposite prices while they cross, and any remainder rests in the book. Every order is logged first, so the book can be rebuilt.

followUps.a: Matching must be strictly ordered and repeatable. One thread per stock avoids locks and is very fast.
Better prices match first; at the same price, the order that arrived first matches first.

practice.explain: Explain price-time priority with a small example of 3 sell orders.
practice.draw: Draw the order book (bids and asks by price level) before and after a large buy order.
practice.apply: Add sell() and cancel() to the order book below, and test partial fills.
practice.tradeoffs: Heaps or a sorted map of price levels: which makes cancel fast?

resources.title: How to build a fast limit order book

explain.answer:
Three sell orders are waiting in the book:
• S1: sell 5 shares at £101, placed at 09:00.
• S2: sell 3 at £100, placed at 09:01.
• S3: sell 4 at £100, placed at 09:02.

A buy order arrives: buy 10 at up to £101.

Price-time priority means the best price goes first, and at the same price, the earliest order goes first. For a buyer the best price is the lowest, so the £100 level goes before £101, even though S1 was placed first.
1. £100 level, oldest first: S2 fills 3 (7 still wanted), then S3 fills 4 (3 still wanted).
2. £101 level: S1 fills 3 of its 5.

Trades: 3 @ £100, 4 @ £100, 3 @ £101. Each trade happens at the price of the order that was already waiting. S1 stays in the book with 2 shares left.

The rule is what makes the exchange fair and deterministic: improving your price gets you served first, and at equal prices, whoever came first wins.

draw.answer: Asks (sell orders) are listed from the cheapest upwards, bids (buy orders) from the highest down; the gap between the best ask and the best bid is the spread. The incoming buy at £101 takes everything at £100 and part of £101; the bids are untouched, and the £102 sellers are above the buyer's limit, so they stay.

apply.answer:
sell() mirrors buy(): it fills against the highest bids while they are at or above its price, oldest first at each price, and rests whatever is left. cancel() uses lazy deletion: finding an order inside a heap is slow, so the id is just marked as cancelled, and cancelled orders are thrown away whenever they reach the top. Each trade is (buyer, seller, price, quantity), at the resting order's price.

The test: three sells (two at £100, so time decides between them), then one buy that fills partly at each level and leaves 2 shares of S1. After S1 is cancelled, a buy at £105 finds nothing to match and rests as a bid; a later sell at £99 fills against it at £105, its price.
apply.code:
import heapq
import itertools


class OrderBook:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bids, self.asks = [], []            # heaps of (price key, time, qty, id)
        self.clock = itertools.count()
        self.cancelled = set()

    def _top(self, heap):                        # skip cancelled orders lazily
        while heap and heap[0][3] in self.cancelled:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        return heap[0] if heap else None

    def buy(self, order_id, price, qty):
        trades = []
        while qty and (top := self._top(self.asks)) and top[0] <= price:
            ask_price, t, ask_qty, ask_id = heapq.heappop(self.asks)
            fill = min(qty, ask_qty)
            trades.append((order_id, ask_id, ask_price, fill))
            qty -= fill
            if ask_qty > fill:
                heapq.heappush(self.asks, (ask_price, t, ask_qty - fill, ask_id))
        if qty:
            heapq.heappush(self.bids, (-price, next(self.clock), qty, order_id))
        return trades

    def sell(self, order_id, price, qty):
        trades = []
        while qty and (top := self._top(self.bids)) and -top[0] >= price:
            neg_price, t, bid_qty, bid_id = heapq.heappop(self.bids)
            fill = min(qty, bid_qty)
            trades.append((bid_id, order_id, -neg_price, fill))     # buyer, seller, price, qty
            qty -= fill
            if bid_qty > fill:
                heapq.heappush(self.bids, (neg_price, t, bid_qty - fill, bid_id))
        if qty:
            heapq.heappush(self.asks, (price, next(self.clock), qty, order_id))
        return trades

    def cancel(self, order_id):
        self.cancelled.add(order_id)


book = OrderBook()
book.sell("S1", 101, 5)
book.sell("S2", 100, 3)
book.sell("S3", 100, 4)                          # same price as S2, but later
print(book.buy("B1", 101, 10))
# [('B1', 'S2', 100, 3), ('B1', 'S3', 100, 4), ('B1', 'S1', 101, 3)]
print(book._top(book.asks))                      # (101, 0, 2, 'S1'): 2 of S1 left

book.cancel("S1")
print(book.buy("B2", 105, 1))                    # []: S1 is cancelled, so B2 rests as a bid
print(book.sell("S4", 99, 3))                    # [('B2', 'S4', 105, 1)]: 2 of S4 rest as an ask

tradeoffs.answer:
A sorted map of price levels makes cancel fast.

Heaps of individual orders:
• The best order is always at the top: O(1) to look at, O(log n) to remove.
• But cancel is slow: a heap isn't searchable, so finding one order is O(n), and removing it from the middle needs a re-heapify. The usual workaround is lazy deletion (mark it cancelled and skip it when it reaches the top): cancel becomes O(1), but cancelled orders stay in memory, the top must skip them, and the book's real depth at each price is hard to read.

A sorted map of price levels (a balanced tree or skip list: price → a first-in-first-out queue of orders, as a doubly linked list), plus a hash map from order id to its node:
• Cancel: look the order up by id, unlink it from its level's queue: O(1). If the level is now empty, remove it from the map: O(log P), for P price levels.
• The best price is the first or last key; matching walks the queue at that level in time order.
• Depth per price (the market-data feed) is just each level's total.

Real exchanges use the second shape (often with an array indexed by price tick instead of a tree), because traders cancel far more often than they trade.

phases.title: High-level design questions
phases.goal: Practise the classic HLD questions with the full framework: requirements, estimates, API, data model, design, deep dives and trade-offs.
phases.bigPicture: Each question reuses the core concepts. URL shortener is caching and IDs; chat is real-time connections and partitioning; news feed is fan-out; payments are transactions and idempotency. Try each one yourself for 30 minutes before reading the notes.

topics.name: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly)
topics.definition: Turn long URLs into short links, like bit.ly/x7Kp2a, that redirect to the original.
topics.problem: It's the classic first HLD question: small enough to finish, and it covers APIs, unique IDs, caching, database choice and read-heavy scaling.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U["User"] --> LB["Load balancer"] --> API["App servers"] API -->|"GET /x7Kp2a"| C[("Redis cache")] C -.->|"miss"| DB[("Database
code → long URL")] API -->|"new link"| IDS["ID range allocator
(Base62 codes)"] API -->|"click event"| Q[["Queue"]] --> AN["Analytics workers"]
diagram.caption: Redirects are served from the cache whenever possible. New links get codes from an ID allocator, and clicks are counted in the background.

functional: Create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias and expiry).
Redirect from the short URL to the long URL.
Optional: click analytics.
nonFunctional: Very read-heavy: about 100 redirects per new link.
Redirects in under about 50 ms; highly available.
Codes must be unique and, ideally, hard to guess.
estimates: 100 million new links a month ≈ 40 writes per second; × 100 reads ≈ 4,000 redirects per second on average (peak maybe 10,000–20,000).
Over 5 years: 6 billion links × about 500 bytes ≈ 3 TB.
Base62 with 7 characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, which is plenty.
dataModel: urls: code (primary key), long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at
Either SQL or a key-value store works, because all reads are by code.
evolution: Version 1: one server and one database table mapping code → URL, with a counter in the database for IDs.
Version 2: a Redis cache for redirects, so most requests never touch the database.
Version 3: many stateless app servers behind a load balancer, with ID ranges reserved per server so there's no single counter.
Version 4: shard the table by code when it outgrows one database, and send click analytics through a queue.
design: Write: the API generates a unique code and stores code → long URL.
Read: GET /{code} → check the Redis cache → on a miss, read the database → redirect.
Code generation: a distributed counter (ID ranges per server) encoded in Base62, or a hash of the URL cut to 7 characters, with collision checks.
Very popular links can also be cached at the edge.
deepDives: Counter + Base62: no collisions. Each server reserves a block of IDs from a coordinator, so servers don't fight over one counter.
Hashing: the same URL always gets the same code (no duplicates), but collisions need check-and-retry.
301 (permanent; browsers cache it, so less load but no analytics) or 302 (temporary; every click reaches you, so analytics work).
Analytics: log each click to a queue and aggregate in the background.
mistakes: Hashing the URL without handling collisions.
No caching, for a workload that's 100 times more reads than writes.
Using 301 redirects, then wondering why the analytics are empty.
topics.interviewAnswer: It's a read-heavy key-value lookup. Writes generate a unique 7-character Base62 code from a distributed counter, with ID ranges reserved per server, and store code → URL. Reads go through a Redis cache in front of the database and return a 302, so we can count clicks; click events go onto a queue for background analytics.

followUps.q: How do you stop people guessing other people's links?
followUps.a: Use random codes, or scramble the counter with a reversible shuffle, instead of handing out sequential codes.
302 if you want analytics or may change the target later; 301 if you want browsers to cache the redirect and reduce load.

practice.explain: Explain the full read path and write path in 2 minutes.
practice.draw: Draw the architecture: load balancer, API servers, ID-range allocator, cache, database and analytics queue.
practice.apply: Write Base62 encode and decode functions in Python, and encode the numbers 1, 61, 62 and 3,500,000,000.
practice.tradeoffs: Counter-based codes or hashing the URL: compare collisions, duplicates and guessability.

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a URL shortener

explain.answer:
Write path (creating a short link):
1. POST /urls with the long URL reaches a load balancer, then one of many stateless API servers.
2. The server checks the URL (valid, not on a blocklist) and, if given, that the custom alias is free.
3. It takes the next number from its reserved block of IDs (each server gets a block, say 1,000 at a time, from a small allocator, so servers never compete for one counter) and encodes it in Base62: a short code like "3ORDSU".
4. It stores code → long URL (plus owner, created and expiry times) in the database, and returns the short URL.

Read path (the redirect), about 100 times more frequent:
1. GET /3ORDSU reaches the load balancer, then an API server.
2. The server looks the code up in Redis; most popular codes are there (a hit in well under a millisecond).
3. On a miss it reads the database by primary key, then fills the cache.
4. It replies 302 with the long URL in the Location header (or 404, or 410 if expired).
5. It puts a click event on a queue for analytics, without waiting for it.

Everything is read by one key, the code, so the database scales easily (replicas, or sharding by code), and the cache does most of the work.

draw.answer: Creating a link touches the ID allocator only once per block of IDs, not per link. Redirects are served from the cache whenever possible, and click analytics happen off the request path, through the queue.
draw.code:
Client
  │
  ▼
Load balancer
  │
  ├──► API server ──┐  (stateless, many of them)
  └──► API server ──┤
                    │
  create:           │ 1. take an ID from my block
                    ├──► ID-range allocator
                    │    ("give me IDs 5,000–5,999")
                    │ 2. save code → long URL
                    ├──► Database (key: code)
                    │
  redirect:         │ 1. look up the code
                    ├──► Redis cache ── miss ──► Database
                    │ 2. reply 302 to the long URL
                    │ 3. log the click (async)
                    └──► Queue ──► Analytics workers
                                    └──► Analytics store

apply.answer:
Base62 uses the digits 0–9, then a–z, then A–Z: 62 symbols. Encoding repeatedly divides by 62 and keeps the remainders (like writing a number in base 10, but with 62 digits); decoding multiplies back.

1 is "1", 61 is "Z" (the last symbol), 62 is "10" (one 62 and nothing more), and 3,500,000,000 is "3ORDSU": 6 characters. Seven characters cover every number below 62⁷, about 3.5 trillion.

tradeoffs.answer:
Counter + Base62:
• Collisions: none. Every number is used once, so every code is unique by construction; there is no need to check the database before saving.
• Duplicates: the same long URL shortened twice gets two codes. Fine (often wanted: different owners, different stats), or look it up first if you want one code per URL.
• Guessability: bad by default. Codes are sequential, so anyone can count through them and scrape every link, and they reveal how many links you have. Fix: scramble the number before encoding (a reversible shuffle such as multiplying by a large prime modulo 62⁷), or add a few random characters.
• Cost: needs coordination, though handing out ID ranges keeps that rare.

Hashing the URL (for example MD5, keep the first 7 Base62 characters):
• Collisions: yes. With 3.5 trillion possible codes, collisions become likely after only about √3.5 trillion ≈ 1.9 million links (the birthday paradox). Every write must check whether the code is taken and, if so, retry with a salt.
• Duplicates: the same URL always gives the same code, so de-duplication comes free.
• Guessability: good: codes look random.
• Cost: no coordination, but an extra read on every write.

The usual choice is counter-based with ID ranges, plus a scramble so codes aren't sequential.

topics.name: Design a distributed rate limiter
topics.definition: A service that limits how many requests each client can make, enforced consistently across many API servers.
topics.problem: It tests algorithms (token bucket and windows), shared state across servers, atomic updates and failure handling, all in one small system.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Clients"] --> G1["Gateway node 1
(limiter)"] C --> G2["Gateway node 2
(limiter)"] G1 <-->|"atomic update"| R[("Redis cluster
token buckets")] G2 <-->|"atomic update"| R G1 --> S["Services"] G2 --> S CFG["Rules config"] -.-> G1 CFG -.-> G2
diagram.caption: Every gateway node checks the same buckets in Redis, so a client's limit is shared across all nodes.

functional: Limit requests per user, API key or IP address per time window (for example 100 per minute).
Different rules for different endpoints.
Reject with 429 and tell the client when to retry.
nonFunctional: Adds very little latency (1–2 ms at most).
Highly available, and accurate enough across servers.
Handles millions of clients.
estimates: 10 million active clients × one counter each × about 100 bytes ≈ 1 GB in Redis: it easily fits in memory.
dataModel: One Redis key per client per rule: tokens and last refill time (token bucket), or a counter with a TTL (fixed window).
evolution: Version 1: an in-memory counter per user on one server.
Version 2: many servers, so the counters move to Redis.
Version 3: atomic updates with a Lua script, a token bucket for bursts, and rules from configuration.
Version 4: several regions, a fail-open fallback, and monitoring of rejected requests.
design: The limiter runs as middleware in the API gateway.
Rules are loaded from a config store and cached locally.
Counters live in a Redis cluster and are checked and updated atomically with a Lua script (or INCR plus EXPIRE for fixed windows).
Over the limit → 429 with Retry-After.
deepDives: Race conditions: two servers reading and writing the same counter at once → use atomic Redis operations or a Lua script.
Multiple regions: a limit per region (slightly inaccurate) or a global store (slower).
Redis failure: fail open, with a local in-memory limit as a backup.
Hot clients: spread counters across Redis nodes by client ID.
mistakes: Read-then-write counters with no atomicity.
Limiting per server instead of across all servers.
No answer to 'what if Redis is down?'.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd enforce limits in the API gateway using a token bucket per client and rule, with state in a Redis cluster updated atomically by a Lua script, adding about a millisecond. Rules come from configuration. Requests over the limit get 429 with Retry-After. If Redis is unavailable, the gateway fails open with a local backup limit.

followUps.a: It runs the read, the refill and the decrement as one atomic step inside Redis, so two requests can't both take the last token.

followUps.q: How accurate is it across regions?
followUps.a: Per-region limits are fast but can let a client go slightly over the global limit; a global store is accurate but adds cross-region latency.

practice.explain: Explain where the limiter sits and what happens on each request.
practice.draw: Draw clients → gateway (with the limiter) → services, with Redis beside the gateway.
practice.apply: Implement a sliding-window-log limiter in Python, then sketch the Redis commands you would use for it.
practice.tradeoffs: Token bucket or sliding window for an API that should allow short bursts?

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a rate limiter
Scaling your API with rate limiters

explain.answer:
The limiter sits in the API gateway, as middleware that runs before the request is passed to any service, so blocked requests never cost the services anything.

On each request:
1. Identify who is asking: the API key, the user ID from the token, or the IP address if there is no login.
2. Find the rule for this endpoint and client tier (for example, "search: 100 per minute"). Rules come from a config store and are cached in the gateway's memory.
3. Check and update the client's counter in Redis in one atomic step (a Lua script, or INCR for a fixed window), so two gateways can't both think there is room.
4. Allowed: forward the request, adding headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining.
5. Not allowed: reply 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and don't call the service.

The whole check should add a millisecond or two. If Redis is down, fall back to a local in-memory limit per gateway (fail open, but not unlimited).

draw.answer: The limit is checked once, at the edge, and shared through Redis, so it holds whichever gateway a request lands on. Rules are read from the config store occasionally, never on every request.
draw.code:
Clients
  │
  ▼
Load balancer
  ├──────────────┬──────────────┐
  ▼              ▼              ▼
Gateway 1      Gateway 2      Gateway 3
[limiter]      [limiter]      [limiter]
  │  ▲             │              │
  │  │ atomic check and update    │
  └──┴──────► Redis cluster ◄─────┘
     │        (one counter per client per rule)
     │
     ├── over the limit → 429 + Retry-After
     └── allowed ──► Services

Config store ── rules, cached in each gateway

apply.answer:
The sliding-window log keeps, per client, the times of the requests it allowed in the last window. Each new request first forgets times older than the window, then is allowed only if fewer than the limit remain. Unlike a fixed window, there is no edge where a client can fire twice the limit.

With a limit of 3 per 60 seconds: requests at 0, 10 and 20 s pass; 30 and 59 s are refused; at 60.5 s the request from 0 s has dropped out, so one more passes; at 61 s the window is full again; at 75 s the 10 s request has dropped out.

In Redis, keep one sorted set per client, with timestamps as scores, and run these steps atomically in a Lua script:
• ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:{client} 0 (now − 60000): drop entries older than the window.
• ZCARD rl:{client}: count what is left.
• If the count is below the limit: ZADD rl:{client} now {unique request id}, then PEXPIRE rl:{client} 60000, and allow; otherwise refuse.

The cost: memory for every allowed request, per client. At high limits, a sliding-window counter (two fixed-window counts, weighted) is the cheaper approximation.
apply.code:
from collections import deque


class SlidingWindowLog:
    def __init__(self, limit, window_s, clock):
        self.limit, self.window, self.clock = limit, window_s, clock
        self.logs = {}                              # client -> times of allowed requests

    def allow(self, client):
        now = self.clock()
        log = self.logs.setdefault(client, deque())
        while log and log[0] <= now - self.window:  # forget requests outside the window
            log.popleft()
        if len(log) < self.limit:
            log.append(now)
            return True
        return False


now = [0.0]                                         # a fake clock, in seconds
limiter = SlidingWindowLog(limit=3, window_s=60, clock=lambda: now[0])
results = []
for t in [0, 10, 20, 30, 59, 60.5, 61, 75]:
    now[0] = t
    results.append((t, limiter.allow("key-1")))
print(results)
# [(0, True), (10, True), (20, True), (30, False), (59, False), (60.5, True), (61, False), (75, True)]

tradeoffs.answer:
Token bucket.

It is built for exactly this: the bucket's size is the burst you allow, and the refill rate is the steady limit. A client that has been quiet can fire, say, 20 requests at once; a client that keeps hammering is held to 10 a second. Per client it stores just two numbers (tokens and last refill time), so it is cheap in memory and in Redis.

Sliding window (log or counter) is about fairness over a moving window: never more than N in any 60 seconds. It allows a burst of up to N at once too, but then the client must wait for the whole window to slide before it gets capacity back, which feels stricter than a refill. The log version is exact but stores a timestamp per request; the counter version is cheap but approximate.

So: token bucket when bursts are welcome and you care about the long-run rate (most public APIs); sliding window when the hard rule is "never more than N per window" (for example, a contract with a partner, or login attempts).

topics.name: Design a notification system
topics.definition: Send notifications (mobile push, SMS, email) to users reliably, at large scale.
topics.problem: It tests queues, priorities, third-party integrations, retries and avoiding duplicates — everyday problems in real products.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR P["Order, login and
marketing services"] --> N["Notification service
preferences · templates · limits"] N --> QH[["High-priority queue
(passcodes)"]] N --> QL[["Low-priority queue
(marketing)"]] QH & QL --> W["Channel workers"] W --> PUSH["Apple and Google push"] W --> SMS["SMS provider"] W --> EM["Email provider"] W -.->|"failed too often"| DLQ[["Dead-letter queue"]]
diagram.caption: Messages are checked once, then queued by priority, so a marketing blast never delays a passcode. Workers deliver through outside providers.

functional: Services trigger notifications (order shipped, one-time passcodes, marketing).
Channels: push, SMS, email; respect each user's preferences and opt-outs.
Templates, scheduling, and retries on failure.
nonFunctional: Millions a day, with big spikes during campaigns.
Passcodes must arrive in seconds; marketing can be slower.
Delivered at least once, without spamming duplicates.
estimates: 10 million push + 1 million SMS + 5 million emails a day ≈ 200 per second on average; campaigns can be 10–100 times higher.
api: POST /notifications {user_id, type, template_id, data, channels?, send_at?}
dataModel: user_preferences (user_id, channel, opted_in)
devices (user_id, push_token)
notification_log (id, user_id, channel, status, created_at)
evolution: Version 1: the order service calls the email provider directly.
Version 2: a notification service with templates and user preferences.
Version 3: a queue per channel, workers, retries and a dead-letter queue.
Version 4: priority lanes, idempotency keys, provider failover and per-user rate limits.
design: A notification service checks preferences and rate limits, and fills in the template.
It puts messages onto separate queues per channel (push, SMS, email) and per priority (passcodes ahead of marketing).
Channel workers call the providers (Apple and Google push services, an SMS gateway, an email service).
Retries with backoff; repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue; every status is recorded in a log.
deepDives: De-duplication: an idempotency key per notification, so retries don't send twice.
Separate priority queues, so a marketing blast never delays a passcode.
Provider failover: a second SMS provider.
A per-user rate limit, so nobody gets spammed.
mistakes: Sending inside the user's request.
One queue where marketing messages block passcodes.
Retries without idempotency, so users get duplicates.
topics.interviewAnswer: Producers call a notification service that checks preferences, fills in templates and puts messages on queues per channel and priority. Workers deliver through providers like Apple and Google push services and SMS gateways, with retries, dead-letter queues and idempotency keys to avoid duplicates. Passcodes get a high-priority lane, so campaigns never delay them.

followUps.q: How do you avoid sending the same notification twice?
followUps.a: An idempotency key per notification, checked in a store before sending; the worker records 'sent' only after success.

followUps.q: What if a provider goes down?
followUps.a: Retry with backoff, then fail over to a backup provider, and circuit-break the failing one.

practice.explain: Explain the flow from 'order shipped' to a phone notification.
practice.draw: Draw the service, the queues per channel and priority, the workers and the providers.
practice.apply: Design the data model for preferences, devices and the delivery log, with keys.
practice.tradeoffs: One queue for everything, or separate queues per channel and priority?

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a notification system

explain.answer:
1. The order service marks order 105 as shipped and publishes an "OrderShipped" event (through its outbox, so the event can't be lost). The notification service consumes it, or the order service calls POST /notifications, with an idempotency key such as "order-105-shipped".
2. The notification service checks the key against its log: if this notification was already handled, it stops (no duplicates).
3. It checks the user's preferences: is push allowed for order updates? Is the user opted out of everything? It applies a per-user rate limit.
4. It looks up the user's active devices and their push tokens.
5. It fills in the template ("Your order 105 has shipped") in the user's language.
6. It puts one message per device on the push queue for normal priority, and records "queued" in the log.
7. A push worker takes the message and calls Apple's (APNs) or Google's (FCM) push service with the device token.
8. The provider delivers it to the phone. The worker records "sent". If the provider says the token is no longer valid, the device is marked inactive. A temporary failure is retried with backoff; after several failures, it goes to a dead-letter queue.

draw.answer: Separate queues per channel and priority mean a marketing blast can't delay a passcode, and each worker pool can be scaled and rate-limited to match its provider. Every step updates the delivery log.
draw.code:
Services ── events / POST /notifications ──► Notification service
(orders, auth, marketing)                     1. de-duplicate (key)
                                              2. preferences, opt-outs
                                              3. per-user rate limit
                                              4. fill in the template
                                                 │
       ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼           ▼           ▼
  push: high     push: low     SMS: high    email: high  email: low
  (passcodes)   (marketing)   (passcodes)   (receipts)  (newsletters)
       │              │              │           │           │
       ▼              ▼              ▼           ▼           ▼
  Push workers                  SMS workers   Email workers
       │                             │             │
       ▼                             ▼             ▼
  APNs / FCM                SMS gateway (+ backup)  Email provider

Failures: retry with backoff ──► dead-letter queue
Every status ──► delivery log

apply.answer:
• user_preferences is keyed by (user, channel, category), so a user can turn off marketing emails but keep order texts, and security messages can be treated as always on.
• devices has its own id, because one user has several phones; the push token is unique, and tokens the provider rejects are marked inactive rather than deleted.
• notification_log uses the notification's id as its primary key, which doubles as the idempotency key: retrying the same notification can't create a second row. It is indexed by user and time for "what did we send this person?".

At millions of rows a day, the log would be partitioned by day (and old partitions dropped after, say, 90 days), or kept in a wide-column store.
apply.code:
-- PostgreSQL
CREATE TABLE user_preferences (
  user_id     BIGINT  NOT NULL,
  channel     TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('push', 'sms', 'email')),
  category    TEXT    NOT NULL,          -- 'security', 'orders', 'marketing'
  opted_in    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, channel, category)
);

CREATE TABLE devices (
  device_id   UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  platform    TEXT   NOT NULL CHECK (platform IN ('ios', 'android', 'web')),
  push_token  TEXT   NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  active      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,     -- false once the provider rejects the token
  last_seen   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX devices_by_user ON devices (user_id) WHERE active;

CREATE TABLE notification_log (
  notification_id  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,             -- also the idempotency key
  user_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  channel          TEXT   NOT NULL,
  template_id      TEXT   NOT NULL,
  priority         TEXT   NOT NULL,              -- 'high' or 'low'
  status           TEXT   NOT NULL,              -- queued, sent, delivered, failed, skipped
  provider_msg_id  TEXT,
  attempts         INT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX log_by_user_time ON notification_log (user_id, created_at DESC);

tradeoffs.answer:
One queue for everything:
• Simple: one thing to run, monitor and scale.
• But head-of-line blocking: a 10-million-email newsletter sits in front of a one-time passcode, and the passcode arrives an hour late, so the user can't log in.
• One slow provider (an SMS gateway limiting you to 100 a second) backs up push and email too.
• You can't scale or rate-limit one channel without the others.

Separate queues per channel and priority:
• Isolation: passcodes have their own fast lane; a struggling SMS provider only slows SMS.
• Each worker pool is sized and rate-limited to match its provider's limits.
• Retries and dead-letter queues per channel, so failures are easier to see and fix.
• The cost: more queues to set up and monitor, routing logic, and a rule so low priority isn't starved forever (for example, workers take 9 high-priority messages for every 1 low).

For notifications, separate queues are clearly worth it: different channels and priorities really do have different speeds, limits and urgency.

topics.name: Design a chat app (like WhatsApp)
topics.definition: One-to-one and group messaging, with delivery receipts and online status.
topics.problem: It tests real-time connections, routing between servers, storage for enormous write volumes, ordering and offline delivery.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["User A"] <--> G1["Gateway 1"] B["User B"] <--> G2["Gateway 2"] G1 --> CS["Chat service"] CS --> MS[("Message store
by conversation")] CS --> R[("Redis
who is connected where")] CS --> G2 CS -.->|"B is offline"| PN["Push notification"]
diagram.caption: The chat service stores every message first, then routes it to the recipient's gateway, or sends a push notification if they're offline.

functional: Send and receive messages in real time, one-to-one and in groups.
Message history across devices; delivery to users who were offline.
Sent, delivered and read receipts; online and last-seen status.
nonFunctional: Low latency (under about 200 ms).
Messages are never lost, and stay in order within a conversation.
Billions of messages a day.
estimates: 500 million daily users × 40 messages ≈ 20 billion messages a day ≈ 230,000 per second on average.
20 billion × about 100 bytes ≈ 2 TB of text a day.
api: WebSocket events: send_message {conversation_id, client_msg_id, text}, ack, receipt
dataModel: messages: partition key conversation_id, sort key message_id (time-ordered), in a Cassandra-style store
conversations and members; user → connected gateway (Redis)
evolution: Version 1: one server; clients poll a database for new messages.
Version 2: WebSockets to that server, pushing instead of polling.
Version 3: many gateway servers plus a registry of who is connected where, with messages routed between gateways.
Version 4: a partitioned message store, push notifications for offline users, receipts, presence and groups.
design: Each client keeps a WebSocket connection to a chat gateway server.
Sending: gateway → chat service gives the message a time-ordered ID and stores it, then routes it.
Routing: look up the recipient's gateway in Redis and push to it; if they're offline, keep it stored and send a push notification.
Groups: send a copy to each member (small groups), or have members fetch it (very large groups).
Receipts and presence are small events that travel the same path.
deepDives: Ordering: a sequence number per conversation; clients sort by it.
Retries without duplicates: the client creates a message ID, so resending is idempotent.
Presence: heartbeats with a TTL in Redis; don't broadcast every status change to everyone.
End-to-end encryption: the server only ever stores ciphertext.
mistakes: Polling at scale.
Forgetting offline users.
No plan for ordering or duplicates.
topics.interviewAnswer: Clients hold WebSocket connections to gateway servers, and Redis maps each user to their gateway. The chat service stores every message in a Cassandra-style store partitioned by conversation, with a time-ordered ID, then routes it to the recipient's gateway — or keeps it and sends a push notification if they're offline. Client-generated message IDs make retries safe.

followUps.q: How do you handle a group with 100,000 members?
followUps.a: Don't write a copy for every member. Store the message once and let members fetch it, or deliver lazily as they come online.

followUps.q: How does a new phone get old messages?
followUps.a: History is stored on the server by conversation; the device syncs from the last message ID it has.

practice.explain: Explain how a message reaches a user on a different gateway, and what happens if they're offline.
practice.draw: Draw the clients, gateways, Redis routing and presence, chat service, message store and push service.
practice.apply: Choose the partition key and sort key for messages, and explain the main query they serve.
practice.tradeoffs: Fan-out on write or on read for group messages?

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a chat system

explain.answer:
Asha (on gateway 1) sends Ben (on gateway 7) a message:
1. Asha's app sends it over her WebSocket, with a message id it created itself (client_msg_id), so a resend can't create a duplicate.
2. Gateway 1 passes it to the chat service, which gives it a time-ordered id and the next sequence number for the conversation, and stores it in the message store. Only then does Asha get an acknowledgement ("sent", one tick).
3. The chat service looks Ben up in the routing store (Redis: user → gateway). He is on gateway 7, so it forwards the message there, and gateway 7 pushes it down Ben's WebSocket.
4. Ben's app acknowledges it, and "delivered" (two ticks) travels back the same way to Asha; "read" follows when he opens the chat.

If Ben is offline: Redis has no gateway for him (his entry expired when his heartbeats stopped). The message is already safely stored, so nothing is lost. The chat service asks the push service to send a notification. When Ben reconnects, his app sends the last sequence number it has for each conversation and fetches everything after it, in order; then the delivered receipts go back to Asha.

draw.answer: Gateways hold the long-lived connections and nothing else; the chat service decides where each message goes, using the routing table in Redis. A message is stored before it is acknowledged, so a crash anywhere after that point loses nothing.
draw.code:
Asha ══ WebSocket ══ Gateway 1        Gateway 7 ══ WebSocket ══ Ben
                        │                 ▲
                        │ send            │ 4. push to Ben
                        ▼                 │
                     Chat service ────────┘
                      │  │  │  3. where is Ben?
                      │  │  └──────► Redis
                      │  │            · user → gateway
                      │  │            · presence (heartbeat, TTL)
                      │  │ 2. store first
                      │  └─────────► Message store
                      │              (partition: conversation)
                      │ Ben offline?
                      └────────────► Push service ──► APNs / FCM

apply.answer:
Partition key: the conversation (plus a time bucket); sort key: the message id, newest first.

The main query is "show the latest 50 messages in this chat", then "older ones as I scroll up". With conversation_id in the partition key, all of a chat's messages live together on the same nodes, so that query reads one partition, with no scatter across the cluster. With the time-ordered message id as the clustering (sort) key, they are already stored in order, so reading the newest 50, or the 50 before a cursor, is a single sequential read.

Why add a bucket (such as the month)? A very busy group chat that runs for years would otherwise become one enormous partition. Splitting it by month keeps partitions bounded; reading older history moves to the previous bucket.

Message ids are Snowflake-style: unique and time-ordered, so they double as the sort key and the pagination cursor.
apply.code:
-- Cassandra (CQL)
CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id  UUID,
  bucket           INT,          -- e.g. year * 100 + month; bounds the partition size
  message_id       BIGINT,       -- Snowflake-style: unique and time-ordered
  sender_id        BIGINT,
  body             BLOB,         -- end-to-end encrypted
  PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

-- The main query: the newest page, then older pages using a cursor
SELECT message_id, sender_id, body
FROM messages
WHERE conversation_id = ? AND bucket = ? AND message_id < ?
LIMIT 50;

tradeoffs.answer:
Fan-out on write: when a message is sent to a group, put a copy (or a pointer) into every member's inbox, and push it to each online member straight away.
• Reads are trivial: each member reads their own inbox, and unread counts are easy.
• Writes multiply by the group size: one message to a 256-member group is 256 writes, and a 100,000-member channel is 100,000 writes per message.

Fan-out on read: store the message once, in the group's timeline; each member fetches from the timeline using their own "last read" cursor.
• Writes are a single row, whatever the group size.
• Reads do more work, and every member's unread count and receipts need separate tracking.

The usual answer depends on group size. Small groups (WhatsApp caps them at around a thousand members) use fan-out on write: the multiplication is bounded and the experience is instant. Huge broadcast channels use fan-out on read, with online members notified that "there is something new" rather than sent a copy each.

topics.name: Design a news feed (like Twitter or Instagram)
topics.definition: Show each user a feed of recent posts from the people they follow.
topics.problem: It tests the fan-out trade-off — do the work when posting or when reading — plus caching and the celebrity problem.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD P["A normal user posts"] --> FW["Fan-out workers"] FW --> F1[("Followers' feed lists
in Redis")] CEL["A celebrity posts"] --> CP[("Celebrity post store")] R["A user opens their feed"] --> FS["Feed service"] FS --> F1 FS -->|"merge at read time"| CP
diagram.caption: Normal posts are pushed into followers' feeds when written. Celebrity posts are pulled and merged in when a feed is read.

functional: Create posts; follow and unfollow users.
View a personalised feed (newest first, or ranked), with pagination.
nonFunctional: The feed loads fast (under about 200 ms); very read-heavy.
Eventual consistency is fine: a post can appear a few seconds later.
estimates: 300 million daily users × 10 feed views ≈ 35,000 reads per second; 2 posts each a day ≈ 7,000 writes per second.
dataModel: posts (post_id, author_id, content, created_at)
follows (follower_id, followee_id)
feed cache: user_id → recent post IDs (Redis)
evolution: Version 1: fan-out on read: query the posts of everyone you follow, sorted by time.
Version 2: fan-out on write into per-user feed lists in Redis.
Version 3: a hybrid that handles celebrities differently.
Version 4: ranking, media through a CDN, and skipping inactive users.
design: Fan-out on write (push): when someone posts, add the post ID to each follower's feed list. Reads are fast.
Fan-out on read (pull): build the feed at request time from the followed users' recent posts. Writes are cheap; reads are slow.
Hybrid: push for normal users; for celebrities with millions of followers, pull their posts at read time and merge.
Post content comes from a cache and media from a CDN; a ranking service can reorder the feed.
deepDives: The celebrity problem: pushing to 50 million followers for every post is far too expensive → use the hybrid.
Each user's feed list keeps only the latest few hundred post IDs.
Skip pushing to inactive users; build their feed when they log in.
Ranking: gather candidates → score them with a model → re-rank for variety.
mistakes: Push-only fan-out that ignores celebrities.
Storing whole posts in every feed instead of post IDs.
Offset pagination on a feed that keeps changing.
topics.interviewAnswer: I'd use a hybrid fan-out. When a normal user posts, workers push the post ID into each follower's feed list in Redis, so reading is a fast cache lookup. Celebrity posts aren't fanned out; their recent posts are fetched at read time and merged in. Post bodies come from a cache and media from a CDN.

followUps.q: Why not fan out on write for everyone?
followUps.a: A celebrity with 50 million followers would cause 50 million writes per post: slow and wasteful.

followUps.q: How do you paginate a feed that keeps changing?
followUps.a: With a cursor: continue from the last post ID the user saw, so new posts don't shift the pages.

practice.explain: Explain push, pull and hybrid fan-out, and the celebrity problem.
practice.draw: Draw the write path and the read path for the hybrid design.
practice.apply: Estimate how many writes one celebrity post causes with push fan-out, and compare with the hybrid.
practice.tradeoffs: A chronological feed or a ranked feed: what changes in the architecture?

resources.title: Hello Interview: design a news feed system
Hello Interview: design a news feed

explain.answer:
• Push (fan-out on write): when someone posts, add the post's id to the feed list of every follower straight away. Reading a feed is then just reading one ready-made list: very fast. The cost is at write time: one post makes as many writes as the author has followers.
• Pull (fan-out on read): store each post once. When someone opens their feed, fetch the recent posts of everyone they follow and merge them. Posting is cheap, but every feed load does a lot of work, and feeds are read far more often than posts are written.
• Hybrid: push for ordinary users, who have hundreds of followers; pull for the few accounts with millions. At read time, the pre-built feed list is merged with the recent posts of the celebrities you follow.

The celebrity problem: with pure push, one post from an account with 50 million followers means 50 million feed writes. It swamps the fan-out workers and delays everyone else's posts, and most of those followers won't even open the app today. The hybrid avoids it: celebrities' posts are fetched when someone actually reads.

draw.answer: On write, only ordinary authors' posts are fanned out to followers' feed lists; a celebrity's post is just stored. On read, the ready-made feed list is merged with the latest posts of the few celebrities the reader follows, then hydrated (ids turned into full posts) and optionally ranked.
draw.code:
WRITE
Author ── POST /posts ──► Post service ──► Posts DB + post cache
                             │
                             ├─ ordinary author ──► Fan-out queue
                             │                        │ workers
                             │                        ▼
                             │        each follower's feed list (Redis)
                             │        user → [latest ~500 post ids]
                             │
                             └─ celebrity ──► only their own post list

READ
Reader ── GET /feed ──► Feed service
                          1. read my feed list (Redis)
                          2. + latest posts of celebrities I follow
                          3. merge by time (or rank)
                          4. hydrate: post cache, media via CDN
                          ──► page of posts + cursor

apply.answer:
With pure push, one post from an account with 50 million followers is 50 million feed-list writes; at 5 posts a day, 250 million writes a day from one account.

To put that in proportion: all ordinary posting (7,000 posts a second × about 200 followers each) is about 1.4 million feed writes a second. One celebrity post is 50 million ÷ 1.4 million ≈ 36 seconds of the whole system's normal fan-out capacity, arriving all at once, and delaying everyone else's posts behind it.

With the hybrid: the post is written once (to the celebrity's own post list): 1 write instead of 50 million. The cost moves to reads: each follower's feed load does one extra lookup, "latest posts of the celebrities I follow", which is a few hot keys that sit in a replicated cache.

(Even with push, skipping inactive followers helps: if only 30% open the app today, that is 15 million writes, not 50; the others' feeds are built when they log in.)
apply.code:
followers = 50_000_000
posts_per_day = 5
normal_fanout_per_s = 7_000 * 200                 # every ordinary post, ~200 followers each

print(followers * posts_per_day)                  # 250000000 feed writes a day, pure push
print(round(followers / normal_fanout_per_s, 1))  # 35.7 seconds of normal fan-out, per post

tradeoffs.answer:
Chronological feed:
• The feed list is just post ids in time order, so fan-out stores them sorted and reading is a range read.
• Caching is simple, and pagination is a simple cursor ("posts older than this one").
• Behaviour is predictable and easy to explain.

Ranked feed: the architecture grows several new parts:
• Candidate generation: gather a few hundred possible posts (the fan-out list, plus celebrity posts, plus recommended posts from accounts you don't follow).
• Features: a feature store with signals per post and per user (likes so far, how often you interact with the author, the post's age), fetched at read time.
• A ranking service that scores candidates with a model, inside the latency budget (tens of milliseconds).
• Re-ranking for variety and rules (not five posts in a row from one author; remove what you have already seen).
• Logging of what was shown and what was clicked, to train the next model, plus experiment infrastructure for A/B tests.
• Pagination gets harder: the ranked list changes between requests, so you store the ranked result for the session and page through that.

In short: chronological is a data-structure problem; ranked is that, plus a machine-learning system on every read.

topics.name: Design a video streaming platform (like YouTube or Netflix)
topics.definition: Upload, process and stream videos to millions of viewers.
topics.problem: It tests large-file handling, background processing pipelines, CDNs and adaptive streaming — dealing with petabytes, not just requests.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR U["Uploader"] -->|"pre-signed URL"| RAW[("Raw video
object storage")] RAW -->|"event"| Q[["Queue"]] --> T["Transcoding workers
segments × qualities"] T --> ENC[("Encoded segments
and manifest")] ENC --> CDN["CDN"] --> V["Viewers
adaptive bitrate"]
diagram.caption: Upload, then convert in the background, then deliver from the CDN. Viewers' players pick the quality that suits their connection.

functional: Upload videos and process them into several resolutions.
Stream with quality that adapts to the viewer's connection; search and view details.
View counts and likes.
nonFunctional: Smooth playback worldwide; enormous bandwidth.
Uploads are never lost; processing may take minutes.
Reads are highly available.
estimates: 5 million daily viewers × 5 videos × about 300 MB ≈ 7.5 PB of video sent a day — which is why CDNs are essential.
dataModel: videos (id, owner_id, title, status, manifest_url)
Raw and encoded files in object storage.
evolution: Version 1: upload a file to a server and serve it as it is.
Version 2: files in object storage, details in a database.
Version 3: a transcoding pipeline driven by a queue, producing several qualities.
Version 4: segments with HLS or DASH, adaptive bitrate, CDN delivery, and view counts in the background.
design: Upload: the client gets a pre-signed URL and uploads in parts straight to object storage.
An event on a queue triggers transcoding workers, which cut the video into short segments and encode several resolutions and bitrates (a graph of tasks).
The outputs go to object storage, with a manifest (HLS or DASH) listing the segments for each quality.
Playback: the player fetches the manifest and segments from a CDN and switches quality as bandwidth changes (adaptive bitrate).
Video details live in a database with a cache; view counts are aggregated in the background.
deepDives: Adaptive bitrate: small segments (2–10 seconds) at several qualities.
Transcoding runs in parallel per segment, with retries per task.
Popular videos sit on the CDN; rarely watched ones are served from origin.
Resumable uploads for big files.
mistakes: Streaming from your own servers instead of a CDN.
Transcoding inside the upload request.
One quality for every device and connection.
topics.interviewAnswer: Uploads go straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs. A queue triggers transcoding workers that encode short segments at several bitrates and write HLS or DASH manifests. Viewers stream the segments from a CDN with adaptive bitrate. Video details live in a database behind a cache, and view counts are aggregated in the background.

followUps.a: Segments can be transcoded in parallel, cached by the CDN, and let the player switch quality in the middle of a video.

followUps.q: How do you count views at this scale?
followUps.a: Send view events to a stream, aggregate them in batches, and update the stored total periodically.

practice.explain: Explain the pipeline from upload to playback in 2 minutes.
practice.draw: Draw the upload, the transcoding pipeline, storage, the CDN and the player.
practice.apply: Estimate the storage for one 10-minute video encoded at 4 qualities: 0.5, 1, 3 and 6 Mbps.
practice.tradeoffs: Build your own CDN (like Netflix) or use a commercial one?

explain.answer:
Upload: the app asks the API for a pre-signed upload URL and sends the video straight to object storage, in parts, so a dropped connection resumes instead of restarting. The API records the video as "processing".

Processing: the upload triggers an event on a queue. Transcoding workers split the video into short segments (a few seconds each) and encode every segment at several qualities (say 240p up to 4K, each at its own bitrate). This is a graph of tasks: split, encode in parallel, package. Each task is retried on its own if it fails. Thumbnails are made too.

Output: the encoded segments go into object storage, along with a manifest file (HLS or DASH) that lists, for each quality, the segment files in order. The video's status becomes "ready", with the manifest's URL.

Playback: the player fetches the manifest and the segments from a CDN close to the viewer. It measures how fast segments arrive and picks the quality for the next one: if the connection slows, it drops to a lower bitrate without stopping (adaptive bitrate streaming). Views and likes are counted asynchronously; video details come from a database behind a cache.

draw.answer: Uploads and playback both bypass the API servers for the heavy bytes: uploads go straight to object storage, and playback comes from the CDN. The transcoding pipeline sits between the two, driven by a queue.
draw.code:
UPLOAD
Creator app ── 1. ask for an upload URL ──► API ──► Videos DB (status: processing)
     │ 2. upload in parts (pre-signed URL)
     ▼
Object storage: raw video
     │ 3. "video uploaded" event
     ▼
Queue ──► Transcoding pipeline
           split into segments
             ├─► encode 240p ┐
             ├─► encode 720p ├─ in parallel, retried per task
             └─► encode 4K   ┘
           package: HLS/DASH manifest + segments, thumbnails
     │
     ▼
Object storage: encoded segments ──► Videos DB (status: ready)

PLAYBACK
Viewer's player ── manifest + segments ──► CDN edge
     ▲                                       │ miss
     │ picks the quality for                 ▼
     │ each segment by bandwidth      Object storage (origin)
     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

apply.answer:
Storage = bitrate × duration. 10 minutes is 600 seconds; bitrates are in megabits a second, so divide by 8 for megabytes.

• 0.5 Mbps: 37.5 MB
• 1 Mbps: 75 MB
• 3 Mbps: 225 MB
• 6 Mbps: 450 MB

Total: 787.5 MB, about 0.8 GB for one 10-minute video, and about 2.4 GB with 3 copies for durability. Add the original upload (often kept, at a high bitrate) and thumbnails. Notice that the top quality alone is more than half the total, which is why rarely watched videos are sometimes kept only at lower qualities, or re-encoded on demand.
apply.code:
seconds = 10 * 60
bitrates_mbps = [0.5, 1, 3, 6]
megabytes = [rate * seconds / 8 for rate in bitrates_mbps]   # megabits → megabytes
print(megabytes)                          # [37.5, 75.0, 225.0, 450.0]
print(sum(megabytes), sum(megabytes) * 3) # 787.5 2362.5: MB once, and with 3 copies

tradeoffs.answer:
Use a commercial CDN (Akamai, Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront…), and build your own only at Netflix's scale.

Commercial CDN:
• Global reach on day one, paid per gigabyte, with nothing to build or run.
• Proven security and DDoS protection.
• Downsides: at enormous volume, per-gigabyte prices add up to a very large bill, and you have less control over caching, placement and hardware. Many large companies use several CDNs at once, for price and resilience.

Your own CDN (Netflix's Open Connect puts its own servers inside internet providers' networks):
• At the scale where you are a large share of all internet traffic, owning the boxes is far cheaper per gigabyte.
• Full control: tomorrow's popular shows are copied to the boxes overnight, when networks are quiet; tuned hardware and software.
• Downsides: huge upfront cost, agreements with thousands of internet providers, teams to run hardware around the world, and years to build.

It only pays off when traffic is huge, predictable, and mostly a known catalogue that can be placed in advance, which describes Netflix and very few others.

topics.name: Design a ride-hailing app (like Uber)
topics.definition: Match riders with nearby drivers in real time, track trips and charge fares.
topics.problem: It tests geospatial search, very high-volume updates, real-time matching and preventing double-booking.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR D["Driver apps"] -->|"location every 4 s"| LS["Location service"] --> GEO[("Geo index in memory
geohash cells")] R["Rider app"] -->|"request a ride"| M["Matching service"] M -->|"search nearby cells"| GEO M -->|"offer and lock a driver"| D M --> TS["Trip service"] --> DB[("Trips database")]
diagram.caption: Driver locations flow into a fast in-memory map. A ride request searches nearby cells, then offers the trip to one driver, locked so nobody else can book them.

functional: Drivers send their location every few seconds.
A rider requests a ride; the system finds nearby drivers and offers the trip.
Track the trip live; work out the fare and take payment.
nonFunctional: Matching within seconds; a very high volume of location updates.
A driver must never be given two trips at once.
estimates: 1 million active drivers × one update every 4 seconds ≈ 250,000 location writes per second.
dataModel: Live driver locations in memory, indexed by geohash cell.
trips (id, rider_id, driver_id, status, fare) in a relational database.
evolution: Version 1: driver locations in a database; for each request, compute the distance to every driver.
Version 2: a grid or geohash cells, searching only the nearby cells.
Version 3: an in-memory geo index, a matching service and atomic driver locking.
Version 4: a trip state machine, surge pricing, payments, and analytics on location history.
design: A location service takes driver updates and keeps only the latest position in an in-memory geospatial index (geohash cells, for example Redis GEO).
A matching service searches nearby cells, ranks drivers by arrival time, and offers the trip to one driver at a time with a timeout.
The offered driver is locked with an atomic status update, so they can't be double-booked.
A trip service tracks the trip's state; pricing (including surge) and payment services handle the money.
deepDives: Geohash: nearby places share a prefix; search the rider's cell and its neighbours.
Location updates are short-lived: keep only the latest in memory, and stream the history to cheap storage for analytics.
Surge pricing from supply and demand in each area.
Driver assignment uses an atomic compare-and-set.
mistakes: Scanning every driver for every request.
Saving every location update permanently in the main database.
Offering one ride to several drivers without locking.
topics.interviewAnswer: Drivers stream their location to a location service that keeps only the latest position in an in-memory geospatial index. A ride request searches nearby cells, ranks drivers by arrival time and offers the trip to one driver at a time, locking that driver atomically to prevent double-booking. Trips and payments live in a transactional database.

followUps.a: A short string that encodes latitude and longitude as nested grid cells. Nearby places share a prefix, so 'nearby' becomes a prefix lookup plus the neighbouring cells.

followUps.q: Why not save every location update in a database?
followUps.a: That's 250,000 writes a second of data that's out of date within seconds. Keep the latest in memory and stream the history to cheap storage.

practice.explain: Explain how 'find nearby drivers' works with geohashes.
practice.draw: Draw driver app → location service → geo index, and rider → matching → trip service.
practice.apply: Bucket 10,000 random points into a simple grid (or with a geohash library), then find the neighbours of one point.
practice.tradeoffs: Geohash or quadtree for a city where driver density is very uneven?

resources.title: Hello Interview: proximity service, and nearby friends

explain.answer:
A geohash turns a latitude and longitude into a short string by repeatedly halving the map: is the point in the west or east half? Then the north or south half of that? Each answer is one bit, and the bits are written in base 32. Each extra character makes the cell smaller: 5 characters is roughly a 5 km square, 6 characters roughly 1.2 km by 0.6 km.

The useful property: points close together usually share a long prefix, so "drivers near here" becomes "drivers whose geohash starts with the same 6 characters as the rider's".

Finding nearby drivers:
1. Every few seconds, each driver's location update moves them into the right cell in an in-memory index (Redis GEO, or cell → set of driver ids).
2. For a ride request, compute the rider's cell at a suitable precision.
3. Look in that cell and its 8 neighbours. Neighbours matter: a rider near the edge of a cell may be closest to a driver just across the line, whose geohash looks quite different.
4. Work out the real distance (better, the estimated arrival time by road) for those candidates, rank them, and offer the trip to the best one first.
5. If too few drivers are found, widen the search: a shorter prefix, or more rings of neighbours.

draw.answer: Two independent flows meet in the geo index: drivers write their position into it every few seconds; the matching service reads from it when a ride is requested. Only the latest position is kept in memory; the history is streamed off to cheap storage.
draw.code:
Driver app ── location every 4 s ──► Location service
                                       │ keep only the latest
                                       ▼
                                  Geo index (in memory)
                                  cell → drivers (Redis GEO)
                                       ▲      │ history
                                       │      └──► stream ──► analytics store
Rider app ── request a ride ──► Matching service
                                  1. rider's cell + 8 neighbours
                                  2. rank by arrival time
                                  3. offer to one driver, with a timeout
                                  4. lock the driver (atomic status update)
                                       │
                                       ▼
                                  Trip service ── trip state ──► Trips DB
                                       ├──► Pricing (surge)
                                       └──► Payments
Rider app ◄══ WebSocket: live trip updates ══ Trip service

apply.answer:
10,000 random drivers are spread over a box around London. Each goes into a grid cell of 0.01° × 0.01° (about 1.1 km by 0.7 km here): a simple stand-in for a geohash, using the same idea of a key per cell.

That makes 800 cells, about 12 drivers each. For a rider at Trafalgar Square, the search reads only the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours: 108 drivers instead of 10,000. Real distances (the haversine formula) are worked out only for those, and the nearest three are 0.15, 0.17 and 0.23 km away.
apply.code:
import math
import random

random.seed(42)
drivers = [(random.uniform(51.40, 51.60), random.uniform(-0.30, 0.10)) for _ in range(10_000)]

CELL = 0.01                                          # degrees: about 1.1 km × 0.7 km in London


def cell(lat, lon):
    return (math.floor(lat / CELL), math.floor(lon / CELL))


grid = {}
for i, (lat, lon) in enumerate(drivers):
    grid.setdefault(cell(lat, lon), []).append(i)


def km(a, b):                                        # great-circle distance
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(math.radians, (*a, *b))
    h = math.sin((lat2 - lat1) / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(lat1) * math.cos(lat2) * math.sin((lon2 - lon1) / 2) ** 2
    return 6371 * 2 * math.asin(math.sqrt(h))


rider = (51.5080, -0.1281)                           # Trafalgar Square
row, col = cell(*rider)
nearby = [i for dr in (-1, 0, 1) for dc in (-1, 0, 1) for i in grid.get((row + dr, col + dc), [])]
nearest = sorted(nearby, key=lambda i: km(rider, drivers[i]))[:3]

print(len(grid), len(drivers) / len(grid))           # 800 12.5: cells, drivers per cell
print(len(nearby))                                   # 108: candidates in the 9 cells
print([round(km(rider, drivers[i]), 2) for i in nearest])   # [0.15, 0.17, 0.23] km

tradeoffs.answer:
Geohash (fixed-size cells):
• Simple and stateless: a driver's cell is a pure function of their position, so a location update is just moving one key; easy to shard by prefix across machines.
• Copes with 250,000 updates a second, because nothing needs rebalancing.
• Uneven density hurts: a city-centre cell may hold thousands of drivers (the search returns far too many), while a suburban cell holds none (you must widen the search ring by ring). You can compensate by choosing the search precision by area, or with a hexagonal grid like Uber's H3.

Quadtree (cells split where it is busy):
• Adaptive: a cell splits into four when it holds more than, say, 100 drivers, so dense areas get small cells and quiet areas big ones, and every search returns a sensible number of candidates.
• But drivers move constantly, so the tree is always splitting and merging; it is harder to update concurrently, and harder to spread across machines.

For moving drivers with very uneven density, the common answer is geohash (or H3) with an adaptive search radius: you keep the cheap updates and handle density at query time. A quadtree shines for points that rarely move, such as restaurants or shops.

topics.name: Design a payment system
topics.definition: Process payments reliably: charge customers, record every money movement, and never lose money or charge twice.
topics.problem: It tests correctness under failure — retries, timeouts, idempotency, transactions and audit trails — where a small bug means real money.

diagram.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant P as Payment service
  participant DB as Database
  participant PSP as Payment provider
  C->>P: pay £50 (idempotency key k1)
  P->>DB: insert payment PENDING (key k1 must be unique)
  P->>PSP: charge £50 (key k1)
  PSP-->>P: succeeded
  P->>DB: one transaction - status SUCCEEDED, ledger debit and credit
  P-->>C: paid
  Note over P,PSP: every night, reconcile the ledger with the provider's reports
diagram.caption: The unique key stops double charges, the status and ledger change together in one transaction, and a nightly check catches any mismatch.

functional: Accept a payment for an order through a payment provider (PSP) that talks to the card networks.
Record every money movement in a ledger.
Refunds; reconciliation with the provider's reports.
nonFunctional: Correctness over speed: no double charges, no lost money.
Strong consistency and a full audit trail.
Secure (PCI DSS rules for card data) and highly available.
estimates: 1 million payments a day ≈ 12 per second on average: the volume is modest; correctness is the hard part.
api: POST /payments {order_id, amount, currency, idempotency_key} → payment status
Webhook from the provider: payment succeeded or failed
dataModel: payments (id, order_id, amount, currency, status, idempotency_key UNIQUE)
ledger_entries (id, account_id, payment_id, debit, credit, created_at), append-only and double-entry
evolution: Version 1: call the payment provider and mark the order 'paid'.
Version 2: a payments table with statuses and idempotency keys.
Version 3: a double-entry ledger, written in the same transaction as the status change.
Version 4: webhooks, an outbox, reconciliation, and handling results that are unknown.
design: The payment service receives the request with an idempotency key; a unique constraint in the database blocks duplicates.
It creates a PENDING payment record, then calls the payment provider. The provider handles the card details, so you never store raw card numbers.
The provider's result (response or webhook) updates the status, and balanced double-entry ledger rows are written in the same transaction.
The order service is told through an outbox event.
